Title: Critical Langflow flaws enable authentication bypass and RCE
Context: Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication
Full Text:
IBM patched critical vulnerabilities in Langflow, an open-source framework for building AI agents, LLM-powered workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The flaws could allow attackers to bypass authentication, leak API credentials, and execute arbitrary code.

Langflow, now owned by IBM, is popular in enterprise environments because it offers a visual experience that doesn’t require coding knowledge to create AI workflows and agents. Vulnerabilities in the framework have been exploited in the wild to steal AI and developer credentials before, most recently in August.

This latest round of security patches fix four vulnerabilities, two of which are rated critical with 9.8 CVSS score. One flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-93680, stems from an incomplete remediation of a previous auto-login security issue. Exploiting it could allow attackers to bypass security restrictions and gain access to features that would normally require authentication.

Another flaw, CVE-2026-110186, allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code through Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool enumeration. A third vulnerability, CVE-2026-110193, which is rated as high severity, also allows for code and command execution on the server due to an issue in a third-party library used by the Agentic Assistant. However, exploiting this flaw requires authentication with at least a low-privileged account.

The fourth vulnerability, CVE-2026-110192, is an information disclosure issue due to insufficiently protected API credentials. It is rated as 6.5 on the CVSS scale.

The flaws affect Langflow OSS versions 1.0.0 to 1.12.8 and were fixed in the newly released 1.13.0 version, which is available both from the PyPI repository and as a Docker image.

“Before upgrading, back up the database, secret key, and uploaded files,” IBM said in its advisory. “If the deployment uses automatic login, prepare the existing account for password sign-in as described in the installation and Docker upgrade instruction.”

The company also released patches for three medium-severity flaws in Hono, an API and web application development framework used inside Langflow for request routing and backend web server tasks. The company advises users to upgrade Hono to version 4.13.5.

Title: Barracuda Flaws Could Be Chained to Bypass Authorization and Gain Root Access
Context: "If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device
Full Text:
Barracuda has disclosed details of two vulnerabilities affecting its products that, if chained together, could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to a susceptible device.

The vulnerabilities, a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability and a command injection vulnerability, have been assigned the CVE identifiers CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS score: 9.3) and CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS score: 8.6), respectively.

While CVE-2026-116606 only affects Email Security Gateway, CVE-2026-111560 impacts the following Barracuda products -

Email Security Gateway

Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller

Message Archiver

WAF Control Center

Web Application Firewall

Web Security Gateway

"Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product," Barracuda said. "If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device."

Barracuda said that organizations that do not expose their administrative interfaces to the internet are less vulnerable to the attack path, urging customers to follow the steps below -

Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks

Use appropriate network access controls to limit exposure

"Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches," it added. "If firmware on a device is multiple versions out of date, customers may need to perform more than one update."

Title: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency
Context: 1 or earlier of the open-source payment platform, and that attackers had used a different method to exploit a vulnerability fixed in version 2
Full Text:
Hackers have stolen cryptocurrency from hot wallets on outdated BTCPay Server instances, with blockchain analysis tracing about $1.63m in Bitcoin and Litecoin to addresses linked to the thefts.

BTCPay Server said in an incident update on November 2 that the thefts hit servers running version 2.4.1 or earlier of the open-source payment platform, and that attackers had used a different method to exploit a vulnerability fixed in version 2.4.2, released on August 7.

It had seen no impact on servers already running 2.4.2 or later when it issued its warning.

An analysis by blockchain intelligence company Bitquery traced 18.38 Bitcoin and 3405 Litecoin to two addresses named by BTCPay Server, moved in 682 sweeps between October 30 and the morning of November 2. It said the thief signed in to the servers as an administrator and swept their hot wallets.

The flaw had already been exploited in August to steal funds through LND, a Lightning Network implementation, though BTCPay Server said at the time that on-chain wallets, including hot wallets, were not affected.

Read more on hot wallet breaches: Bitget Restarts Bitcoin Withdrawals Following $387.5m Wallet Breach

Sweeps Continued After BTCPay's Warning

Bitquery said 87% of the traced funds moved in a single wave on the afternoon and evening of November 1. It counted 267 further sweeps, worth about $150,000, after BTCPay Server told operators at 22:25 UTC that night to shut down their instances.

The firm could not tell how many servers were hit, since the blockchain records wallets rather than systems. It also left out other addresses and coins, including Lightning funds, making its figure a floor.

BTCPay Server added that some activity at the two addresses appears to predate the reported thefts, so their balances should not be treated as confirmed losses. The project has not published a loss total.

BTCPay Server Urges Hot Wallet Users to Rebuild

BTCPay Server urged operators of version 2.4.1 or earlier to move to a fresh server with a new wallet and seed, even if they had since updated, warning that "updating alone cannot remove access an attacker may already have gained."

It said wallets whose spending keys are held off the server, including hardware wallets, were unaffected, and advised keeping only operational funds on the server.

Operators should also preserve logs and transaction records, replace exposed credentials and avoid restoring the old server onto a new one, the project said.

The fix had been available since August 7. The wallets that were emptied sat on servers that had never installed it.

Title: Introducing Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities
Context: Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level...
Full Text:
You run security at your organization. It’s 7:00 am, and you’re having breakfast. You receive a ping: a new critical vulnerability has been disclosed. Your team scrambles to compare vendor advisories, read technical research, check which systems run the affected software, and answer familiar questions from the business: are we affected, and what are we doing about it? Another disclosure arrives before that work is finished.

AI is changing both the volume and speed of critical vulnerability discovery. It can analyze large codebases at scale and surface deeply nested flaws that may have existed for years without being found through human review. That discovery momentum will put more pressure on security teams to understand the impact of each disclosure on their infrastructure.

To help security teams prepare, today we’re introducing Zero Wire: a public vulnerability intelligence feed on Cloudflare Radar, bringing the clarity of a news wire service to critical security developments. It helps security leaders and practitioners understand significant vulnerabilities and decide what to do next.

How it works

Zero Wire lives inside Cloudflare Radar under the security section.

Each briefing brings together a plain-language explanation of the vulnerability, who should investigate it, recommended actions, and links to the evidence and vendor guidance. The format is deliberately simple: an index card with what you need to know, without the drama. A CISO should be able to understand the issue quickly and ask the right questions. An engineer should be able to follow the same briefing to the technical guidance needed to investigate and remediate it.

We also offer a pre-compiled prompt you can use with your agent to assess the impact on your infrastructure. Cloudflare contributes security research, observations from our network, and practical knowledge of the controls that can help reduce exposure. The information is useful whether or not you are a Cloudflare customer.

Zero Wire brings that context together with authoritative external sources, giving readers a starting point for assessment and a place to return as an issue develops.

Our focus

Rather than a catalog of every CVE, Zero Wire complements vendor advisories and vulnerability databases, linking readers to the evidence and technical guidance needed to act. Zero Wire focuses on critical CVEs in Internet-facing software, such as vulnerabilities in web applications, the runtimes and libraries they depend on, and services exposed to the Internet, where a proxy can help mitigate exploitation.

We select significant issues that security teams need to understand and assess. Each briefing explains the potential impact, which deployments should be investigated, what is known about exploitation, and the available mitigation and patching guidance. A vulnerability’s severity and evidence of active exploitation are distinct: readers need both to make informed decisions.

A dedicated Cloudflare protection, such as Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules, is not a prerequisite for inclusion. Some issues require vendor updates or changes beyond the traffic Cloudflare can inspect. Where Cloudflare controls can help, we explain their scope and configuration requirements.

A walk through Zero Wire

Start on the Zero Wire homepage. Each card introduces an issue, identifies associated CVEs where applicable, and summarizes why it matters and what to do. You can search for a published briefing using a CVE or issue name, and follow technology tags to related entries. One briefing can cover several related CVEs when understanding them together makes the response clearer.

Find what needs attention

The homepage separates briefings into two categories. “Needs attention” brings together issues requiring active assessment or action, including those with known exploitation or developing guidance. “Reference” keeps briefings available when guidance has stabilized. Moving to “Reference” does not mean every affected system has been patched: an older vulnerability can still matter to an organization that has not completed remediation.

The status and last-checked date help you interpret each card. Known exploitation, an ongoing investigation, and an available vendor fix describe different things. Read them alongside the briefing’s evidence rather than treating them as a verdict on your own environment.

Understand what happened and who should investigate

When you open a briefing, the overview tells you what happened, why it deserves attention, and which teams should investigate. The explanation connects the technical issue to its practical consequences, such as service disruption or risk of data exposure.

For example, the recent php2shell vulnerability concerns flaws in the PHP runtime. That distinction matters for teams running applications such as WordPress or Magento: updating application code or a plugin alone does not repair the underlying runtime. The briefing helps readers identify the right system owners and directs them to the PHP security guidance for affected versions and remediation.

Turn the briefing into an action plan

What to do now gives your team a short set of next steps. Depending on the issue, that can mean identifying affected deployments, checking versions with a hosting provider, applying vendor updates, reviewing suspicious activity, or keeping compensating controls in place while patching.

The purpose is to make the next conversation concrete. For a PHP deployment, ask which runtime is actually running, whether the vendor’s fix has been applied, and who owns the update. Follow the linked vendor advisory for detailed applicability and remediation instructions, which can change as the investigation develops.

Assess your exposure with an AI agent

In this section, we share a prompt that can be used with your AI agent to quickly assess the impact on your infrastructure. The prompt asks for a read-only assessment of deployed software, relevant vendor fixes, exposure, and compensating controls, with per-asset evidence, unknowns, and next actions. It helps your team investigate its own environment; copying the prompt does not itself scan or change systems.

Check the evidence and follow what changed

To help you learn more about the vulnerability, each briefing links to external documents such as CVE records, research, and relevant exploitation evidence, including CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog. These sources answer different questions. A vendor advisory establishes affected versions and remediation guidance. An exploitation report provides evidence of attacker activity.

If applicable to a briefing, Cloudflare can add context about traffic seen on our network, for example by showing traffic matching WAF rules that indicates exploitation attempts. Those distinctions matter. Observing an attack attempt does not establish that a particular organization was compromised. Equally, a lack of observed attempts on Cloudflare’s network does not establish that exploitation is absent elsewhere. Briefings distinguish what the sources establish from what remains unknown.

Where available, charts add context to that evidence. The php2shell briefing shows the volume of HTTP requests matching Cloudflare WAF managed rules over time. Note that requests matching these rules are not a count of compromised systems or successful exploits; the chart aims at providing practitioners a sense of what the focus level is by threat actors on a particular vulnerability.

Finally, update chronology records important developments, such as new advisories or changes to the evidence and response guidance. Together with the last-checked date, it helps returning readers understand what has changed since their previous visit.

Understand Cloudflare’s role

The Cloudflare section provides links to whether we offer compensating controls or provide a way to mitigate the vulnerability impact on your infrastructure.

If a particular CVE can be addressed with a WAF rule, the briefing reports its availability and essential configuration requirements. When applicable, paid Plans and free Plans links take customers to the relevant dashboard configuration. The next step is explicit: “Review your WAF configuration to determine whether you are protected”. A link allows you to review your security posture, it does not automatically enable a rule or verify a deployment.

Note that a WAF mitigation is a compensating control for the traffic it covers, it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Blocking the requests can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. The security teams should always follow the vendor remediation guidance.

Stay informed with Zero Wire

A useful vulnerability briefing should leave you with a clearer understanding of the issue and a concrete next step. Day Zero brings those essentials together: what happened, who should investigate, what to do now, and where to find the evidence.

Visit Zero Wire vulnerability intelligence, share the relevant briefings with the teams responsible for your systems, and return for new entries and updates. When the next disclosure arrives, we want you to spend less time assembling the basic facts and more time acting on them.

Follow Cloudflare Radar on X @CloudflareRadar and Bluesky @radar.cloudflare.com for updates.

Title: Attackers exploit critical Node-RED flaw to deploy Linux bot and backdoors (CVE-2026-58115)
Context: Attackers are exploiting an authentication flaw (CVE-2026-58115) in Node-RED, a programming tool built into some industrial control products, to install a Linux bot and...
Full Text:
Attackers are exploiting an authentication flaw (CVE-2026-58115) in Node-RED, a programming tool built into some industrial control products, to install a Linux bot and backdoors on unprotected servers, VulnCheck has found.

Node-RED is a flow-based programming tool built on Node.js that lets users wire together event-driven applications in a browser-based editor. It can run on small devices such as the Raspberry Pi or in the cloud, and it is used in manufacturing, healthcare, and home and industrial automation.

The tool is also part of critical infrastructure, embedded in commercial ICS/OT products such as Siemens’ SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced, which is affected by the flaw. Siemens disclosed it in August and gave it a CVSS score of 10.0, warning that devices running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed, in versions before V4.3.4.1, are vulnerable.

The bug “could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to create malicious flows and execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with maximum privileges,” Siemens said at the time of disclosure.

Caught by a decoy

More than two months after Siemens’ disclosure, the flaw is being exploited in the wild.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” wrote VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity.

“The attacker’s request was a complete exploit. It deployed a Node-RED flow, triggered it automatically, and pulled a binary from an attacker-controlled server, all behind three layers of encoding,” added Garrity.

“Two built-in node types make this trivial to weaponize. An inject node fires a message on a schedule or once at startup, and an exec node runs a shell command. Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” he explained.

The flow downloaded a file named bot-linux-amd64 from a separate server, saved it under a hidden name in a memory-backed location and ran it in the background. VulnCheck did not retrieve the binary, so the company can’t say whether it is a cryptominer, a DDoS bot, a reverse shell or something else.

One address, eight CVEs

The request came from an IP address in Microsoft’s network that geolocates to Brazil. “It didn’t just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity stated.

The same address went after the Node-RED flaw 16 times between October 30 and November 1, and in VulnCheck’s wider canary data it logged 125 hits against 8 different CVEs, old and new, in Apache Solr, Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik and Joomla.

Garrity describes this as opportunistic mass scanning, and notes that an address in a large cloud provider’s range is usually a rented or compromised virtual machine and says little about who is behind the attacks.

Later requests brought new payloads. One fetched a shell script from the same download server, and another pulled a file from a second server and saved it under a name made to look like a kernel worker thread. Several requests installed webshells that let the attackers come back and run commands at will. The bot is stored in memory and is lost on reboot unless it sets up persistence some other way, while the webshells stay in place after a restart.

The exploitation activity (Source: VulnCheck)

Check your instances

VulnCheck added the flaw to its KEV catalog after spotting the in-the-wild attempt and noted that CISA had not listed it in its own KEV catalog at the time of writing.

“Node-RED instances without adminAuth are being found and exploited automatically,” Garrity warned.

“If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post.

The VulnCheck post lists indicators of compromise, including the IP addresses of the attack source and both payload servers.

Title: Network appliances go more than a year without patches as exploits speed up
Context: The researchers also cited VulnCheck’s State of Exploitation 2026 report, which found that 29% of exploits in 2025 were launched within a day of CVE publication
Full Text:
The median vulnerability on enterprise network appliances stays unpatched for more than a year, Microsoft’s own telemetry shows, even as the most damaging software flaws are being weaponized within days of disclosure.

Microsoft Security Research reported the findings Monday in an analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026. It shows that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. The period is more than a month for Windows servers, over 10 weeks for Linux servers and applications running on macOS, and about two weeks for Windows workstations.

“That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest,” Microsoft Security researchers Yair Tsarfaty and Or Begam wrote in a blog post detailing the findings. They were referring to the distance between how fast flaws are exploited and how slowly critical systems are patched.

Patching measured in weeks and months

Microsoft drew its patching figures from 2026 data in its Security Exposure Management product. The median vulnerability is fixed in about two weeks on Windows workstations but takes more than a month on Windows Server, according to the post. The delay stretches beyond 10 weeks on Linux servers and for applications running on macOS, and past a year on network appliances.

Vibhum Dubey, a cybersecurity researcher and red teamer, said the findings reflect what he sees across enterprise environments. In those environments, change approvals, application dependencies, maintenance windows, and legacy infrastructure routinely hold up fixes.

“Network appliances are particularly difficult because firmware upgrades can affect critical business operations,” Dubey said. “In many cases, the challenge is not identifying vulnerabilities, but getting the right teams to remediate them without disrupting business services.”

Exploitation measured in days

Exploitation runs on a far shorter clock, Microsoft wrote in the post. Citing CISA figures, the researchers said the mean time from CVE publication to listing in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. For 2026 through September, the mean has dropped to 20 days and the median to three.

“Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure,” the post said.

The researchers also cited VulnCheck’s State of Exploitation 2026 report, which found that 29% of exploits in 2025 were launched within a day of CVE publication. Industry research points to advances in AI as a significant factor in cutting the time needed to develop exploits, Microsoft wrote in the blog post.

In some cases, defenders have hours rather than weeks, Dubey said. Vulnerabilities can be exploited before public disclosure or before organizations have completed their initial assessment.

He said enterprises need to move away from relying entirely on monthly scans and scheduled patch cycles. In their place, he said, they need continuous monitoring, emergency patching procedures, virtual patching through WAF and IPS controls, and clear remediation ownership.

“The priority should be to reduce the window of exposure, because by the time a vulnerability reaches the regular patching queue, attackers may already be exploiting it,” Dubey said.

Where the exploits land

The vulnerabilities attackers actually use look very different from the CVE population as a whole, the analysis found. Server-side remote code execution (RCE) flaws make up 20% of all published CVEs but 37% of those exploited in the wild. Local privilege escalation climbs from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%.

Cross-site scripting drops from 15% of published CVEs to 4% of exploited ones, and denial-of-service flaws drop from 16% to 7%, according to the researchers. Operating system vulnerabilities make up 23% of the overall population but account for 41% of exploited CVEs.

“These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control,” the researchers wrote.

Together, RCE, authentication bypass, and local privilege escalation account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, the post said. Windows ranks as the most affected platform among exploited CVEs in Microsoft’s data.

Prioritizing by exposure

A vulnerability’s value to an attacker depends on its impact and its exposure, according to Microsoft. Impact is what successful exploitation delivers. Exposure is the identities, privileges, and network connections reachable from the compromised asset.

Servers frequently run service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with more permissions than they need, the post noted. Taking over one of them can open paths to sensitive data, administrative rights, and trusted networks.

“CVSS scores alone are no longer sufficient,” Dubey said. Organizations should prioritize vulnerabilities based on active exploitation, internet exposure, asset criticality, and potential attack paths, he said. “A medium-severity vulnerability on an internet-facing system with a known exploit can present a greater risk than a critical vulnerability on an isolated asset,” he said.

Title: Android’s November 2026 Updates Patch Over 200 Vulnerabilities
Context: “The most severe of these issues is a critical security vulnerability in the Framework component that could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges...
Full Text:
Google on Monday announced new security updates for Android that resolve more than 200 vulnerabilities, including two dozen critical-severity issues.

The first part of the patches arrives on devices as the 2026-11-01 security patch level and resolves 119 security defects across Android runtime, Framework, and System.

Framework received fixes for the largest number of flaws, namely 65, followed by System with 53. Google resolved one high-severity information disclosure bug in Android runtime.

According to Google’s security bulletin, the most severe of the patched weaknesses resides in the Framework component and is tracked as CVE-2026-58868.

“The most severe of these issues is a critical security vulnerability in the Framework component that could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation,” the company says.

Critical-severity remote code execution (RCE), elevation of privilege (EoP), and denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerabilities were addressed in the System component as well.

Google rolled out patches for 17 of these flaws ahead of the monthly rollout, as part of Google Play system updates.

The second part of Android’s November 2026 security updates arrives on devices as the 2026-11-05 security patch level and fixes 97 bugs in Kernel, Arm, Imagination Technologies, MediaTek, Unisoc, and Qualcomm components.

While most of the fixes target high-severity issues, more than a dozen of them resolve critical-severity weaknesses in subcomponents such as Bluetooth, pKVM, HID, MediaTek modem, and a Qualcomm closed-source component.

“Security patch levels of 2026-11-05 or later address all of these issues,” Google notes.

On Monday, Google also published security bulletins for Android XR and Wear OS. In addition to the bugs described in the November 2026 Android bulletin, the Android XR update resolves a high-severity flaw in Framework, while the Wear OS patch addresses two high-severity issues in Framework and System.

Title: Google adds new $250,000 Cloud VRP reward for Root-in-Cloud bugs
Context: 6 million since launching its first Vulnerability Reward Program in 2010
Full Text:
Google has expanded its Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) with a new top-tier reward for high-impact architectural security flaws.

Starting this month, researchers can earn $250,000 for Root-in-Cloud bugs, including tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws that let attackers gain full administrative control over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations.

"To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of 'roles/owner' or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup," said Chris Betz, Google Cloud's Chief Information Security Officer (CISO).

"Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility."

However, to qualify for this reward, the exploits cannot depend on prior access to the victim project, compromised credentials, social engineering, or user interaction.

Additionally, security researchers who achieve execution on Google's production infrastructure must stop probing since escalating, obtaining production credentials, or lateral movement are not allowed and will result in disqualification.

"High incentives require clear, safe rules of engagement. We never want researchers testing exploits against real customer projects," added Cloud VRP Lead Michael Cote.

"Instead, we created a deterministic proof-of-root mechanism using a designated service account. Researchers can cryptographically prove unauthorized access against that identity."

More details on the Google Cloud VRP, including endpoint specifications, JSON payloads, and CLI examples, are available on the rules page.

This follows Google's suspension of submissions to its Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program (OSS VRP) in October after a flood of AI-generated reports.

Google has rewarded thousands of security researchers worldwide with more than $81.6 million since launching its first Vulnerability Reward Program in 2010.

In 2025, Google awarded a record-breaking $17.1 million to over 700 security researchers, a 40% increase from 2024, when it awarded $12 million in total.

Title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
Context: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation
Full Text:
CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-119977 WordPress Core Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Red Hat Patches 9.8-Rated Linux TCP RCE Flaw While Ubuntu Releases Fixes for Testing
Context: Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its...
Full Text:
Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its three newest long-term-support releases remain in its opt-in testing channel with no date for a regular update.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, can be reached by a remote, unauthenticated attacker and can lead to remote code execution, Red Hat and Canonical said.

The Linux kernel's own CVE team rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Red Hat, which initially rated it Moderate at 5.9, has raised its score to 9.8 and now calls it Critical. The bug has been present since Linux 4.4, and the upstream fix landed in October.

What the Flaw Is

When a server accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, the kernel passes IP options from the incoming request to the new socket without copying them. If the client retransmits its connection request while another processor still reads those options, the kernel can read memory it has already freed.

An attacker triggers the race by sending connection requests that carry IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options to any listening TCP port. No login is needed. IPv6 is not affected on the main path.

Red Hat shipped RHSA-2026:93414 (RHEL 8), RHSA-2026:93412 (RHEL 9), and RHSA-2026:93413 (RHEL 10) on November 1. A reboot is needed after installing the update.

Canonical tests kernel updates across more than 2,000 certified servers and devices before releasing them to the regular update channel, and no release date has been given.

sudo add-apt-repository --component main --pocket proposed https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install -t $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)-proposed --only-upgrade sudo reboot

To check whether a system is running a fixed kernel, compare the output of uname -r against the versions in the tables above.

Ubuntu 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 have no fix yet. Older releases require Expanded Security Maintenance through Ubuntu Pro.

Cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernel variants for Ubuntu are listed as work in progress on the Ubuntu CVE page with target versions, but Canonical's blog post covers only the generic kernel.

Interim Mitigation

Red Hat published an nftables rule on October 30 that drops inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. The rule blocks the known trigger for the race but cannot fully prevent exploitation and may break workloads that depend on IPv4 options, Red Hat said.

table inet cve_2026_98432 { chain input { type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept; ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop } }

The filter applies only to the host where it is loaded. Traffic between containers on the same host can bypass it, a member of the CIQ kernel team noted on the oss-security mailing list.

Several sources have recommended disabling Multipath TCP (MPTCP) as a workaround. The flaw is in the IPv4 TCP path, not in MPTCP, and that advice alone is not enough, Canonical said. "The Ubuntu Security Team believes that security updates are the only appropriate mitigation."

Exploitation Status

No vendor, CERT, or the kernel CVE team has reported attacks using this flaw. It was not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of the catalog's October 30 release.

Anthropic said on October 27 that an unreleased, internal Claude research model wrote a remote root exploit for the flaw that works against Linux servers with an MPTCP listener, with no credentials and no user interaction. In its proof of concept, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes and reaching a root shell took another 5 minutes. Anthropic has not published the exploit code.

Proof-only code that triggers the race and detects the kernel echoing freed memory in a SYN-ACK has appeared on GitHub. It does not implement code execution.

Amazon Linux scored the flaw 8.1 and rated it Important, saying the main outcome is a crash with possible memory corruption. Debian, Oracle Linux, and SUSE shipped fixes in October. Amazon Linux was fixed across all packages between October 24 and 30.

Title: OpenAI raises top bug bounty payout to $172,000 with bonuses
Context: Short-term campaigns will have dedicated bonus pools for researchers who test newly launched features
Full Text:
OpenAI increased its security bug bounties to encourage independent researchers to find vulnerabilities in its software. The program now offers bonuses for high-quality reports.

The program encourages researchers to disclose vulnerabilities responsibly and complements OpenAI’s Defense Factory, where engineers use the company’s models to find and reproduce vulnerabilities and test fixes.

New bounty payouts and bonuses

The midpoints of the reward ranges for medium, high, and critical findings more than quadrupled on average. High-quality reports are eligible for a multiplier on the base bounty. OpenAI says a reliable proof of concept helps engineers develop a fix by isolating the bug, showing when it can be exploited, and demonstrating its impact.

OpenAI introduced a five-tier loyalty program that offers larger bonuses at higher tiers. Short-term campaigns will have dedicated bonus pools for researchers who test newly launched features.

Updated payout calculation examples (Source: OpenAI)

“If you’ve already submitted a report and we haven’t yet awarded a bounty, we’ll apply the new reward ranges,” OpenAI said.

For bounties awarded in the 30 days before the announcement, the company will pay the difference if the finding would have earned more under the new ranges. The calculation includes base and loyalty awards.

Title: Attackers Target Unpatched CryptoPayment Gateway Flaw That Can Expose Wallet Credentials
Context: Threat actors are attempting to exploit an unpatched maximum-severity security vulnerability in the CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin, according to findings from Defused Cyber
Full Text:
Threat actors are attempting to exploit an unpatched maximum-severity security vulnerability in the CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin, according to findings from Defused Cyber.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-81648, which carries a CVSS score of 10.0. Successful exploitation of the flaw could permit unauthenticated users to delete arbitrary files on the server and extract sensitive data, including stored wallet credentials.

"The CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin from 1.2.1 to 1.2.2 does not apply an authorization check on one of its AJAX endpoints, allowing unauthenticated users to invoke administrative operations, including deleting arbitrary files on the server, overwriting the payment gateway configuration and recovering stored wallet credentials in cleartext," according to a description of the flaw on the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The vulnerability affects versions 1.2.1 through 1.2.2, which is the latest version. There are no known fixes for the flaw, according to WP Scan. As of August 28, 2026, the plugin has been closed on the WordPress Plugin Directory and is no longer available for download due to an unspecified "security issue."

Statistics show that the plugin has been collectively downloaded 1,845 times, including 20 downloads over the last seven days. It's unclear if it's actively installed on any WordPress sites.

"We are observing in-the-wild exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-81648, a critical (CVSS 10.0) flaw in the CryptoPayment Gateway for WordPress," Defused Cyber said in an X post. "The attacks we recorded came from infrastructure that markets themselves as 'Anonymous KYC-Free VPS Hosting.'"

In the absence of a fix, site owners are advised to remove the plugin, rotate wallet keys, and audit for any suspicious changes.

Title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
Context: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow...
Full Text: Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot. Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating. Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday. “On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.” One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said. Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer. The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote. While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted. Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher. One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote. The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote. “If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post. While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

Title: What exploited vulnerabilities have in common: A data-driven analysis of real-world attacks
Context: Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead,...
Full Text:
In this article

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

References

Learn More

The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation.

Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond.

Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack.

Classifying the vulnerability landscape

To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform.

Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve.

Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction.

Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content.

Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold.

Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges.

Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls.

Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen.

Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets.

Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state.

Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability.

Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context.

Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files.

Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception.

We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population.

Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware.

This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis.

Figure 1 – The full published-CVE population as of September 2026, broken down by impact class and affected platform, and an OS vs. application split. Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code.

Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild

The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure.

The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities.

These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise.

Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization.

Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall.

Where defenders should focus

Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast

Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest.

Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck, 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly.

Impact, exposure and where to focus

Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it.

Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise.

Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment.

Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment.

Next in line

A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above.

Figure 3 – The three remote-takeover classes analyzed across 1,239 exploited CVEs), each drilled down by affected platform and split into OS vs Application code. Bar length is the CVE count per platform; the dark segment is OS/system, the light segment is application.

How Microsoft Security helps defenders act

Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point.

Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations.

Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure.

An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud.

Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands.

Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets.

Title: Armadin Tests Find 88% of Severe Flaws Outside Vendor Advisories
Context: Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or...
Full Text:
Some 88% of the critical and high-severity weaknesses found in live attack tests on enterprise environments this year would not have been identified through vendor advisories or other outside sources, new data has suggested.

The figure comes from a report published on November 2 by Armadin, the offensive security startup launched by Mandiant founder Kevin Mandia, based on AI-driven attacks against its clients' live systems.

The clients span nearly a dozen industries, but Armadin did not disclose how many organizations or findings the data covers.

Read more on exposure management: AI Threats and Alert Fatigue Challenge Cybersecurity Teams

Most Severe Findings Sat Beyond Advisories and Logins

Defects in software the clients had written themselves made up 67% of the critical findings and 78% of the high findings that advisories could not cover. Vendor products deployed in ways no advisory describes, such as administrative consoles exposed to the internet, accounted for 24% and 22%.

The remaining 9% of critical findings, and under 1% of high ones, were zero-days Armadin found itself, including one in an identity governance platform whose vendor took almost four months to issue an advisory.

Nearly 70% of critical and high findings sat on the unauthenticated attack surface. Of the documented attack chains, 82% began without credentials, and 56% of those went on without a password or key ever being presented.

In more than 70% of client environments, Armadin said it reached a critical outcome in three steps or fewer without valid credentials.

Exposed Service Accounts Created Further Attack Paths

Just under half of the chains that started without authentication relied on an exposed credential, 71% of which belonged to applications or service accounts rather than people. Nearly 90% were reachable without extraction, often in repositories, configuration files, backups, logs or cloud settings.

In one engagement, Armadin started from an unprivileged domain account and used a flaw in backup software to read the credentials it held. That led to a hypervisor management server and, via a domain controller backup, to domain administrator hashes.

Fixing the severe findings meant shipping application code in 51% of cases, changing a setting, permission or policy in 43% and rotating an exposed credential in 32%, with many needing more than one step.

Armadin's recommendations included policies for provisioning, storing and rotating service account credentials, and checks of pipelines and code repositories for exposed secrets.

By its count, 93% of severe findings needed no third party to act, leaving the fix in each organization's own hands.

Context: Clive Robinson • November 2, 2026 11:45 AM @ Jeff, ALL, With regards, “More bugs aren’t necessarily being found because there’s more of them being created than before, the more...
Full Text:
Clive Robinson • November 2, 2026 11:45 AM

@ Jeff, ALL,

With regards,

“More bugs aren’t necessarily being found because there’s more of them being created than before, the more likely explanation is that the bugs were already there and now we’re closing them at the fastest pace in history! “

Actually both points are true…

Yes we are finding “new instances of bugs from known classes of bugs” at a much higher rate.

But that does not mean we are finding “new classes of bugs” (ie black swans).

But also “vibe coding” by AI is certainly generating “new instances of bugs” at a more alarming rate.

It’s why quite a few employers are now seeing “laying off humans with AI” as being not just horrifically unprofitable, but extremely dangerous to the business.

Yes, AI has niche advantages, but those niches are invariably not general in nature.

Even China is begining to see the dangers of even low cost AI.

None of this was unpredictable and quite a few have called it that way. However when you’ve handed over everything for a few tulip bulbs you had better be sure not only are they going to grow but that people are going to by the result sufficient to pay a “Return on Investment”(ROI).

Right now the ROI in “General AI” is not a certainty or even a likely hood based on the current economy…

Then there is “clearing up the mess of harms” the rush for AI has created… How many billions if not trillions that is going to cost companies that are already by normal forecasting methods “bankrupt”…

Title: Additional Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527)
Context: Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3
Full Text:
Overview

On October 29, 2026, Ivanti updated its security advisory for Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) to include two additional vulnerabilities and released fixes for both. Ivanti rates CVE-2026-111357, a missing authentication for critical function vulnerability (CWE-306), with a CVSSv3.1 score of 8.8; it allows a local authenticated attacker to escalate privileges. CVE-2026-118527, classified as generation of predictable numbers or identifiers (CWE-340), has an Ivanti-assigned CVSSv3.0 score of 4.3 and, according to CISA's KEV entry, allows a remote authenticated attacker to upload attacker-controlled content to a known location on disk.

Per Ivanti, exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers when these flaws are chained with CVE-2026-104935, an authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290). Rapid7 covered the original disclosure on October 13, 2026, when a fix for CVE-2026-104935 was available but the privilege escalation component remained unpatched. Fixes are now available for all three vulnerabilities.

On October 30, 2026, CVE-2026-111357 and CVE-2026-118527 were added to the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) list of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEV), based on evidence of active exploitation.

The following scores and classifications are from Ivanti's updated advisory:

Note: The CVE record and Rapid7's vulnerability database rate CVE-2026-111357 at 7.0, using high attack complexity and unchanged scope. Ivanti assesses low attack complexity and changed scope, resulting in its score of 8.8. The table follows Ivanti's scores and classifications.

In its investigation, Volexity reports that UTA0576 used an exploit chain to gain unauthenticated root access to an appliance running 22.8R2.4, beginning on October 3, 2026. Its write-up identifies CVE-2026-104935 and CVE-2026-111357; Ivanti's updated advisory identifies CVE-2026-118527 as an additional component of the chain. Volexity observed credential theft and Active Directory queries for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys.

The combined impact warrants emergency remediation despite the individual CVSS ratings. Ivanti Connect Secure is an enterprise VPN solution deployed at the network edge and has a history of zero-day exploitation, including in 2024 and 2025.

Mitigation guidance

Rapid7 recommends applying the available updates on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. The October 13 fixes in 25.1.1.2 and 22.8R2.5 do not remediate CVE-2026-111357 or CVE-2026-118527.

Rapid7 also recommends investigating for compromise after patching. Volexity reports that the observed activity evades Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, so a clean result does not rule out compromise. Preserve memory and logs before rebooting or resetting where feasible. If compromise is suspected, follow Ivanti's recovery steps and rotate potentially exposed credentials.

For current fixed versions and mitigation guidance, refer to Ivanti's security advisory. Its linked recovery procedure includes older release references.

/home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog and /var/log/audit/audit.log: investigate evidence of selective deletion.

Title: CVSS 10.0 LXD, MicroCloud Flaw Lets Attackers Impersonate Trusted Clients Without a Private Key
Context: A critical flaw in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud let an attacker log in as a trusted client without holding that client's private key
Full Text:
A critical flaw in Canonical's LXD and MicroCloud let an attacker log in as a trusted client without holding that client's private key. To do it, the attacker had to reach their HTTPS API over the network and have the trusted client's public certificate.

Once in, the attacker would act as that client, with access to the cluster and its virtual machines. If the impersonated account is privileged, the attacker could gain "root access to the host machine," Canonical said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-112816, carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and Canonical has released fixed versions of both products.

How the Flaw Works

LXD and MicroCloud let remote clients access their APIs over mutual TLS, a setup in which the client presents a certificate to prove who it is. A client is trusted when its certificate is in the server's trust store, the list of identities the server will accept.

The flaw was in how the server checked that certificate. It compared every certificate the client sent against the trust store, but a TLS connection only proves the client owns the private key for the first certificate in the chain, the leaf. The rest of the chain is whatever the client chose to attach.

So an attacker could take a trusted client's public certificate, which is not secret, attach it to the chain behind their own, and the server would accept them as that client.

Who Is Affected

Using the flaw takes two things: network access to the HTTPS API, and the public certificate of a client the server already trusts.

A standalone LXD server does not expose that API by default. It listens only on a local socket unless an administrator turns on the network API with the core.https_address setting.

MicroCloud, which ties several machines running LXD into one cluster, has a specific weak point. Canonical said an attacker who can capture a member's public certificate as it joins the cluster can then log in as that member.

The CVE record lists LXD 4.0.14, 5.0.10, 5.21.8 and 6.9 as affected, each before the fixed release that follows. Canonical lists these fixed snap versions:

The bug did not start at Canonical. The Incus project, which began as a community fork of LXD, reported it, and Canonical confirmed it affected LXD as well. Incus fixed the same flaw in version 7.6.0.

Ubuntu's own archive packages of LXD are listed as not affected or not shipped, so the fixed releases are the snaps.

There is no public sign the flaw has been used in an attack. The CVE record carries a U.S. CISA assessment, dated October 30, that the flaw is not known to have been exploited; it is not on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and no working exploit has been published.

What to Do

Update LXD and MicroCloud to the fixed versions. On a snap install, run sudo snap refresh lxd and sudo snap refresh microcloud.

Canonical said the fixed LXD point releases were still rolling out from the candidate channel to stable at the time of its advisory, so check the version you actually have after the refresh rather than assume the fix arrived.

Canonical's advisory gives no temporary workaround for LXD. Because the attack requires network access to the API, limiting who can reach it reduces risk until you update. The Incus project, reporting the same flaw, said there is no configuration fix and that the only step is to restrict network access to the listener.

Incus users should move to 7.6.0, which fixed this flaw along with 17 other security issues.

Title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys
Context: While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained...
Full Text:
On October 19, 2026, we learned about eMudhra’s eight shockingly weak keys: where eMudhra was trusted to pick a 115-digit number for their virtual combination lock protecting the Internet, they picked the number 4. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. Now, we are sharing a more in-depth follow up on the evidence we’ve seen of exploitation, and the progress seen on visitors patching their systems.

Let's start with the scale of the problem. A certificate authority (CA) with weak keys this serious is unprecedented, and the potential consequences are significant. While there have been plenty of compromised certification authorities in the past (such as DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, and TrustWave), access to their keys has always been contained to a degree; these incidents gave a limited set of attackers or organizations the ability to issue fraudulent certificates. The eMudhra incident is fundamentally different; the affected intermediate private keys could be recovered almost instantly by anyone from the public certificates themselves. Anyone can independently recover these same signing keys and create certificates for any domain that an unpatched client not enforcing Certificate Transparency would accept.

eMudhra announced they’re exiting the public CA business and have claimed a mistake in a key generation script, but have not yet shared the script. They signed a certificate revocation list (CRL) with what might’ve been a correctly generated key, and subsequently corrected it to be signed with the weak key.

How did that come to be and why didn’t that set off alarms? Much has to be cleared up, including the role of the auditors and cross signers. This blog proposes the fixes and next steps for organizations to ensure they are secure.

Patching Cloudflare

Our primary concern remains the security impact on Cloudflare, our customers, and the Internet as a whole. At the time of writing, all high priority Cloudflare systems have been patched. A small number of confirmed low impact tickets is being worked on.

We started patching high-impact systems immediately on October 19. These included customer origin-facing proxies using Pingora, responsible for most of our outbound connections. These were patched in hours to reject the vulnerable eMudhra keys. At the same time, we started an AI-assisted analysis of our source code to find all other systems that trust these weak keys. Within four hours we had a full analysis. We assigned a ticket with preliminary analysis for each system, and asked the team to confirm and/or adjust the analysis before the end of the day. Where high impact was identified, we asked to patch immediately, and for the lower impact, remediation was due at the end of last week.

Has Cloudflare seen exploitation across its network?

To track whenever a customer’s server (or attacker) presents a certificate signed by eMudhra’s weak keys, we added logging to Pingora. As this outbound service accounts for the vast majority of outgoing TLS connections from a Cloudflare machine, any attacker attempting to snoop using the eMudhra keys would trigger this logging. The logging finished rolling out October 21.

At the time of writing, a week later, we’ve seen about 22,000 attempted handshakes with the weak eMudhra keys. Two-thirds of the attempts were fetches of test sites such as emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (which we mentioned in the developer guidance in our earlier post). Almost all of the remaining third went to origins who appeared to set up a certificate for themselves using the weak intermediate. Every handshake configured to verify the certificate was refused, as we already patched.

About 160 of these handshakes stood out: the certificates’ Subject Alternative Names (SANs) were naming other organizations’ domains, unrelated to the Server Name Indication (SNI) requested in the handshake. Some of those names were domains related to consumer IoT devices. We noticed as well that those forged certificates were made after the keys leaked and some were valid for over two years, longer than any public CA may issue. However, these certificates looked like the servers' own default certificates rather than part of an attempt to intercept our connections. They named domains other than the ones being connected to, so they would have failed hostname verification anyway. And in several cases, a server presented the same certificate to connections from many of our locations, which means it came from the server itself rather than from something on a single network path.

Thus while there is no evidence of the weak keys being used to intercept Cloudflare's connections so far, these keys appear to have been used to forge certificates within hours of the weakness becoming public: one of the forged certificates we saw was dated October 20 at 18:19 UTC, less than an hour after Mozilla's bug report was made public. This does not exclude carefully targeted interception. For that we have to rely on the usual indirect signals of system compromise — and so far, we have not seen any such signals.

How many visitors are still vulnerable?

So much about patching Cloudflare, but what about our visitors? We cannot directly test whether a visitor still trusts the weak keys without breaking connections, so we have to do something more indirect. For that we used our challenge pages:

We rolled out an update to send out two probe connections on a fraction of challenge pages: one probe to ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and one to ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com. Initially we installed an eMudhra signed certificate on ca1.cloudflarecaptcha.com and a regularly signed certificate on ca2.cloudflarecaptcha.com as control. Then we record whether these probes succeeded. This allows us to see if visitors that are served a challenge page still trust the weak eMudhra keys.

What did we find? With 50 million probes over the last week, we see this:

Big caveat upfront: by design the traffic to these challenge pages is highly skewed. There are many (unconfirmed) bots in there. Also, only clients that execute JavaScript (like browsers) will send probes.

The jump in the data is due to the following changes—all times are UTC:

October 23 15:30, we changed our control endpoint to also serve an eMudhra certificate, but this time without signed certificate timestamps (SCTs). There were some differences in acceptance, but not large. We could’ve added a new endpoint, but that would’ve required a slow release of our challenge platform. Changing the endpoint was easier.

October 23 16:30, our challenge platform rolled back to a previous version because of an unrelated issue. The probes returned October 27 at 10:00.

October 27 16:37, we noticed we did not send the G3 cross-sign, which not all clients knew about, and added it to both endpoints. We removed SCTs from both.

October 27 16:49, we switched ca2 to chain up to the AAA Certificate Services root.

October 27 18:18, we ramped up probes to be included from 1% to 10% of all challenge pages served on non-paying customer zones.

With those caveats out of the way: what do we notice? Up-to-date modern browsers are mostly patched, but bots and old browsers are not. Also embedded browsers, like Android WebView, lag behind patching with 30–40% still accepting. Over the first weekend (with the monitoring gap), we see clear evidence of patching, but afterwards we see little movement.

On October 29 around 18:00 UTC, we released a detection that caught a large influx of bot traffic identifying as Chrome 150-154 on macOS. This can look like patching in the top graph, but it is actually a change in traffic classification: the same user agents show a corresponding increase in acceptance among traffic with bot signals detected in the bottom graph.

Chrome 150-154 on Linux is the notable exception: its acceptance continues to decline, consistent with further patching in that cohort. Given the bot-heavy and changing traffic mix, that evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive. Otherwise, we still see little movement.

Breaking down by network (ASN) we see:

Across the large networks, more than half of probes still accept the compromised chain, both among traffic with no bot signals detected (top graph) and traffic with bot signals detected (bottom graph). Over the weekend we saw some patching, but afterwards the trend has been flat.

The big caveat still holds: traffic is skewed by (unconfirmed) bots. But bots are also just software that need security updates. And if they’re in any way representative of overall software updates, then the picture is quite dire indeed.

What can you do?

Patch! Dennis Jackson has a great crowdsourced website with instructions. Especially if you’re a developer on macOS, you want to follow these instructions. If you’re a Cloudflare customer, check out last week’s blog post on what needs to be done on your end when using certain products like WARP or Tunnel.

Looking ahead

At Cloudflare, we have a quick-revocation mechanism in place in some products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys. As vulnerabilities are discovered at a faster pace than ever, it is vital that they can be addressed quickly and effectively.
