Title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempt Detected by Amazon Four Days Before Vulnerability Disclosure
Context: Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17
Full Text:
Someone tried to exploit two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language four days before the vulnerabilities were published and the flaws are now being exploited in the wild at scale, according to Amazon.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell,’ could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) and server takeover on any websites relying on any PHP version released in the last decade – going back to version 5.4.

PHP is used by approximately 69.7% of websites whose server-side programming language is known, according to recent W3Techs data. These include many content management systems (CMS) like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento as well as e-commerce and web services platforms.

The bugs were discovered by security researchers at California-based security firm Calif and Google Cloud’s Wiz, with collaboration from OpenAI’s Patch the Planet project, in August. Public disclosure was scheduled for October 21, when the PHP Foundation planned to release the security patches.

However, on October 20, a pseudonymous user of the Hacker News forum leaked some information about the flaws before the patches were ready.

This led to many organizations across the world, including French public administrations, the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre and the University of Vienna taking their websites offline to prepare for and then apply the patches.

Now the patches have been released, the Amazon Threat Intelligence team has publically confirmed they observed a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating October 17. The attempt occurred in MadPot, an internal honeypot system created by Amazon Web Services (AWS) to monitor, study and disrupt global cybercrime.

Early Exploitation Attempt Likely From A “Threat Actor”

The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. According to the Amazon researchers, this suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

In addition, they said they identified multiple proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for PHP2Shell on October 21, around 12 hours before the vulnerability’s scheduled disclosure at 2pm GMT.

The earliest exploit was detected at approximately 2am GMT, with further attempts targeting the company’s MadPot sensors between 2am and 8am GMT from additional infrastructure.

According to the researchers, variations in the payloads and anonymization infrastructure suggested that multiple threat actors were involved. However, it was unclear whether the attempts would have succeeded against real-world systems.

Further PoC exploits emerged within hours of the release of the PHP2Shell patches, which were used against Amazon’s sensors almost immediately.

The researchers warned that PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Emerging Evidence of PHP2Shell Exploitation Attempts

Other security and threat intelligence teams have started to report active exploitation attempts of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in the wild.

Matthew Prince, co-founder and CEO of Cloudflare, said on X his company saw “thousands of attempts to exploit” the vulnerabilities within the 10 hours that preceded the disclosure.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now,” he added.

Other security firms, including Beelzebub, Ellio, Recorded Future, VulnCheck, WatchTowr and Wiz have also observed evidence of exploitation attempts in the wild for both vulnerabilities.

Title: ZDI-26-790: OpenSSL CMS AuthEnvelopedData Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value Vulnerability

Full Text:
Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to tamper with CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages on affected installations of OpenSSL. An attacker must first obtain the ability to modify CMS AuthEnvelopedData messages in order to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of AES-GCM message authentication codes. The issue results from an improper integrity check. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to tamper with authenticated data.

OpenSSL has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20260609.txt

Title: Turn Your Vulnerability Backlog Into Pull Requests With Agentic Remediation
Context: For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization
Full Text:
The Evo Remediation Agent is now in Open Preview, bringing automated dependency resolution to Evo Agentic AppSec. AppSec teams can now run ongoing remediation campaigns across repositories and deliver proposed fixes to developers through validated pull requests.

Fixing a dependency vulnerability can mean choosing an upgrade, resolving dependency conflicts, adapting the application, and/or checking the result. That work competes with everything developers are already building. As teams introduce code and new vulnerabilities at increasingly exponential rates, AppSec needs a way to accelerate remediation across the applications they protect.

With the help of agentic remediation, AppSec teams can start by leveraging campaigns targeting a defined set of repositories and vulnerabilities. Snyk supplies the model and hosted sandbox environment, and developers receive proposed changes through their existing source code management (SCM) workflow. The developers continue to retain control over final review and merging.

Give AppSec a way to drive fixes

A remediation campaign defines which vulnerabilities the agent works on, in which repositories, and on what schedule. AppSec teams set the scope, and Evo Remediation Agent works through eligible vulnerabilities and opens pull requests for developers to review.

For example, an AppSec team can launch a campaign targeting high- and critical-severity dependency vulnerabilities across repositories in a Snyk Organization. Recurring campaigns repeat that work on a schedule as repositories and vulnerability findings change.

That gives AppSec teams a way to initiate remediation without asking each developer to install and run an agent. Teams can follow repository outcomes across a campaign, review where the agent produced fixes, and investigate where remediation efforts still need attention.

Snyk first brought automated dependency updates into developer workflows with automatic Fix PRs across SCA and Container. Agent Fix extended remediation to source-code vulnerabilities detected by Snyk Code, our first AI-native solution generating and checking proposed fixes. The initial Evo Remediation Agent then brought a broader workflow into the CLI and ADE: plan the fix, apply changes, and validate the result in the developer’s environment. Now, fully validated, the next iteration of the Evo Remediation Agent brings campaigns that automate agentic remediation to AppSec teams.

Starting once again with Open Source vulnerabilities, teams can put the agent to work across repositories and make remediation an ongoing part of their security program.

Security context guides the work

A dependency update can require changes throughout an application. The agent uses Snyk findings to plan updates, applies changes in a hosted sandbox, and checks its work with builds, available tests, and rescans. This feedback helps the agent work through the changes an upgrade requires.

When the agent produces a fix, it opens a pull request and records each action attached to the change. Teams can restrict campaigns to fixes assessed as non-breaking, and the agent does not merge changes. Developers review the proposed changes and decide whether to merge them.

Evidence behind the remediation engine

Generating a fix only helps reduce risk if a developer can merge it. A pull request that breaks the build, fails existing tests, or leaves the vulnerability in place adds review work and doesn’t shrink the backlog. A high mergeable fix rate is what turns agent fix suggestions into backlog reduction because more of the fix pull requests actually get merged with less developer rework.

The VulnBump benchmark tests the mergeable fix rate of the engine that powers Evo Remediation Agent. Across 307 dependency-upgrade tasks, the CLI-based Remediation Agent passed all four verification checks on 90.2% of tasks. Claude Code with Snyk findings passed 77.5%, and Claude Code alone passed 59.6%. All three used the same model.

Those checks cover the outcomes that matter to a dependency fix: dependencies resolve, the targeted vulnerabilities disappear on rescan, the application builds, and previously passing tests still pass. The results show the value of combining security context with a purpose-built remediation workflow.

Fix first. Prioritize the rest.

Remediation programs usually start by deciding what to fix. Evo Remediation Agent reverses that order, giving AppSec teams another way to act on the backlog. Recurring campaigns work through eligible vulnerabilities in scope, so what reaches your team is then the work that needs human judgment.

Repository outcomes and journals help teams understand where the agent made progress and where further work remains. AppSec teams get a running view not only of the backlog, but also the pull requests opened, while developers get a record of why each change was made. Remediation consequently becomes an ongoing part of the security program, with your team setting the standard for what ships.

Bring remediation to your team

Workspaces

Title: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
Context: The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack,...
Full Text:
The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.

Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.

But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.

AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.

“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.

Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, tells WIRED that the organization was unaware of AWS's research prior to publication and did not immediately have a comment on the findings. She added, “Although we agree that upgrading is absolutely imperative, to our knowledge, there has been no successful attempt at remote code execution.”

Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”

Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up, given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.

Title: A patched PHP server can still be a compromised one by Lucie Cardiet
Context: Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad...
Full Text:
On October 20, details of two critical flaws in PHP leaked online before the fixes were ready. PHP, the scripting language behind a large share of the web, moved its patch release up a day and shipped it on October 21. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed php2shell), let an attacker run commands on a web server through PHP itself, with no login needed.

Patch now. CISA added both flaws to its list of exploited vulnerabilities on October 26. That advice is right, and it leaves a gap. This post is about the gap.

Attackers were testing the flaw before the fix existed

Fixes are out for PHP 8.2 to 8.5,and PHP says PHP 8.1 and older will not get updates. One estimate counts about 884,000 such servers still online, a rough figure from a single source.

Amazon's honeypots (decoy servers built to attract attackers) recorded the first attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure, and by October 21 Amazon was seeing broad exploitation attempts in the wild. Cloudflare saw early attacks, and the UK National Cyber Security Centre warned organizations to update immediately or take systems offline. How many real servers were taken over is still unclear. Amazon says it does not know whether the attempts it saw would have worked outside a honeypot.

On October 23, CrowdStrike and Flare still reported only probing and failed attempts, many of which crash PHP rather than give an attacker control. The next day, Perplexity's Adel Karimi recorded successful remote code execution on a honeypot, and on October 26 CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities, with a federal patch deadline of October 29. Karimi's test used a deliberately favorable setup, so it shows the flaw works, not how often attacks like it succeed.

Every flaw has been out there for a while before anyone announces it

A flaw becomes news on the day it is announced, not the day it appears. PHP's own maintainers first spotted signs of this problem in a 2024 audit, and attackers reached it before the public did.

We have seen this pattern before. When Log4j hit in December 2021, Vectra wrote that the first sign of an attack was hard to spot and that the safest assumption was that at least one server in an estate was already compromised. Other flaws in the software your business runs are very likely in the same position today: known to someone, announced to no one. Patching deals with the ones you hear about. It cannot help with the rest.

The PHP servers you miss matter most

PHP runs WordPress,Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, hosting control panels, and a lot of software that never mentions PHP. The servers you know about will get patched. The ones you do not know about are the ones attackers find first, because nobody is watching them.

Appliances and management interfaces that ship PHP are the likeliest place an attempt becomes a compromise, and they are rarely monitored like web servers. Flare, relaying one researcher's report, says some ship PHP without address randomization, which removes the main obstacle for an attacker. Ask your vendors which of their products include PHP.

No team patches everything on the day a fix ships. Knowing which servers face the internet, and which hold the most valuable data, turns a backlog into a short list of decisions, including which services to switch off until they are fixed. On any server you suspect was hit, save logs and a snapshot of memory before restarting, because a restart erases traces.

‍

What happens after a PHP server falls

An attacker who gets code running through PHP usually does not need malware. The web server already has a shell, a network connection and access to files, so they can use the tools already installed on the machine to look around, find credentials and move from one system to the next. Nothing looks wrong, because the web server is doing web server things with slightly different commands. That is the first of the three detection gaps I write about: nothing looks wrong.

What changes is where the server talks to. A web server that has served the same pages for years suddenly reaches places it never did before, calls out to unfamiliar addresses, or starts talking to internal systems. That behavior shows up in network traffic, not in patch status. A view of the network is how you see what a server is actually connecting to, whether or not anyone is watching the server itself.

What Vectra AI can and cannot see

Vectra AI is not really concerned about what the initial attack vector is. What we see is what happens afterward.

PHP is the story today. Next week it will be something else: another flaw, a phone call to a help desk, someone on the inside. What we look at does not depend on which door was used. We watch what a system does once an attacker is inside, so we do not need the way in to be known or the flaw to be published. That matters most when the entry point is unknown or the vulnerability has not been announced yet.

Uncovering Potential PHP Servers and Shadow IT

One of the challenges in securing PHP infrastructure is knowing where it exists in the first place. Forgotten applications, unmanaged servers, and shadow IT can create security blind spots, even after known vulnerabilities have been patched.

Vectra AI's PHP Server Visibility dashboard provides an additional investigative tool to help security teams identify potentially overlooked PHP servers using indicators observed in unencrypted HTTP traffic, such as .php endpoints and PHPSESSID cookies. Analysts can then investigate whether these hosts are also receiving externally originated encrypted traffic, helping prioritize potentially exposed systems for further investigation.

The dashboard is not intended to provide a complete inventory of PHP servers. It can only identify systems exhibiting observable PHP-related indicators, and encrypted traffic or limited network visibility may leave some servers undiscovered. Instead, it acts as an assistant to existing asset discovery and threat-hunting workflows, helping analysts uncover potential shadow IT, investigate exposure, and identify systems that warrant closer examination, even after patching.

Detection rules for known php2shell exploit attempts

Vectra Match now contains rules to detect the PHP2Shell attacker behaviors when proper visibility is provided to the attacker traffic. They flag known exploit attempts in network traffic when that traffic is visible to us, so they catch attempts at the door, while the detections above catch what follows. An attempt is not a compromise. A match is a reason to look at that server, not proof that it was taken over. This is available for all Vectra Match customers.

The rules, by ET rule number:

2072548: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Handler-mismatch Session Injection (CVE-2026-109619)

2072549: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Header Amplification OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072550: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Nested Empty File Control OOM (CVE-2026-109618)

2072551: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Chunked Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072552: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Binary URL-Encoded POST for $_POST Corruption (CVE-2026-109618), commented out in the rule set, so off by default

2072553: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Multipart Request without Content-Length (CVE-2026-109618)

2072554: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Code Injection in Filename (CVE-2026-109619)

2072555: ET HUNTING PHP Generic Upload Progress Session Manipulation, a hunting rule, not an exploit rule, so treat a match as a lead

2072556: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Multipart Part Count (CVE-2026-109618)

2072557: ET EXPLOIT PHP php2shell Excessive Empty Multipart File Controls (CVE-2026-109618)

What a compromised PHP server reveals about your resilience

The old measure of success was whether attackers get in. The better one is how far they get. Patching, a sound network design, splitting the network into zones, least privilege and knowing which systems carry your most important business processes all limit that distance. The network record can show whether anyone came through the door before it closed, and where they went next.

The three gaps are walked end to end in the Mind Your Gaps in the Age of AI-Powered Attacks white paper.

Title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: PHP Vulnerable to Unauthenticated RCE Attacks

Full Text: *October 26, 2026: This advisory has been updated to clarify language describing exploitability and potential impact.*October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours following disclosure.IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to as “PHP2Shell,” were publicly disclosed. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. The PHP security team has released emergency patches and strongly encouraged all PHP users to update immediately. These flaws reside in the PHP core language runtime and successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to achieve remote code execution on any server running a vulnerable version, potentially enabling unauthorized access, data theft, or further system compromise. Given PHP's pervasive deployment across web infrastructure globally - including applications like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, as well as embedded devices and similarly overlooked public-facing platforms - the potential attack surface is significant. The vulnerabilities could enable automated exploitation of exposed, vulnerable PHP deployments without authentication or user interaction. The vulnerabilities therefore may be attractive targets for exploitation.ThreatLabz analysis indicates that attackers began rapidly targeting these vulnerabilities following public disclosure, highlighting the need for organizations to patch vulnerable PHP deployments immediately.Zscaler’s security team has analyzed this issue across both production and corporate environments and has ruled out any impact to Zscaler Cloud Platforms, products, distributed components, services, or our enterprise environment, as detailed in the Trust post. RecommendationsOrganizations running PHP should take the following actions:Patch immediately: Upgrade PHP to one of the fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Linux package maintainers received patches in advance and may already have updated packages available. PHP packages for most Linux distributions may also include the patches backported to previous versions of the software, so consult the release notes for your specific installation to ensure your systems are covered.Deactivate unpatched instances: Consider fully disabling services for any PHP instance that cannot be immediately patched. While this may seem overly cautious, any unpatched instance could be targeted by opportunistic adversaries and result in shell-level access to the vulnerable host. Inventory PHP deployments: Conduct an immediate inventory of all PHP installations across your environment, including standalone servers, vendor appliances, bundled software (WordPress, Magento, WooCommerce, Shopware), and hosting panels (cPanel, Plesk, etc).Migrate off EOL branches: Organizations running PHP 5.4+, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1 must migrate to a supported branch immediately. No official binary patches will be released for these versions.Isolate EOL instances that cannot be immediately migrated: Migrating EOL instances is strongly recommended. If this is not possible, isolating unpatchable applications from the internet and other untrusted networks may provide some level of protection. This should be considered a high-risk mitigation and reserved only for business and mission-critical applications while implementing aggressive monitoring of these instances.Monitor for exploitation: Audit web server logs (including but not limited to Apache, Nginx, etc.) for unusual segmentation faults, crash dumps, or abnormal memory usage patterns that may indicate active exploitation attempts.Mitigate risk through PHP settings: While not a definitive fix, mission critical applications that cannot be disabled or immediately patched may benefit from reviewing and tightening memory_limit and max_execution_time settings in php.ini to avoid triggering OOM conditions. Consult additional guidance regarding mitigations through setting session.upload_progress.enabled = Off and disabling multipart uploads at the service edge. ThreatLabz Observes Exploitation Attempts Within 48 HoursThreatLabz observed scanning activity and possible exploitation attempts targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities using multiple attack tools and exploitation methods, including RCE payloads, PHP object injection, and named exploitation frameworks, indicating rapid, in-the-wild exploitation attempts.In the first 48 hours after the PHP2Shell disclosure, Zscaler’s global decoy mesh observed 1,156 exploitation attempts from 156 unique attacker IPs targeting 70 organizations. As a rapid response measure, a new detection rule for PHP2Shell exploitation has been pushed to all Zscaler Deception customers.Attack chainAutomated scanning activity observed by Zscaler suggests attackers may be attempting to use a two-stage PHP2Shell exploitation chain, as shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Notional exploit chain consistent with scanning and exploit attempts observed by ThreatLabz.Stage 1: State setup and fatal triggerThe attacker sends a crafted multipart/form-data POST request containing:A PHPSESSID field to associate the request with a known session, making the session filename (sess_[PHPSESSID]) predictable.The PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field to force PHP to begin session bookkeeping during multipart parsing, populating vulnerable global state pointers and writing attacker-controlled data into the session file.A file attachment whose filename= parameter contains either PHP code or a serialized object string.A body sized or structured to exhaust memory (CVE-2026-109618) or trigger a fatal error (CVE-2026-109619).When the fatal condition is triggered, longjmp() aborts the request, freeing per-request memory but leaving stale global pointers.Stage 2: Heap reclaim and code executionThe attacker immediately sends a second request to the same worker process. This second request contains the attacker's payload, sized and aligned to reclaim the freed memory slots. When PHP processes the new request and references the stale global state before re-initialization occurs, it reads and executes the attacker-controlled data, achieving arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker process.Zscaler Deception telemetry findingsThreatLabz observed malicious POST requests targeting the PHP2Shell exploitation path across multiple tools and stages of the attack chain. Every observed request is a multipart/form-data POST targeting PHP endpoints, specifically /, /index.php, /api/endpoint.php, and /app/upload.php.Exploitation payloads observed1. ShellFlow PHP2Shell named exploit toolThe most forensically significant artifact is the presence of a multipart boundary string that explicitly names the exploitation tool. This indicator should not be considered durable, as an adversary can trivially replace the known strings with something less obvious. At this time, the ShellFlow tool uses a known boundary value, so it is a useful indicator for detecting the unmodified tool. The exploit tool request is shown below. POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----shellflow-php2shell ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" sf618_ec172709c8b74601 ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" shellflow_poc ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="poc.bin" Content-Type: application/octet-stream AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA[...15485 bytes total...]The multipart boundary shellflow-php2shell identifies the attacking tool by name. The poc.bin file body contains more than 15k bytes of data along with a repeated AAAA... characters, a characteristic heap spray pattern used for memory layout control in the CVE-2026-109618 OOM corruption path.Notable characteristics:The boundary string shellflow-php2shell directly identifies the ShellFlow PHP2Shell attacking tool, which is publicly linked to CVE-2026-109618 scanning activity.The session ID sf618_ec172709c8b74601 contains sf618, possibly reflecting a developer’s shorthand reference to ShellFlow + CVE-2026-109618.The application/octet-stream upload with a repeating AAAAA... buffer is consistent with a heap spray technique used to influence the memory layout when the OOM condition is triggered.2. Active system() command execution payloadThese requests represent the strongest indication of automated exploitation attempts. The filename= field contains a fully formed PHP webshell instruction designed to be written into the PHP session file through the session.upload_progress handler and later executed, as shown in the example below.The filename= value [?php system('echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt');echo 'RCE';?] instructs the PHP runtime to:Execute the OS command echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt, writing a proof-of-compromise marker to disk.Echo the string RCE in the HTTP response body, providing an indication of successful code execution to the attacker. The RCE string may still be returned even if the preceding echo redirection fails.This payload pattern was observed in two separate requests with identical content, consistent with automated retry behavior commonly seen in exploit frameworks.3. Affected VersionsAll PHP versions from 5.4 onward are vulnerable. Only currently supported branches received patches, but package maintainers may also backport the security patches to previous versions. Carefully review the instructions and release notes from the maintainers of your PHP installations to determine what version and release includes the necessary patch.PHP BranchVulnerable VersionsPatch AvailablePHP 8.58.5.0 – 8.5.11Yes (8.5.12)PHP 8.48.4.0 – 8.4.26Yes (8.4.27)PHP 8.38.3.0 – 8.3.35Yes (8.3.36)PHP 8.28.2.0 – 8.2.34Yes (8.2.35)PHP 8.1All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 8.0All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 7.xAll versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 5.4+All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)Table 2: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 Affected PHP Versions and Patch Availability How It WorksBoth vulnerabilities are use-after-free memory safety flaws in PHP's core request-handling engine. All PHP installations serving web requests may be affected regardless of security controls. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory; that memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.CVE-2026-109618: OOM Corruption / Uninitialized Memory UseCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: PHP uses longjmp() to abort a request when it hits its configured memory limit. When a web application receives form input, PHP records new entries in its internal POST data structure before finishing their initialization. If an out-of-memory (OOM) error fires while internal request data is only partially initialized, longjmp() bypasses normal control flow, leaving memory in an inconsistent/uninitialized state. During request cleanup, PHP misinterprets this invalid data as valid and follows an attacker-controlled code pointer, yielding control of execution.Exploit Vector: An attacker can intentionally trigger specific OOM conditions (e.g., via large memory allocations, deeply recursive calls, or maliciously crafted request payloads) to corrupt state and achieve unauthenticated RCE.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code ExecutionCVE-2026-109619: Use-After-Free / Stale Memory AccessCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: When PHP encounters a fatal error and calls zend_bailout() (via longjmp()), request-owned internal state can survive in global memory after its backing allocation has been freed. PHP workers process multiple requests in sequence, and certain internal pointers persist between requests. If a request crashes or exhausts memory at the right moment, those pointers are left pointing to already-recycled memory. A subsequent request processed by the same worker may access this stale memory before re-initialization occurs.Exploit Vector: This vulnerability is chainable with CVE-2026-109618. The partial initialization in CVE-2026-109618 allows an attacker to shape the freed memory contents and gain control of the instruction pointer, potentially enabling RCE. Chaining these two CVEs requires no authentication and no user interaction.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution and memory/credential disclosure ConclusionPHP2Shell represents a significant security issue because of the severity of the vulnerabilities and PHP’s broad deployment. The combination of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 could provide an unauthenticated path to RCE and potentially broader server compromise without user interaction.Organizations are strongly urged to treat this as an emergency patching event. Title: Arctic Wolf Labs: Finding, Prioritizing, and Patching PHP2Shell Exposure
Context: On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race...
Full Text:
On Tuesday, October 20, threat actors gained advance visibility into two critical PHP vulnerabilities after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure, accelerating the race between defenders and attackers. The flaws are tracked as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Together they’re known as PHP2Shell. Both carry a 9.2 rating on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) version 4.0 scale. For both vulnerabilities, Arctic Wolf’s Aurora® Agentic SOC helps organizations rapidly identify affected assets, correlate exploitation signals across the environment, and accelerate investigation and response before attackers can establish persistence.

An unauthenticated attacker can use either flaw to run code on a vulnerable server. On Wednesday, October 21, the PHP project released patched versions. PHP2Shell shows how AI is changing the threat landscape. Attackers can now find and weaponize old flaws in widely used technology faster than ever before. Arctic Wolf recommends treating every PHP installation that serves web requests as at-risk presently. Internet-facing Linux web servers without endpoint monitoring carry the highest risk of quiet compromise.

Patching remains the recommended remediation. Security teams should assess exposure immediately, identify likely attack paths, and segment critical systems to limit an attacker’s ability to move through the environment. If attackers exploit PHP2Shell, Aurora Agentic SOC is designed to detect the activity that follows, including webshell deployment, unauthorized command execution, persistence attempts, and lateral movement, enabling rapid investigation and response before attacks can escalate.

Overview and Impact

All PHP installations that serve web requests are at risk. That includes PHP-FPM (FastCGI Process Manager), Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP rates the risk highest for mod_php. In PHP’s demonstrated exploit, an unauthenticated request triggers the attack before any application code runs.

PHP runs WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, and control panels like cPanel and Plesk. Many vendor applications bundle PHP without saying so, which makes the affected assets hard to find. Bundled standalone binaries such as php.exe and php-cgi.exe on Windows are easy to miss.

Understanding the Root Cause

CVE-2026-109618 is an out-of-memory handling flaw. PHP can stop while internal request data is only partly set up. Request cleanup may then treat that invalid data as valid.

CVE-2026-109619 is a stale state flaw. Request-owned internal state can survive after its memory is freed. A later request on the same worker may use that stale state before normal setup resets it. The PHP session upload progress feature is one confirmed path to this flaw, and it’s enabled by default.

Guidance for Arctic Wolf Customers

Inventory every system that runs PHP. Include package-based installs, containers, appliances, and hosting panels. Include vendor software that bundles PHP. Include continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) images.

Identify the PHP branch and package source on each system.

Update to the patched version or confirm your vendor has backported both fixes. Patch internet-facing systems first.

Restart every affected service. That covers PHP-FPM, Apache, NGINX upstream pools, application workers, and containers.

Rebuild container images from patched upstream bases. Patching only the running containers leaves the image exposed.

Move end-of-life PHP to a supported branch.

Record the patched version, vendor advisory, restart time, and validation evidence for each host or image. If a workload can’t be patched right away, document compensating controls and an approved exception with an expiry date.

Use stopgaps to reduce exposure while you patch

Configuration changes such as memory_limit or session.upload_progress.enabled are not remediation. PHP states that only an update is a complete solution. The required fix is a patched PHP runtime or a vendor package that explicitly backports both fixes.

If you can’t update right away, PHP lists measures that reduce exposure to specific attack paths. These measures do not make an installation safe.

For CVE-2026-109618

Set memory_limit=-1 in a way applications can’t override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration.

Set a low post_max_size. PHP suggests 8M for applications without uploads and 32M for those with uploads. Keep upload_max_filesize below it.

Enforce request size, field count, and header limits at the web server or proxy.

Skip RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA because they can trigger the vulnerable allocation failure.

Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or in an FPM pool or server configuration that applies before request parsing. Then restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed session paths but not other variants.

On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 and restart every worker.

Fix attacker-reachable fatal errors and execution timeouts.

How Arctic Wolf Labs turns telemetry into outcomes

Arctic Wolf Labs is our threat intelligence and research team. Global SOC telemetry visibility drives a shared defense, while active network monitoring gives Labs an early warning system across our global customer base. Using telemetry from across the Arctic Wolf customer community, researchers identify spikes in scanning activity, analyze exploitation attempts, and uncover attacker payloads associated with PHP2Shell. We use those findings to develop and fine-tune detections to respond to malicious activity faster. This means customers gain coverage against PHP2Shell activity they may have not observed yet in their unique environment.

Labs researchers also replicate attacker techniques against PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in controlled environments. Arctic Wolf Labs leverages resulting artifacts from these simulations, as well as observed exploit techniques, attacker tradecraft, and emerging indicators of attack/compromise (IOA/IOC), to develop new detections, threat hunt queries, and inform customer remediation guidance

As threat behavior evolves, we continuously apply the latest intelligence across customer environments. Arctic Wolf Labs’ initial investigation has identified numerous scanning efforts as well as malicious exploitation attempts, including passing wget requests to retrieve both ELF and Golang binaries associated with commodity malware.

How the Aurora Superintelligence Platform keeps customers protected

The Aurora Superintelligence Platform helps organizations reduce PHP2Shell risk before and after exploitation. Aurora Vulnerability Management identifies and prioritizes affected assets using live exploit activity and threat intelligence, helping security teams focus remediation efforts where risk is highest.

PHP2Shell vulnerability detections in Aurora Vulnerability Management

The Aurora Agentic SOC monitors the behaviors attackers rely on after exploitation, including webshell deployment, suspicious processes spawned by PHP or web servers, malicious command execution, persistence activity, and lateral movement.

Together, these capabilities help organizations quickly identify exposed systems, prioritize remediation, detect malicious activity, investigate potential compromise, and contain threats while vulnerable systems are being patched. As the threat evolves, Arctic Wolf continuously incorporates new intelligence across the platform to strengthen proactive cyber risk remediation and detection and response capabilities for all customers.

Title: TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions
Context: Vendor Breach Puts TiDB Customers at Risk In a security notification published 12 days after first having discovered the incident, PingCAP acknowledged that hackers had access...
Full Text:
UPDATE

A breach of an open source database provider may have inadvertently highlighted a serious gap in the way companies think about their cloud security.

On Oct. 19, software maker PingCAP, which sells an SQL database program called TiDB, disclosed that it had been breached. According to PingCAP's website, it serves major American corporations like Atlassian, Square, and Pinterest, as well as major players in China's AI space, including Manus, Kimi, and more.

The perpetrator — the somewhat deceptively named "Fulcrum Security," or FulcrumSec, for short — is a relatively new extortionist group whose leak site already includes major organizations like LexisNexis, Novo Nordisk, and the Manchester Airports Group (MAG). Earlier this fall, FulcrumSec appears to have compromised PingCAP, enjoying something shy of unfettered access to all of its cloud management, financial, analytics, storage, and other systems for a month or more.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

The even bigger issue is whether the breach exposed downstream customers' sensitive data. Investigators are still working out the details, but early evidence suggests that customers may be at some risk. Though their actual databases weren't breached, the information their vendor stored about them may have been enough to cause serious issues.

Vendor Breach Puts TiDB Customers at Risk

In a security notification published 12 days after first having discovered the incident, PingCAP acknowledged that hackers had access to its systems from Sept. 9 to Oct. 7. Using stolen service account credentials, the company wrote, the unauthorized party accessed internal company systems and then copied data and source code.

PingCAP's own third-party-assisted investigation found no evidence that attackers ran malicious commands or maintained persistent access in their systems, nor did they access any customers' databases. Instead, it said, the threat actors accessed customers' billing and other business data, such as contract terms and pricing, as well as various information pertaining to cloud accounts and product usage — email addresses, SQL editor text and errors, etc. They also exported a table with encrypted API keys, though investigators said the encryption protected the keys from actually being used maliciously.

Dark Reading reached out to PingCAP for comment. A company spokesperson provided the following statement:

"Between September 9 and October 7, 2026, an unauthorized party used stolen service account credentials to access certain PingCAP internal systems, copy data, and obtain source code. PingCAP identified the activity on October 7 and began disabling the affected credentials that day. As of October 14, all identified compromised credentials have been invalidated, all identified unauthorized access paths have been blocked, and four vulnerabilities reported by our external incident response firm have been fixed and independently verified as remediated.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

"Our investigation, supported by outside counsel and third-party forensic specialists, has found no evidence that data stored by customers in our TiDB cloud production services was impacted, and no evidence that the attacker ran commands or maintained persistent access in the production systems reviewed. Exported records included certain TiDB Cloud account information, business and billing details. API-key values in the exported data were encrypted, and we have found no evidence that any were decrypted or used. As a precaution, we have advised all customers to rotate their TiDB Cloud management API keys and remain alert to targeted phishing attempts. We will notify affected customers directly as customer-specific impact is confirmed, and we will continue to share verified updates on our Trust Hub: pingcap.com/trust-hub."

FulcrumSec, however, painted a bleaker picture.

Related:Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Attackers Leak TiDB Customer Data

In a name-and-shame post to its leak site, the hackers claimed to be in possession of all of PingCAP's service management records, its financial records, its files stored within Google Cloud, Jira support tickets, customer relationship management (CRM) data, analytics data, source code, plus a four-year-long log of every connection every one of its customers ever made to the TiDB Cloud service.

Crucially, the hackers did not claim to have stolen any TiDB databases straight up. Instead, they indirectly obtained a wealth of potentially exploitable user data like those aforementioned API keys and other secrets, and potentially sensitive internal data exposed by cloud database commands.

The attackers fingered individual enterprises caught in the crossfire: brand-name US companies like Airbnb and Booking.com, Asian corporate giants like Baidu and Fujitsu, and a few of the world's biggest video game companies, including Capcom, Konami, and Square Enix. Asia represented the biggest slice of the pie, with nearly 2,000 affected organizations in Japan, China, and Hong Kong, with another 500 from India.

Additionally, FulcrumSec said its unauthorized access lasted for nearly two months, not just one. It was so comprehensive and unthreatened that, in the meantime, they were able to stand up a mirror of PingCAP's own service management system. Instead of having to manually exfiltrate data, their replication feed automatically pulled fresh copies of the company's internal database every six hours, for 22 days.

Claims made by threat actors must always be met with a degree of skepticism, and Dark Reading did not independently confirm FulcrumSec's. Still, the group does have some record of reliability.

Last summer, for example, the group breached Manchester Airports Group (MAG), claiming to have stolen 86GB of data. That data turned out to contain far more genuine personally identifiable information (PII) than MAG copped to, according to reporting by BleepingComputer. And whereas some hackers exaggerate their winnings, this case was something of the opposite: That initial 86GB claim represented compressed data. The hackers clarified that the actual, uncompressed total stolen was 640GB.

Orgs: Be More Critical of Your Service Providers

Even if one were to completely ignore the hackers' account and take PingCAP's more limited assessment as the truth, it would still represent a potentially serious risk to customers.

Arguably the most acute dangers — more than the broad customer data, or the API keys if they are in fact protected — lie in the less obvious exfiltrated data. This includes Jira tickets, SQL histories, and places where organizations unknowingly leak internal data. For instance, when customers use their cloud-managed database services, they send commands to the vendors' servers. Those interactions can often carry corporate secrets or sensitive data of many other types.

"Vendors don't typically set out to store secrets. However, customers often pass them over to use features built for convenience, and the data can settle in places few people think of as credential stores," explains Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at Sysdig.

Take PingCAP's SQL editor text and errors, for example, she says. "That's query history and error output, which is where secrets can accumulate when someone pastes a connection string to debug something on the fly," Morin adds. In FulcrumSec's name-and-shame post, for example, it highlighted exfiltrated SQL statements that listed in full view one medical clinic's roster of patients, and another's list of medical professionals.

Keeper Security chief information security officer Shane Barney seconds Morin's point. "The PingCAP incident illustrates a daily reality in enterprise security: Attackers do not need to compromise a customer's primary database directly if they can systematically harvest upstream credentials," he says. "In modern software-as-a-service (SaaS) ecosystems, customer metadata, API keys, and diagnostic query logs routinely seep into vendor environments through everyday operational telemetry. When service account credentials or administrative API tokens are stolen from a provider, that aggregated operational data transforms into a road map for exploitation."

Barney emphasizes the importance of cloud security hygiene — such as rotating vendor-facing API keys and eliminating hardcoded and long-lived secrets in developer workflows — and vetting one's managed service providers by demanding continuous third-party risk assessments and independent certifications and attestations such as SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001.

Morin urges organizations to ask a few specific questions when vetting cloud providers. "Teams should seek to understand what customer-provided data the vendor retains and what its retention policy is. They should also ask whether they scan for secrets at ingest and redact what they find," she says. "Teams may also want to understand how service account credentials are handled, whether they’re short-lived, how they’re scoped, how often they rotate, and what detections fire on anomalous credential or account use."

And, she says, don't forget: "Inquire about breach notification, specifically the timeline and what triggers it."

This story was updated at 9 p.m. ET on Oct. 22 to reflect a statement from PingCAP.

Title: PHP2Shell: How to Protect Vulnerable PHP Workloads While Patching
Context: Aquasec provides vulnerability detection and runtime controls to help identify exposure and restrict supported unauthorized activities while customers apply security updates
Full Text:
How does Aquasec protect PHP workloads?

Aquasec enforces security policies inside running workloads, allowing security teams to restrict supported unauthorized actions without depending exclusively on vulnerability specific signatures.

Four runtime control areas are particularly relevant to PHP workloads.

Restrict unauthorized process execution. Runtime policies can restrict PHP workloads from launching unnecessary shells and download utilities such as `sh`, `bash`, `curl` and `wget`. This can interrupt certain attempts to execute additional commands or retrieve malicious payloads.

Prevent unauthorized executable changes. Aquasec Drift Prevention can block execution of executable files that were not present in the original container image. This helps restrict newly introduced malicious binaries, although it does not independently prevent a PHP script from running through the existing interpreter.

Restrict unauthorized network activity. Appropriate runtime network controls can restrict unnecessary outbound connections and help limit certain reverse shell activities or communication with attacker controlled infrastructure.

Protect application files. File integrity monitoring can detect unauthorized modifications to sensitive application directories. File modification restrictions can prevent changes when properly configured, including changes to PHP web roots where malicious scripts might be introduced.

The effectiveness of these controls depends on workload coverage, policy configuration and the attack technique. In enforcement mode, validated policies can block supported unauthorized actions. They should not be represented as complete protection against either PHP2Shell vulnerability, particularly the reported memory disclosure path.

Title: Limits of Java Certificate Bypass: Fingerprint Blocklist Insights
Context: TL;DR Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked
Full Text:
TL;DR

Sonatype's tests found that Java's blocked.certs rejected the listed certificate encodings but accepted re-encoded versions that still validated in the tested configurations.

We reproduced the behavior with ECDSA- and RSA-signed intermediates associated with the eMudhra incident. Each re-encoded certificate had a different SHA-256 fingerprint.

The results apply to the JDK versions and trust-store configurations tested. Follow current vendor guidance and verify the protections in the runtimes and trust stores you deploy.

A certificate blocklist can reject a known-bad certificate and still miss another encoding of it.

We saw this while examining Java's response to the eMudhra certificate incident. The mitigation uses SHA-256 fingerprints to identify compromised intermediate certificates. But a certificate’s fingerprint is calculated from its exact encoded bytes.

During an AI-assisted review, Sonatype Research Labs asked Opus 5.5 whether Java's exact-fingerprint blocking could be bypassed. The AI model flagged that exact-byte matching might leave room for equivalent certificate encodings.

We confirmed the behavior for both ECDSA and RSA certificates: re-encoded intermediates had different SHA-256 fingerprints, yet still validated in our Java trust-store tests. This points to a limit in exact-fingerprint blocking: it can identify the certificate bytes it knows about without necessarily covering every equivalent encoding.

Here, we’ll explain how the re-encoding works, what the tests show, and what teams should check before relying on a certificate blocklist as their only mitigation.

How It Started: eMudhra Certificates Compromised

Several eMudhra intermediate certificate authority keys were compromised on October 20, 2026, allowing anyone who obtained a key to create certificates that could be trusted as part of a chain to a trusted root. Browser and platform vendors responded with blocks and trust-store changes.

This also prompted a Java mitigation: add the affected intermediates to blocked.certs. Our research began with a narrower question: does that fingerprint-based block reject every valid encoding of those certificates?

How Exact-Fingerprint Blocking Works

A certificate is a structured document: it contains information such as the subject, public key, issuer, validity period, and a digital signature. In Java, blocked.certs identifies certificates by their SHA-256 fingerprints. The fingerprint is calculated from the certificate's encoded bytes, so even a small change to those bytes produces a different fingerprint.

This makes fingerprint blocking precise, but the match depends on the exact encoding in the blocklist. If a certificate can be re-encoded and still pass signature validation, the new encoding may have a different fingerprint and may not match the listed entry. To test whether an alternate encoding could still validate in practice, we examined two signature formats: ECDSA and RSA.

Changing the Encoding Changes the Result

We tested two certificate chains from the eMudhra incident advisory: one with an ECDSA-signed intermediate and one with an RSA-signed intermediate. For each, the reproduction added the original intermediate's SHA-256 fingerprint to a copy of a JDK's blocked.certs file, changed the intermediate's encoding without its private key, then checked whether the chain still validated.

The two encoding changes were:

ECDSA: The script changes the signature value from s to n − s, another valid representation of the signature.

RSA: It removes the NULL parameter from the outer signature algorithm identifier. The signature over the certificate data remains unchanged.

Both tests produced the same result:Java rejected the original chain whose intermediate fingerprint was listed, but trusted the chain with the re-encoded intermediate, whose fingerprint was different. After the relevant roots were removed from the copied JDK’s trust store, both chains were rejected.

Verify the Mitigation in Your Runtime

Teams should verify certificate mitigations in the Java runtimes and trust stores they deploy. Removing the relevant roots rejected both chains in our tests, but it can also interrupt legitimate TLS connections. Before changing a trust store, identify dependent services, test their certificate chains, and monitor for TLS failures after deployment.

Follow current vendor guidance and document any exceptions. These results cover only the JDK versions and trust-store configurations we examined, so validate the controls separately for other runtimes and TLS paths in your environment.

Title: PHP2Shell Makes PHP Inventory and Patch Ownership Urgent
Context: As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet
Full Text:
Updated October 23, 2026: PHP disclosed a related follow-on issue, CVE-2026-115560, involving an unlikely remote code execution (RCE) vector under unusual session settings. PHP recommends disabling session.upload_progress.enabled until the next regular bugfix release. See our research and recommendation in Sonatype Guide for more details.

TL;DR

PHP2Shell is the name being used for two critical PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Both can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

PHP says all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, with the highest risk in Apache configurations using mod_php. Fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

Organizations should inventory PHP across their environments, prioritize internet-facing systems, monitor for suspicious activity, and apply the update through PHP or the relevant distribution or product vendor. If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

On October 23, 2026, PHP disclosed CVE-2026-115560, a separate follow-on RCE issue. Temporarily disable session.upload_progress.enabled as PHP recommends, then apply the complete PHP fix when available.

PHP2Shell Is Two Critical Flaws in the PHP Runtime

PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in PHP's internal request handling. Because PHP is used in websites, applications, and products, affected installations may be managed by different teams or supplied through different vendors.The urgent work is to find those systems, establish who owns each one, and verify that the fix reaches every deployment.

Sonatype's PHP2Shell Security Event tracks current guidance and response recommendations.

CVE-2026-109618 involves out-of-memory handling: PHP may interrupt a request while internal data is only partly initialized, then handle that data incorrectly during cleanup.

CVE-2026-109619 involves a stale global state that can persist after its underlying memory has been freed.

PHP says CVE-2026-115560 can occur when an application configures session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, switches it to php at runtime before calling session_start(), and leaves session upload progress enabled. PHP had already listed disabling upload progress as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619. This setting does not cover every affected path, and that a PHP release containing the complete state-reset patch is the reliable remediation.

Under affected conditions, the flaws can allow a remote attacker to execute code without authentication.

Ilkka Turunen, Sonatype's Field CTO, puts the operational priority plainly: "The immediate priority is clear accountability: know where PHP is used across your services and products, who owns remediation, and how quickly fixes can be deployed."

The Hard Part Is Finding Every PHP Installation

Organizations may know that their public websites use PHP but have less visibility into internal portals, older services, appliances, or software that bundles its own runtime. Different teams may also install and maintain PHP through separate operating system distributions, hosting providers, or third-party vendors.

Turunen expects remediation to extend beyond visible websites and services. PHP is bundled into other products and remains in older environments, creating what he calls "a long tail of environments needing to apply this patch."

A complete response starts with an inventory that connects each runtime to an owner and a patch path. Teams should identify:

Which internet-facing and internal systems run PHP.

The PHP version and how it is supplied or maintained.

Which applications, containers, images, appliances, and products include a PHP runtime.

The business or service owner responsible for remediation.

Whether a fixed package is available from PHP, the operating system distributor, hosting provider, or another vendor.

Include systems that are easy to overlook: older applications with little traffic, test environments that remain reachable, and deployments maintained outside the central platform team. An incomplete inventory can make an organization believe remediation is finished while vulnerable installations remain online.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project. PHP says some distributions and long-term support vendors provide backported fixes, and it has also published source backports for selected older branches. Organizations using these versions should confirm the status with their distribution or vendor, or plan an upgrade to a supported release. Do not assume an upstream version number alone tells you whether a vendor-maintained package includes the fix.

Patch, Verify, and Monitor Across the Estate

PHP says updating to a fixed release is the only complete solution. Temporary controls can reduce exposure to specific attack paths, and a web application firewall can add protection for traffic routed through it. Cloudflare reported deploying protections and seeing attack traffic aimed at its customers, while urging users to patch.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, the UK National Cyber Security Centre advises organizations to consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated. If it must remain available, assign an owner and document interim protections and a reassessment date.

The discovery and response also highlight the role AI is playing in vulnerability research. The Wall Street Journal reported that Calif and Wiz researchers used AI tools during a PHP source-code audit, and that developers, researchers, and distributors coordinated on fixes after details leaked ahead of the planned disclosure.

As Turunen warns: "The age of AI has also sped up exploitation where it's likely we are going to see scaled up attacks imminently across the internet."

What Organizations Should Do Now

PHP2Shell is a test of whether organizations can find, own, and update the software running across their environments. PHP has published fixes, but a release only reduces risk when the update reaches every affected runtime, including those inside products and services maintained by other vendors.

Organizations should:

Inventory systems running PHP, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

Monitor internet-facing PHP systems for suspicious activity.

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or apply the relevant vendor backport. Include products and services that bundle PHP.

Check PHP, distribution, and third-party vendor advisories for updates, especially when running PHP 8.1 or older.

If a system cannot be remediated promptly, consider taking it offline until it is fully mitigated.

For ongoing details and links to current advisories, see the official PHP security advisory.

Title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
Context: Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server
Full Text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

Title: “Next Exploit Opportunities”: How a Threat Actor Used AI to Help Plan and Execute Multiple Types of Cybercrime Activities
Context: Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

“Can you find about like what scam or thing they done in past like spoofing calls or somthing [sic],” the threat actor typed. The conversation was with one of several AI assistants that the actor was using to get advice on planning and executing a variety of cybercrime activities.

Our visibility into this specific actor's operational environment gives us unique insights into exactly how threat actors are building, testing and executing agentic attacks across multiple campaign types.

Unit 42’s investigation into the actor’s operational environment and activities makes two things clear:

The attacker used basic tooling and relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports, suggesting they didn’t have the skills these activities would have required before the advent of readily available AI tools.

Despite some apparent bumbling, the actor had an impact, attacking a number of targets in India, including universities. The actor recovered thousands of records revealing personal information and mapped multiple organizations’ attack surfaces.

The attacker’s conversations with jailbroken AI tools included getting step by step advice on how to set up a fraudulent Voice over IP (VoIP) operation. One assistant “helpfully” generated a document including a “NEXT EXPLOIT OPPORTUNITIES” section, outlining planned followup attacks.

Unit 42 identified and investigated this threat actor's operational environment. There, we determined that they had weaponized an AI assistant across several types of cybercrime, including:

Credential theft and data exfiltration

VoIP telecommunications fraud

Wi-Fi password cracking

Cryptocurrency reconnaissance

Command-and-control (C2) operations

An actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor integrated development environment (IDE) as a secondary tool, both with safety controls disabled. The actor ran an AI-generated brute-force campaign against an Indian university’s website. The actor also achieved a confirmed intrusion against a second university, where they exfiltrated a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students.

The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders). Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations.

Multiple, unrelated actors are independently adopting the same Hermes + DeepSeek combination. This suggests we may be witnessing an increasingly prevalent toolchain of choice for cybercriminals adopting AI-enabled capabilities. We assess a key driver is low safety friction at low cost: DeepSeek models are inexpensive and easy to access, and readily jailbroken with a simple system-prompt override.
