Full Text: Title: Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 - command execution Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Linux CVE: pending Description: Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 build 1178, the closed-source incremental backup and file-replication server from Synametrics Technologies, Inc. (United States), written in Java and served by an embedded Tomcat 9.0.113 through the vendor's in-house sradef framework whose single front controller routes every request as /app?operation=<op>&st=<step> to a handler registered in WorkerMappings.xml, contains a path traversal (CWE-22 primary, CWE-269 and CWE-78 contributing for the deployment shape that converts the write into an execution) in the chunked-upload branch of its PublicLink handler. That branch, operation=pb with st=u, reads a length-prefixed binary frame straight from request.getInputStream() rather than through any parameter parser: four big-endian int32 fields for protocol, chunkNumber, totalChunks and size, then a four-byte length prefix followed by UTF-8 filename bytes, then exactly size body bytes. At PublicLink.java:70-110 the decompiled method evaluates new File(base, filename) on that client-supplied filename with no rejection of "..", no rejection of path separators, no base-name extraction and no canonical containment check, creates missing parent directories with target.getParentFile().mkdirs(), opens the result with new FileOutputStream(target, true) in append mode, writes the size bytes it read and returns 0, which the caller at PublicLink.java:127 turns into the client reply code="1" with <payload>0</payload>. base is the authenticated user's own folder at /opt/Syncrify/PublicLinks/<user>/<generated-folder>, five components below the filesystem root, so a chunk name of ../../../../../etc/cron.d/<name> leaves it and lands a cron fragment anywhere the service identity can write. Because the documented Linux deployment shape runs the server process at uid 0 and a cron daemon was active on the verified instance, the host scheduler then reads that fragment as a root-authored job definition and runs its command field through a shell on the next minute boundary. The application never constructs, quotes or invokes a command line and every execution site in the product uses an argument vector with no shell, so the execution happens one component later and argument hygiene at the application layer would not have prevented it. The chain was verified end to end and the identity capture the cron job produced was uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root), established twice over: the fragment landed as -rw-r--r-- 1 root root at mode 0644, a file's owner after creation being the effective uid of its creator, and the scheduled job's own output reported uid 0 because the fragment names root in its user field and a scheduler will not honour that for a job file it does not already trust. The principal required is the product's lowest-trust account type. The gate on operation=pb is a secLevel=0 registration, meaning no administrator session, and the handler's own authentication call validates a credential from the backup-user store at config/UserMappings.xml via syncrify.users.DefaultUserManager rather than from the web-administrator store at config/umap.dat; the two stores are independent and must not be conflated. A backup user's entire legitimate job is to move bytes into its own repository, so the privilege boundary that fails here is inside the product, not a misconfiguration of the host. The defect is an omission rather than an absent control: three sibling families in the same tree, written against the same client protocol, do filter the same kind of field, the profile-upload, profile-fetch and file-splitter handlers rejecting separators with indexOf(47) and indexOf(92), the multipart upload path collapsing the name through getName(), and the download path testing indexOf("..") and answering 404 on a match. The chunk-upload branch calls none of them. There is no decoding step between the socket and the constructor, so no encoding trick is involved or needed. The product does ship a factory administration password of letmein in its first-run install wizard, but the first administrator login is forced through a password change through ChangePassword.jsp, the credential belongs to a different user store than the one gating this sink, and it is documented as a contributing fact only: it appears in no vector, raises no metric, and no conditional reading assumes it has not been rotated. No unauthenticated path to this sink was found and none is claimed. CVSS: 7.5 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding. That is the primary reading, and the two metrics that carry its nuance are AV:N and AC:H: the vulnerable component is an HTTP handler on a network-bound servlet connector and the credential it accepts exists so that remote backup clients can use it, so AV:N is the faithful classification of the component, while the deployment-dependent exposure of the listener carrying the route is priced in attack complexity rather than smuggled into the attack vector. AC:H is High for two reasons outside the attacker's control, that the listener carrying /app?operation= be reachable from the attacker's position and that the host run a scheduler which scans /etc/cron.d. Base = Roundup(5.873119 + 1.620146) = Roundup(7.493265) = 7.5, from ISS = 0.914816 and Impact at S:U = 5.873119. Conditional reading: 8.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), applying only where the listener carrying the /app?operation= surface is reachable from the attacker's network position, which is the normal operating mode for a backup server whose clients push data to it remotely, and computed as Roundup(5.873119 + 2.835255) = Roundup(8.708374) = 8.8. The conditional is labelled conditional everywhere it appears, is never the headline, and the published score is 7.5 rather than 8.8. Two further readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic. The changed-scope variant of the same metrics, 8.6 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H), is rejected because the identity reached is the same root identity the server process already holds on the same host, so no component authority boundary is crossed by the outcome; the privilege gain is carried by PR:L and by C:H/I:H/A:H, which are the metrics meant to express it. The local-vector reading, 7.8 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), is rejected for an evidential reason and it is worth being explicit that this rejection lowers our own number rather than raising it: that reading is what follows if you treat the loopback binding observed in the testbed as the shipped default, and 7.8 is higher than the 7.5 this submission publishes at AV:N. The loopback binding was applied by us in the configuration before any testing began, so the host carried no public exposure while research was in progress, and there is no shipped artifact, no configuration template, no installer script excerpt and no documentation quotation, establishing the factory value of that binding in either direction, not that it binds publicly by default and not that it binds loopback by default. That unestablished reachable-listener premise is the reason AC is High and the reason the 8.8 figure is conditional, and a reader who disagrees with us about the factory default ends up with a larger score than ours, not a smaller one. No version-range claim is made: only 6.2 build 1178 was decompiled and exercised. Impact: arbitrary file write with an attacker-chosen path and attacker-chosen bytes, escalating to command execution as uid 0 on the verified deployment shape. The chunk branch writes exactly the bytes it reads to whatever path the chunk name resolves to, in append mode, creating missing parent directories via mkdirs(), so /etc/cron.d is the demonstrated escalation path and not the limit of the primitive. On this product the weight comes from what the host is for: it is a backup and file-replication server, and root on it means read access to the entire repository tree, every backup belonging to every configured client, which on a multi-tenant server is a confidentiality breach across all tenants rather than within one account, plus the server's own configuration holding administrator and backup-user credential material and transport secrets, the backup-user store comparing passwords in plaintext or storing them under a reversible permutation transform so a read of it hands over credentials directly. It also means integrity control over the replication path itself: repository contents, version and retention metadata and the server's own binaries can be altered in place, and because that path is how clients back up and restore, a modified backup set becomes a distribution channel whose corruption stays invisible until the moment the data is needed. Persistence is structural rather than incidental, a cron fragment running on every minute boundary until it is deleted and surviving restarts of both the service and the host. Availability follows the same authority: the backup service can be stopped, the host rebooted or hung, repositories deleted or truncated, and the scheduler used to keep doing so after the application alone is remediated, which destroys the recoverability that is the entire reason the product exists. All of that beyond the executed identity capture is argued from the identity reached and the deployment layout and was not performed; no repository data was read and no product file was modified or deleted during verification. Verification boundary: static reversal of the decompiled handler tree, then a live run against a single deployed instance of Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 installed from the distributed Linux tarball archive into /opt/Syncrify and started with ./run.sh, behind the embedded Tomcat 9.0.113 announcing itself as Synametrics Web Server v7. Two properties of that instance were the researchers' rather than the product's and both are carried as boundaries. The portal listener was bound to the loopback address by an explicit configuration edit made before testing, so remote reachability of the route is argued from the product's own design and binding configuration, from the front controller being the same listener that serves the client-protocol operations backup clients use, and from the structural fact that a backup server whose clients push across a network must have that listener reachable from them or it cannot perform its function; it is not a measurement from a separate host, and no shipped artifact establishes the factory binding in either direction. The backup-user store did not exist after installation, so the verification account was written into config/UserMappings.xml by hand with plaintext password comparison rather than provisioned through the administrator's user-management operation, which is licence-gated and was blocked by a zero licence count; the encrypted-entry and directory-authentication branches were examined statically and not exercised. The chain was driven from the target host itself over the loopback interface because that is how the listener was bound, so the same chain arriving from across a network segment was not verified and is not claimed. Four controls were exercised: a non-traversing chunk name through identical authentication, framing and routing in the same session, landing inside the user's own PublicLinks folder with an assertion that neither the fragment nor the marker existed, which isolates the traversal as the cause of the outcome and of nothing else; a Java-level confirmation that the multipart family's getName() collapse keeps a traversing name inside the PublicLinks root; a dispatch control against st=f, which reached a different void E() overload that parses an ed parameter as a Long and performed no write anywhere, fixing the sink to the st=u branch rather than to the handler in general after an initial static reading had attributed the upload to the wrong overload; and the four-way authentication reply table showing code="1" for a correct pair, code="-2" for a wrong password so the comparison is live, and code="-1" for an absent password and an absent user so the parameter-presence gate fired before the credential lookup was entered, which is what makes the lookup's no-comparison branch unreachable from this surface. Root execution was observed rather than inferred, and a non-root service deployment was not tested, so no claim is made about what the primitive achieves under an unprivileged service identity, where the escalation demonstrated here would not follow while the file write itself survived. Exactly one payload shape was executed, an identity capture into a marker file, and only that shape is claimed; the advisory reproduces the identity string and the frame field lengths derived from the field values but not the run's own byte capture, which was not preserved, not the generated PublicLinks folder name, which embeds the run's timestamp, not the credential pair, which are mandatory tool arguments with no default, and not the per-run fragment name or marker path. The unauthenticated surface was exhausted first with negative results: thirteen operations answer anonymous requests with real content and no credential check and all thirteen are sink-free; the remaining level-0 operations are not anonymous and answer code="-2" without valid credentials; seventeen Runtime.exec and ProcessBuilder sites exist and none is reachable anonymously; eight deserialization candidates have no network caller and the classpath carries no gadget library, no commons-collections, Jackson, XStream, Kryo or Hessian; and no template engine or naming-service lookup exists in the tree. That enumeration is not a proof the unauthenticated surface is safe, and it surfaced weaknesses deliberately not claimed here and not folded into any metric, being a manualOverride filter-block bypass exposing debug pages with a directory listing and an environment-variable dump, a password-recovery account-enumeration weakness, globally disabled CSRF prevention that is irrelevant to a chain needing credentials the attacker holds, vendor-default credentials for an embedded database that is configured but disabled and was not listening, and a default trial licence serial whose effect was left unresolved. Only Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 is claimed; the same sradef framework underpins the vendor's sibling products and this build's own web.xml still carries the display-name SynaMan, which is recorded to say where else the same construction is worth auditing, and no sibling product was tested. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/synametrics-syncrify-publiclink-chunk-upload-traversal-cron-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/synametrics/syncrify-6.2/publiclink-chunk-upload-traversal-cron-root-rce/exploit/synametrics_syncrify_publiclink_chunk_upload_traversal_cron_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target. It takes host, port, scheme, front-controller route, operation and upload step; a mandatory backup-user credential pair with no default; and the command, marker path, fragment path, fragment user field, fragment schedule, traversal depth, scheduler wait and per-request timeout as arguments, defaulting to the loopback interface, port 5800, a depth of five and an identity capture. It offers an --insecure flag for self-signed TLS on the https scheme, a --control mode that performs the identical authenticated upload with a non-traversing chunk name and then asserts that neither the fragment path nor the marker path exists, a --proof-command argument that reads proof from a local command's standard output for an operator who already holds a shell channel to the host, an --expect-root flag that exits non-zero unless the recovered proof reports uid=0, and a --cleanup mode that removes only the two paths the script created. Nothing destructive is performed and no product file is overwritten or deleted. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Full Text: Title: Edimax BR-6478AC firmware v2.20 - authenticated command injection Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware CVE: pending Description: Edimax BR-6478AC firmware image BR6478AC_v2.20.bin, the closed-source dual-band AC1750 SOHO wireless router from Edimax Technology Co., Ltd. (Taiwan), whose SquashFS root filesystem of roughly 2.3 MB targets MIPS 32-bit big-endian MIPS-I with a uClibc C library and carries an internal build timestamp from 2015, contains an OS command injection (CWE-78) in the WAN-configuration form handler of bin/webs, the embedded GoAhead-style HTTP server serving the management interface on TCP port 80. That binary is ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS, 762904 bytes, SHA256 ec39c0f9332361e37ab92f1999ac5f00f5742dd6db75f7cb26c0652cfedb32a1, reads etc/boa/boa.conf, writes /var/run/webs.pid and is kept alive by the boot path cleanlog.sh:131 invoked from init.sh:1115. The registration websFormDefine("setWAN", ...) at 0x478484, handler at 0x441cec, name string at 0x4a6250, publishes POST /goform/setWAN. Inside the handler the WAN mode is taken from the request and dispatched: websGetVar(wp, "wanMode", "") at 0x441d3c, atoi at 0x441d44, apmib_set(0x102, &wanMode) at 0x441d54, then addiu v1, zero, 2 at 0x441d60 and beq v0, v1, 0x441e74 at 0x441d6c. On the PPP branch, wanMode 2, the username field is read by websGetVar for pppUserName, name string at 0x4953f4, copied with strcpy at 0x441e94 into a fixed stack buffer, measured with strlen at 0x441ea8 and then scanned by an inline byte loop between 0x441ebc and 0x441ee4 whose only comparison is addiu a0, zero, 0x3b, a semicolon; finding one, the loop writes a NUL and stops. That single-character scan is the entire sanitisation on the path. The value is then formatted by sprintf at 0x441ee8 with the format string at 0x49a510, echo %s > /tmp/UserName, and passed to system(buf2) at 0x441f1c through the PLT slot at 0x4c6d60, which hands the line to /bin/sh -c. A pipe, an ampersand, a backtick, a dollar sign with parentheses and an embedded newline are never inspected, so a username containing no semicolon reaches the shell untouched: the payload |id > /tmp/marker # builds the command line "echo |id > /tmp/marker # > /tmp/UserName", in which the shell treats the hash as a comment swallowing the sink's own redirect and runs id as the right-hand side of a pipeline. An escape loop replacing a hash with a backslash-escaped hash does exist between 0x441f4c and 0x441fb0, but the instruction order places it after system() at 0x441f1c with no branch back to it, and it writes the configuration buffer at sp+0x18 that apmib_set(0x6d, ...) stores at 0x44200c rather than the buffer handed to the shell, so the hash character is escaped for storage and for nowhere near execution. Between websGetVar and system there is no regex call, no inet_aton, no isdigit, no isalnum, no strchr, no strcspn, no vendor validation helper and no custom validator; the inet_aton calls that do exist in the function, at 0x441dd0 and 0x441e14, belong to the static-IP branch, wanMode 1, reached via the branch at 0x441d8c, which the wanMode 2 comparison never enters, so a quick read of the decompilation misleads a reviewer into thinking this function validates addresses. The same construction appears three times in this handler and one root cause yields three reachable parameters: pppUserName on wanMode 2 with sink region 0x441e74 to 0x441f1c and configuration object 0x6d written after the sink, pptpUserName on wanMode 3 from 0x4420d0 onward with configuration object 0xf3, and L2TPUserName on wanMode 6 from 0x44246c onward with configuration object 0x128, each selected by a value the request supplies and each using the same immediate-0x3b scan, the same echo format string and the same system() call shape, so a patch confined to the PPP path leaves the PPTP and L2TP paths injectable. Reaching the handler requires a valid administrative session: the gate auth_authorize at 0x404d00 reads configuration object 0x1bc, the setup-wizard flag, through apmib_get, and once past setup the security store at 0x4c7004, a single / entry of type Basic registered from the directive Auth / /etc/boa/boa.passwd, covers every /goform/ path with HTTP Basic authentication. The product has no second lower-privileged role, so Privileges Required is High: one realm entry, one password file, one account, an Allow directive handler at 0x407688 that is a stub answering "This version of Boa doesn't support access controls", a type-None string at 0x49070c never passed to auth_add, and a shipped configuration carrying one Auth directive and no Allow directive. The route is not one of the four carrying a post-boot uptime gate, /mp.asp, /goform/mp, /advanced_management.asp and /goform/formAdvManagement, which redirect to /index.asp once /proc/uptime exceeds 600 seconds, so it is reachable at any time the device is up. The calling process is root because etc/boa/boa.conf declares User root, the server performs no setuid, chroot, namespace or capability drop and writes /var/run/webs.pid, which requires root on this filesystem, so the landing identity is uid=0(root) with no escalation step in the chain. This handler is one instance of a broad construction: a count of the shipped registration table found 91 /goform/form* handlers of which roughly 85 reach a system() or popen() call. Two adjacent observations are reported without a score: the strcpy at 0x441e94 copies attacker-controlled bytes with no length argument into a fixed stack buffer, for which no overflow was developed and no exploitability claim is made, and because the semicolon scan writes a NUL at the first semicolon a legitimate username containing one is silently truncated before storage, a correctness defect independent of the injection. The firmware image ships a populated /etc/boa/boa.passwd for the single realm and the model's published factory login is admin:1234; that is reported separately as CWE-798, carries no score, is never described as the vector for this injection, and no cryptographic match against the shipped MD5-crypt digest is claimed because the digest string captured during analysis was recorded incompletely. One detail is left unresolved rather than smoothed over: the single account entry in the image is recorded under the name root while the model's published management login is admin, and because no device was ever authenticated against, which user name the realm accepts was not established. Absence of privilege separation is likewise reported separately as CWE-250. A static comparison against a second firmware image, BR-6208AC_V2_1.03, whose webs is a different build, ELF 32-bit MSB MIPS-I, 816568 bytes, SHA256 3ad10a41d11c8cd59185eab6c9ce67b18cd2118942eb2201f48540d7846a0328, found a setWAN implementation matching instruction for instruction, handler at 0x448710, websGetVar for pppUserName at 0x4488b8, strcpy at 0x4488bc, the same inline immediate-0x3b scan at 0x4488dc to 0x4488fc, the same sprintf at 0x448920 with format string 0x4a6954, system() at 0x448940, the same three parameters on the same three wanMode values and the same single-realm Basic authentication behind the same configuration flag, which points to a shared source component in the vendor's router software base; that model was not tested, nothing was executed from that image, no score covers it and it is not an exploited finding on it. Privileges Required Low is rejected at 8.8 High, Exploitability 2.835255 and Base Roundup(8.708373), because the product has no basic-user role. Scope Changed is rejected at 9.1 High, Impact at S:C 6.128026, Exploitability 2.286496 and Base Roundup(1.08 x 8.414522), because webs is root before the attack and root after it. Attack Complexity High is rejected at 6.6 High, Exploitability 0.705547 and Base Roundup(6.578666), because success depends on no condition outside the attacker's control, the only branch to satisfy, wanMode, being attacker-supplied. An adjacent-vector reading is published as a labelled alternative at 6.8 High, Exploitability 0.900610 and Base Roundup(6.773729), and is the honest description of a stock device whose WAN-side input policy drops new connections, the shipped firewall script dropping WAN-originated SYN at firewall.sh:180, installing a default DROP input policy at firewall.sh:187 and accepting input on other interfaces at firewall.sh:189; AV:N is retained because the service is bound to the device's own network stack and addressable over IP by every host on the segment the router serves, including guest wireless clients and anything bridged or compromised behind it, and because remote management on the WAN side or forwarding port 80 are ordinary documented features. That conditional's Scope Changed variant computes to 10.0 and is deliberately not published, and if the setup window has to be contested rather than found open the reading is 8.1 High from Exploitability 2.221167 and Base 8.094286. No version range is claimed: only firmware BR6478AC_v2.20.bin was examined, and only the wanMode 2 path was replicated, so no claim is made for other BR6478AC builds, for the separately marketed BR-6478AC V2 hardware revision whose firmware line is a different little-endian MIPS-II build of webs, for the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances beyond the structural reading of the same handler, or for any other model. Impact: arbitrary operating-system command execution as root on the router from a single authenticated POST indistinguishable from a legitimate WAN settings submission, since the payload travels in the PPP username field of the form the product's own wan.asp page posts. Root on this device exposes every stored secret, including precisely the PPP, PPTP and L2TP credentials this handler writes into configuration objects 0x6d, 0xf3 and 0x128, so an attacker who reaches the device can read the ISP or VPN account details the owner entered, together with the administrator password file, wireless pre-shared keys and per-station key material, VPN parameters and any certificate or key on the filesystem. It grants control of the configuration and routing plane: firewall and NAT rules, the DNS resolver handed out to clients, DHCP leases and a malicious default gateway, port forwards, wireless SSIDs and the WAN uplink itself, including rewriting the WAN mode, which is exactly the configuration path this handler owns. It grants firmware-level persistence, since root can write the flash-backed configuration area and install a boot-time startup mechanism, so a compromise survives reboots and can survive a partial configuration reset, with recovery requiring a full reflash of a known-good image. It grants availability at will over wireless, routing, DHCP, DNS and the management service. There is no rate limit on the handler and no lockout in the Basic realm, so the route is repeatable and leaves no alert behind. Detection is poor by construction but this sink leaves one usable anomaly: a submitted WAN configuration produces ordinary behaviour and the sink's visible effect, a username written into /tmp/UserName and then into the configuration store, is what a legitimate submission does, so the indicator is the absence of the expected /tmp/UserName destination on a submission that should have created it. An injection also corrupts stored configuration in a way the owner may not notice, the semicolon scan truncating at the first semicolon and a pipe-and-hash payload storing a username the WAN link cannot authenticate with, a self-inflicted availability event that doubles as a fingerprint. One operational caution: the injection is not side-effect free. A successful submission overwrites the stored WAN username and can break the uplink, which is what the handler does on any successful submission, so any demonstration must record and restore the device's original WAN configuration. Verification boundary: no physical device was powered on and no end-to-end HTTP request was ever accepted by the product. The HTTP leg, being request parsing, the authentication gate, form registration, mode dispatch and PPP branch selection, is evidenced at instruction level from the shipped binary, its configuration and its boot scripts. The execution leg is evidenced dynamically by replication of the sink's semantics rather than by detonation, because a MIPS big-endian uClibc userspace with a board-specific bootloader could not be booted end to end in the research environment: the extracted binaries faulted with SIGBUS under the available user-mode translator and full-system emulation of the board was not brought up. The question under test is not the device but whether a shell evaluates a pipeline and honours a trailing comment in a string built by the vendor's own sprintf and handed to /bin/sh -c, which is a question about POSIX shell semantics that are architecture independent, combined with the exact format string read out of the binary. The string sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 was reconstructed byte for byte for a request whose pppUserName field is |id > /tmp/marker_sw # and handed to /bin/sh -c in an isolated POSIX sandbox whose invoking shell ran as root, producing a 39-byte marker file owned by root:root containing uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) with shell exit status 0, while the sink's own /tmp/UserName destination was not created, that absence being the proof that the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment rather than being escaped, since a protected sink would have left the file behind. A benign control submitting an ordinary username created its destination containing that username and produced no marker. The same replication was repeated on a workstation under an ordinary unprivileged user account and reproduced the semantics at that identity, ruling out the alternative explanation that running as root caused the marker to appear. The harness removes any pre-existing marker and destination before each run and deletes its scratch files afterwards. Consequently the on-device landing identity of uid=0(root) is inferred from the shipped User root directive plus the root-identity replication and is not an observation from hardware; AV:N is argued from the product's transport and authentication model rather than measured across a network; the pptpUserName and L2TPUserName instances are a structural reading of the same handler rather than a demonstrated result; the sibling-model comparison is static only with nothing executed from that image and no score covering it; no setup-state request was sent; no dictionary or credential attack was attempted; and no overflow was developed against the unbounded stack copy. Proof-of-concept and full analysis, published unconditionally: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-setwan-command-injection-root-rce Companion advisory, same product and image, different handler: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/edimax-br-6478ac-formwlanmp-command-injection-root-rce PoC location in the public repository: product/edimax/br-6478ac-v2.20/setwan-command-injection-root-rce/exploit/edimax_br6478ac_setwan_command_injection_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish The shipped proof of concept is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target, and it is built so that it cannot be used accidentally against a live network. Its default mode is replication: it reconstructs the exact string the device's sprintf produces at 0x441ee8 and hands it to /bin/sh -c locally, asserting both that the injected pipeline ran and that the sink's own redirect target was not created, which is what proves the trailing hash reached the shell as a comment, then running a benign username as a negative control and asserting the opposite. That replication mode, not a device run, produced the evidence above. Arguments cover target host, Basic realm username and password, the WAN mode to select, which of the three username fields carries the payload, an option to iterate all three modes, a single non-destructive command defaulting to id, the marker path, the submit-url field value defaulting to /wan.asp, a user agent and a per-request timeout. A send mode additionally POSTs the request to the target and is refused for any non-loopback target unless an explicit allow-remote flag is given, and a print-request mode emits the exact HTTP request that would be transmitted while making no connection at all. Safety rails are loopback-only by default, one non-destructive marker command, no callback listener, no reverse shell, no persistence, and removal of every local file the run created. The tool's own documentation carries the warning that sending against a real device does change stored WAN configuration, because that is what the handler does on any successful submission, so the device's WAN settings must be restored afterwards. The model's published factory password appears in the tool only as a placeholder default so the request shape is self-documenting; the injection does not depend on it and the credential is reported as a separate weakness. Use only against systems you own or are authorised to test. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Full Text: Title: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E v2.2.44 - Unsigned Firmware Upgrade Package Executed as Root Author: 0day Rubbish Research Team Contact: disclosure@0day-rubbish.com Type: remote Platform: Hardware Advisory: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce CVE: pending Description: ProSoft RLX-IFH24E, version v2.2.44, the industrial wireless radio from ProSoft Technology, Inc. (United States) whose research designation is RLX-IH 24E, installs and executes code submitted over its management interface without performing any signature, hash or CRC check on it. The appliance is a closed-source embedded device and an OEM build of the MicroHard Systems IPx21 platform on the MHX-910 board design: an Intel IXP425 XScale processor, ARM big-endian, Linux 2.4.24-uc0, with static management pages under /usr/web and 57 ARM big-endian CGI programs under /usr/lib/cgi-bin/ served by boa over HTTP and boa_ssl over HTTPS. The classification is CWE-494, download of code without integrity check, with CWE-345 and CWE-347 co-equal, because the only authenticity check in the path is a non-cryptographic string equality and no signature is verified anywhere. CWE-434, CWE-73, CWE-250 and CWE-269 contribute. It is explicitly not CWE-78 and a command-injection remediation would not fix it: the shared platform helper SubProgram_Start at offset 0xbd5c splits its argument string on spaces with strtok into at most eight tokens and then calls vfork and execvp directly, so no shell is ever invoked and shell metacharacters are inert here. The upload hop is in usr/lib/cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi, routine HandleSubmit at offset 0x8d1c, with its formatting string at rodata offset 0x2b1c. On the file1 part of a multipart/form-data POST to /cgi-bin/tool_reprogramming.cgi it calls cgiFormFileName and cgiFormTempFileName, builds the move argument with sprintf(buf, "%s /upgrade/upgrade/%s", tempfile, origfilename), runs SubProgram_Start("/bin/mv", buf), which must succeed, and then runs SubProgram_Start("/sbin/upgrade", origfilename). The client-supplied original filename is therefore used unmodified twice, once as the destination of the move and once as the installer's only argument, which makes the file extension and so the installer branch entirely the requester's choice. The handler applies no extension whitelist, no digest comparison and no path canonicalisation. The install hop is /sbin/upgrade, a short POSIX shell script shipped in the same package, running with the CGI's own privileges, which are root. It dispatches on ${FILE##*.} and its three consequential branches are: ".pkg", which tests gzip stream integrity with gunzip -t, unpacks with tar -xf into a staging tree, compares the appliance's PRODUCT_NAME read from /etc/MHX_CONFIG against a LOCK_NAME read from a lockfile inside the package itself, prints "Match image." on equality, executes ./pre, applies the inner archive with tar -xf extract/upgradepkg.tar -C /, executes ./post, prints "Upgrade Successful" and then reboots unconditionally; ".passwd", which copies the upload over both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original; and ".factory", which copies the upload over /etc/db1, the configuration store holding the management interface's own transport flags, accounts and radio behaviour. The equality test is the only gate before code execution and both of its operands are available to the requester: the expected value is the compile-time platform constant IPx21PROSOFT recoverable by reading the shipped firmware once, and the asserted value is carried inside the package being installed. A package whose identity is validated against data carried inside that same package cannot be a source of assurance about it. The defect is the absence of an authenticity step, not a weak one, and strengthening the compatibility check would change nothing while both operands come from the same side. Impact: root command execution on the appliance from a single multipart/form-data POST followed by the product's own documented install sequence, with requester-authored shell code running both before and after an unconstrained archive extraction into the root of the filesystem. Attacker code reading the pre-execution state, an arbitrary rootfs write through the inner archive whose entry names are constrained in no way, and attacker code running post-write are all present in one request. The .passwd branch reaches the same privilege ceiling without executing anything, replacing both the live account database and its backup copy so that the device's own recovery path restores the modified database rather than the shipped one; since the factory admin entry is uid 0 with the restricted shell /bin/txtUI, an added uid-0 entry with /bin/sh converts an administratively restricted login into a general root shell at the next interactive login. The .factory branch lets a requester rewrite the device's security configuration, widening or narrowing the exposure of the surface they arrived through and surviving a later reconfiguration by the operator. Persistence is native to the product rather than improvised, because the install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. Availability is controlled at will, both by that reboot and by installing content that stops the device serving traffic, which for a radio carrying traffic between a process network and its field instruments is also a position on the path that traffic takes. Detection is weak by construction: every step is documented product behaviour, the request is an ordinary firmware upload, the response is the vendor's own success page, and a legitimate upgrade prints exactly the same "Match image." and "Upgrade Successful", so the usable indicators are post-hoc and filesystem-level, namely an installed package whose LOCK_NAME and VERSION pair corresponds to no release the operator obtained, an unexpected file under /upgrade/upgrade/, and a uid-0 account whose shell is not the vendor's restricted interface. Verification boundary, stated exactly because it is narrower than the headline suggests, and because the classification above depends on it. The installer half of the chain was measured and the upload half was not. No HTTP request was ever issued at this product and no physical appliance was used at any point, so nothing here is an exploit run against a live device and it is not presented as one. What was executed is the firmware's own /sbin/upgrade, byte-for-byte unmodified, inside an isolated chroot sandbox built on a copy of the upgrade package's own root filesystem. A crafted .pkg printed "Match image." then "Upgrade Successful" and exited 0; the pre script left a marker proving it executed and wrote PRE-RAN-AS-UID=0 into a second marker, the post script left its own marker, and the inner archive applied an entry to the root of the filesystem. The uid marker is the load-bearing evidence: the payload wrote that value at runtime rather than having it read from a configuration file, so it is the executing identity and not an inference about it. The recorded landing identity is uid=0(root). A .passwd run replaced both /etc/passwd and /etc/passwd_original with the uploaded text, proven by a pre-run digest of the pre-seeded database that no longer matched afterwards and by a marker line present in both copies. A negative control was run to establish that none of this came from the harness: a structurally identical package, same outer tar layout, same metadata files, same inner archive, same marker-writing scripts, with exactly one deliberate difference, LOCK_NAME=WRONGPRODUCT, was refused with "This unit doesn't support the image." and produced no markers anywhere. That control also isolates the product-string comparison as the single cause of refusal and makes the positive and negative runs mutually exclusive. Four substitutions existed in the harness and none in the code under test: an x86 busybox build supplied /bin/sh, tar, gunzip, mv and cp because the firmware's own copies are ARM big-endian and the host is not; a stub replaced the platform mhx utility; /etc/MHX_CONFIG was populated with the product identity the firmware itself ships; and /etc/passwd was pre-seeded with three factory-style entries for comparison. Two transcript lines, "logger: not found" and "mhx: not found", are absent helpers in the sandbox PATH and are not product behaviour. The run count is one positive .pkg run, one positive .passwd run and one negative control, in one sandbox on one host, each effect observed once, never repeated across sandbox builds and never performed on hardware. Not measured, and not claimed: the web server and its access control, because /bin/boa lives in the device base flash and is not contained in the system upgrade package, so the access control gating this CGI could be neither proved nor disproved from the artefacts available; the CGI binaries and the firmware's ARM helpers, for the architecture reason; the closing reboot, since the sandbox is a directory tree with no init, though the path up to it was observed; any privilege escalation, the chain starting from the administrative identity the product's own account database already grants uid 0; any reach into the radio baseband image RLX-IFH24E_v5089.mhx, identified but not exercised; and any impact on an attached control system, PLC or historian. Consequently the Type field above reflects the documented delivery vector, a network POST to a CGI on the management listener, and the Platform field reflects a firmware and hardware target; the part that was actually executed was the vendor's own installer acting on a supplied file, and a reader should weight the two halves of this chain differently. That is what the published advisory is written to allow. CVSS: 7.2 High (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) is the single score published for this finding, computed from first principles rather than inherited: ISS = 1 - (0.44 x 0.44 x 0.44) = 0.914816; Impact at Scope Unchanged = 6.42 x 0.914816 = 5.873119; Exploitability = 8.22 x 0.85 x 0.77 x 0.27 x 0.85 = 1.234708; Base = Roundup(7.107826) = 7.2. AV:N because the entry point is a network service and the firmware's own default configuration record inside the shipped package enables the web interface on both transports, UI_Access_HTTP=B and HTTPS=B, with non-default values for the Telnet and SSH entries; that shipped record is the evidence for a default, and the Network classification comes from the transport the artefact establishes rather than from a reach we observed. AC:L because the chain is deterministic, with no race, no timing window, no memory-layout dependency and no on-path position, and the single piece of environment knowledge it needs is a platform string published inside the shipped firmware. PR:H because installing firmware is an administrative function, the handler is a maintenance CGI linked directly from the interface's own menu pages, and the only account model the package documents for that interface is a uid-0 admin entry with a password-change page and a configurable RADIUS mode; no lower-privileged principal was demonstrated reaching the handler. UI:N because once a session holds that privilege the move, the install, both script executions and the reboot all follow from one request with no operator action and no confirmation step in the recovered handler path. Scope Unchanged because the vulnerable component and the impacted component are the same appliance operating system, the CGI already running as root, the installer already running as root and the rootfs extracted by that same root process, so no authority boundary is crossed. Three readings are published as rejected with their arithmetic: low privilege (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 8.8 and is available only by assuming that the shipped uid-500 upgrade account, whose home directory is the upload staging path and which shares the admin password hash, can reach the maintenance handler, which was not tested; Scope Changed (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 9.1 and is rejected because an unproven boundary crossing may not raise a published score; high attack complexity (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) computes to 6.6 and is rejected because the control run isolates a wrong product string as the sole cause of refusal. Two of those rejected readings score higher than the number published, and the advisory says so itself. Two further readings are labelled conditionals and neither is the headline. An unauthenticated HTTP layer (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) would compute to 9.8 and was NOT demonstrated; it is a structural inference that applies only if the management listener does not gate the handler, and the binary that would answer that question is not in the package analysed. The supporting observation about the package is narrower and is weaker than that reading: none of the 57 shipped CGIs imports crypt, none parses or sets a session cookie and no login CGI exists in the directory, so the handler layer adds no authentication of its own, which says nothing about what the web server does before it forks a CGI. A factory credential still in place on a deployed unit would remove the need to discover any secret, but it was not demonstrated either, no authentication was performed against any appliance and no first-login behaviour was tested; under CVSS the metric prices the privilege level of the account used rather than whether its secret was public, so that reading leaves the vector unchanged at 7.2 and is published as a deployment amplifier for operators to assess. The factory password hash is deliberately not reproduced in this submission or in the advisory. No version-range claim is made: only the system upgrade package RLX-IFH24E_v2244.pkg was analysed, no other build of this model, no other version of the OEM IPx21 platform and no other product of either company is claimed as affected, although the upgrade path is a shared platform component rather than a per-product script, so a wider population of devices built on the same OEM platform plausibly shares the root cause, and that is stated as a likelihood rather than scored. Adjacent structural observations recorded in the analysis and deliberately excluded from this finding are a startup configuration that symlink-exposes /etc/MHX_CONFIG, /var/log/messages and /etc/system.debug into the web document root as configuration, syslog and debug views; a legacy debug CGI named request.cgi whose first-argument dispatch includes sending AT commands to the radio module, which was never executed and to which no AT command was sent; and SNMP community strings public and private shipped on the platform, which belong to the configuration plane. Public records were searched by product designation, by the RLX-IH name, by the OEM platform name and by the vendor name with no result describing this appliance and this root cause; the one record associated with the vendor's RadioLinx engineering-software line concerns a pseudo-random number generator in that software family, a different product and a different defect class, and records naming the platform manufacturer's own product families concern different platforms and different chains. Proof of concept, published unconditionally. The shipped script is Python 3 using only the standard library, with no third-party dependency and no hardcoded target: the target address, port, scheme, credentials, command, lock name, product name, uploaded filename, marker token and output path are all command-line arguments and default to inert values, the default target being loopback and the default payload command being true. It builds a gzip-compressed tar containing the file and lockfile metadata the installer reads, the pre and post scripts at mode 0755 and extract/upgradepkg.tar, and can either write that package to disk for inspection or carry it in a multipart/form-data POST under the part name file1. Its modes and the flags that matter: Build the package locally only, performing no network access at all: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --build-only --out demonstration.pkg Refuse a filename that would break the hand-off. The tool rejects any name containing a space or a path separator before it builds anything, because SubProgram_Start splits its argument string on spaces before execvp, so an extra token would change what /bin/mv is asked to do: --filename "payload.pkg" accepted --filename "pay load.pkg" rejected by the tool itself Build the negative control, for an operator who owns the hardware to confirm that the success path really is gated by the product string and by nothing else: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --control --build-only --out control.pkg Build the account-database variant as a local file, which is never sent unless --send is also given: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --passwd-mode --passwd-entry "marker:*:0:0:INERT-DEMONSTRATION-ENTRY:/root:/bin/sh" Deliver the built package to a management listener the operator owns and is authorised in writing to test, over HTTP or HTTPS, with optional HTTP Basic credentials: python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 80 --user <user> --password <pass> python3 prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py --target <address> --port 443 --https --user <user> --password <pass> The default payload is deliberately non-destructive: pre touches one marker file and writes the executing uid into a second, post touches a third, and the inner archive writes a single marker entry under the root of the filesystem. Nothing is deleted, encrypted or modified beyond those markers. The tool also prints the sha256 of what it built, so an operator can record the digest of a package before installing it, which is the one detection control that works after the fact. The script's own documentation carries a warning that applies to every reader of this submission: the network half of this chain was never exercised against an appliance, and running it against hardware you do not own or hold written authorisation to test will reboot and reimage that device, because a successful install rewrites the rootfs and the installer always reboots on success. PoC location in the public repository: product/prosoft-technology/rlx-ifh24e-v2244/unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce/exploit/prosoft_rlx_ifh24e_unsigned_upgrade_package_root_rce.py Repository: https://github.com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish Full analysis, including the sink and source inventories with offsets, the end-to-end data flow marked at the line between measurement and inference, the verification transcripts, the negative control, the authentication boundary and its limits, the detection notes, the remediation set and the derivation of every one of the six CVSS readings: https://0day-rubbish.com/blog/prosoft-rlx-ifh24e-unsigned-upgrade-package-root-rce ProSoft Technology, Inc. was notified unconditionally through the mailbox its own website publishes for reporting a potential vulnerability, under a Security Assurance heading on its Quality and Environment page, with a copy to the North America technical-support address published on its Regional Technical Support page. The research is already public, no permission was asked for, no embargo was requested, nothing is withheld pending a reply and nothing is asked in return. No report was filed with any third party and no national coordination body was involved. -- 0day Rubbish Research Team disclosure@0day-rubbish.com https://0day-rubbish.com

Executive Summary

October 19 Update

Unit 42 has observed attempted exploitation of the May 2026 CVE-2026-0257 by ransomware operators, including Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka Inc).

We’re also aware of public reporting attributing exploitation to threat actors using Settra ransomware.

Fixes for this vulnerability have been available since May 2026. Palo Alto Networks has become aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations applied.

Customers can mitigate the risk of this issue by taking any of the following actions:

Use a dedicated certificate for Authentication Override cookies: Generate a new certificate exclusively for authentication override cookies and store it securely. Do not reuse the portal or gateway certificate, and do not share this certificate with other features or users.

Disable Authentication Override: Uncheck the Authentication Override options (for generating and accepting cookies) in the GlobalProtect portal and gateway configuration.

Key Takeaways

Teams are remediating more than ever, but exposure from the vulnerabilities that matter is still rising faster than they can keep up with.

Mean time to exploitation is about −7 days. Mean time to remediate sits around +30 days.

Qualys research: closures rose from 73M (2022) to 473M (2025) – 6× – while critical findings still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%.

Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited. A volume-and-CVSS program spends most of its effort on the rest.

15% of organizations that operationalized the pipeline patched before a vulnerability hit the CISA KEV list.

October is here, bringing a chill in the air, spooky decorations, and, fittingly, Cybersecurity Awareness Month. It’s a timely reminder for security leaders to revisit and strengthen their strategy. The past 12 months alone show how cyber threats are getting smarter and faster.

There’s a haunting paradox that should be top of mind. Security teams are doing more vulnerability remediation than ever before. They’re patching faster, scanning deeper, and closing more tickets than any team in history, yet attackers exploit systems at an alarming rate, faster than ever before.

Fortunately, with the right cyber risk management plan, security teams can navigate the dark landscape of AI-driven attackers. But before we talk about defense, let’s outline a few of attackers’ tricks.

The Threat Landscape Is Accelerating

Ransomware is one of the leading cyber threats, rising in both frequency and cost. It now factors into 48% of breaches, up from 44% from the previous year, and attacks are projected to occur every two seconds by 2031. If that projection holds, it will put severe pressure on already strained security teams.

AI is escalating the problem rather than easing it. AI-generated attacks have increased 56% between March 2025 and February 2026, adding $1 million in cost per breach to the baseline cost. More attacks are coming, and those powered by AI make each breach more expensive to address.

The increased frequency and sophistication combined result in a spine-chilling number: mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days. Which means, on average, weaponization arrives a week before defenders have anything to deploy. Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days. The attacker’s clock starts before defenders have anything to deploy, so the defenders are already behind before their own 30-day countdown even begins. And there’s a scary price attached.

The Financial Reality

Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead, turning every minute into a running invoice. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident, up 12% from last year.

The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average. The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average.

With costs escalating like this, the expectation would be that a growing volume of patching work is buying that cost down. The data says otherwise.

The Remediation Paradox

Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that while the effort to address vulnerabilities went up, exposure still rose alongside it. According to the research, effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. As a result, enterprises did far more work and ended up further behind. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%. More effort produced less coverage where it counted.

The reason traces back to how that effort gets allocated in the first place. Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, which means a program built around volume and severity score spends the majority of its effort on vulnerabilities attackers were never going to use. The 6x increase didn’t close the gap since most of that work was never aimed at the 1% that mattered.

This misalignment proves detrimental for the vulnerabilities that do get weaponized. Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time, and half were weaponized before a patch existed. Teams were doing the work. They just weren’t always working on the right thing, at the right time.

The light in the dark here is that there are organizations winning this race. 15% of organizations that operationalized their remediation pipeline patched before the vulnerability was even added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list. This is proof that the gap isn’t fixed in place. It closes when the model changes.

As risk accelerates, the organizations that shift away from a ‘fix everything’ mindset to disciplined, continuous, business-impact-based prioritization will be prepared for the unknown. The focus should be on automated, intelligence-driven remediation that assesses risk in real time rather than adding people to a process.

The Path Forward

So what does this shift look like? It starts with context, not more volume. Remediation becomes contextual rather than sequential. Most friction between IT and security doesn’t start with the vulnerability itself. It starts when a ticket arrives without ownership data, gets validated whether or not action is warranted, and then gets reassigned before anything is fixed.

When asset context and risk intelligence route tasks before a ticket is even created, that upstream friction disappears. MTTR drops 30% and response times improve 40%. That’s what happens when decisions about what really matters get made before the backlog forms, instead of getting caught in debates once issues arise.

In a digital age where attacks are happening faster than teams can keep up, the teams still haunted by their own remediation metrics are the ones still asking the old questions: how many vulnerabilities can we close? What’s the CVSS score? How long before we remediate? The organizations that are getting safer are asking a different set of questions: Is this actively being exploited? What’s the evidence? Which assets are at risk? What can we automate?

As we recognize Cybersecurity Awareness Month, it’s crucial to remember that diligence is non-negotiable; the real key lies in prioritizing the vulnerabilities that wield the greatest impact.

Title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
Context: Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild...
Full Text:
Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model.

Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited.

We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines.

With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains.

The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from?

As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions:

If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed?

Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old?

Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed?

How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers?

Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end?

The answer to many of these questions boils down to this: The majority of these vulnerabilities are coming from repositories of old code from large-profile products and systems; and disclosure does not equal weaponization.

Where is it from?

AI is chewing through a backlog of technical debt in libraries and tools used as the dependable, best-practice lynchpins of so many environments. These models have a new perspective, an ability to "think" without some of the hangups or assumptions of human defenders, and they are thorough in listing those vulnerabilities.

Entrenched older tools have always been prime targets because of their predictability; attackers know those tools and all their secrets, and they know what is likely to be present in a network with them. Multi-exploit attacks can be deployed with little variability.

Pre-Mythos threat actors exploited log4j (CVE-2021-44228) to immense success. The library was ubiquitous, included in nearly every environment, but not a component that got cataloged in visibility scans. A combination of scale and low visibility meant defenders were blindsided, scrambling to find out if they even used the log4j library before starting to concoct a mitigation plan.

Talos has ongoing relationships with some of the largest technical vendors (such as the Microsoft Active Protections Process (MAPP) agreement). Organizations share additional information—detection guidance or maybe a POC — for vulnerabilities that are most likely to be exploited, to enable Talos to provide adequate coverage when the advisories are announced. "Microsoft believes it is important for us to provide detection content, based on their guidance," as Yves Younan, Director of Talos Vulnerability Discovery, Detection, and Testing, says.

Talos has needed to invest more resources to get coverage in on time for critical vendors like Microsoft to keep up with notifications coming in fast and often on staggered or out-of-band timelines.

For larger vendors, the pressure is handleable for now. However, open-source projects are getting flooded. Some projects have a trusted group that can combine to tackle patches, and some share with the full community for immediate assistance, but it is up to the project. The internet runs on open-source work.

The pace of discovery presents a challenge for the traditional coordinated disclosure system vulnerability hunters have been using for years, and some are calling it into question.

Security vulnerabilities should be reported, to enable an informed defender base and regular patching, and vendors responsible for vulnerable code need time to create coverage. A timed disclosure model where notifications are sent to a vendor, who then has a set period of time (typically 90 days) to provide coverage before the disclosure is released publicly, has created a more secure online environment for decades.

Now, many practitioners are releasing advisories publicly without a disclosure period beforehand. The reasoning is that if one AI can find a weakness, any other could, so the vulnerability is already, effectively, released.

This conversation is actively changing expectations around vulnerability disclosure, and guidance is in flux.

Will it stay this high?

No one knows the future, but we can always look to the past for insight.

Numbers of vulnerabilities jump drastically when a new bug class is identified, as their possibilities are explored to the fullest. Then the discoveries plateau and drop off.

When format string vulnerabilities were discovered as a new bug class in 2000, the initial influx of discoveries ramped up and up, until reaching a peak in 2005 and then slowly declining over the next couple of years. Format string vulnerabilities are still discovered, but they are a smaller overall fraction of the number of CVEs discovered in a year.

Theoretically, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery could go the same way.

While frontier models have not discovered a new vulnerability class, they are more efficient at discovering known types of software vulnerabilities. Given that a lot of vital software has a long history of code releases, there’s plenty of code to mine for weaknesses. But there’s only so much code… right?

Old and commonly used tools are often under the highest scrutiny, lending them one kind of safety: Because of their popularity, utility, and stability, when popular tools have vulnerabilities, they are discovered fast and patched promptly.

As the historical backlog of essential systems is turned over by AI, vulnerabilities will be found and patched. New code will ideally be run through AI bug-checkers that will prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced. The rate of new vulns should level off and drop accordingly.

There are some caveats. In the past, as vulnerability disclosures increased through coordinated disclosures, we saw increased adoption of mitigations. Exploitation became significantly harder. Attackers often need to chain together 3 or more vulnerabilities to successfully exploit a system.

However, more awareness of vulnerabilities often leads to more exploitation. Attackers often use vendor patches meant to protect customers to discover where vulnerabilities might exist. The frequency of patching has delayed human attackers via parsing bottlenecks, but AI can eliminate that problem.

Are the numbers the real issue?

The volume is certainly up.

Fresh as this blog is being finished, the October Patch Tuesday dropped almost 500 more than last month.

With refinement, any vulnerability could become a link to a path of effect. But... not all vulnerabilities are exploitable. Some are wildly impractical for attacker use. In fact, the percent of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) is vastly smaller than the found vulnerabilities.

Of the 975 vulnerabilities Microsoft reported in September, there were only three in-the-wild exploits detected. When viewed by percentage, vulnerabilities versus KEVs tell a different and perhaps reassuring story.

Compared with the same period last year, additions to the known-exploited vulnerability list increased by 37%, while published CVEs increased by 105%. However, we wouldn't necessarily expect those figures to grow in proportion. Adversaries only need enough useful vulnerabilities to compromise their targets, and the same vulnerabilities can be reused against many organizations. The KEV count tracks distinct vulnerabilities known to be exploited, not the number of attacks or successful compromises.

AI helps ingest code, advisory reports, and attack surfaces with inhuman speed, but it cannot currently make judgment calls about the value of a weakness.

For defenders, the question remains the same: Which vulnerabilities provide a viable path into their environment, and how do you close those paths?

What do we do now?

The undeniable danger here is in exploitation time going down rapidly, while the vulnerabilities that could become exploits is still going up. The biggest hurdle for a defender is determining what is a real vulnerability for their environment, and what is not.

Different defenders have different forms of control depending on their role.

For those who are writing code, the new standard validation chain should include AI evaluation by models at least as up to date as those being used to hunt for vulnerabilities. It is relatively cheap to run new code through AI, but very expensive to run a cumbersome backlog of old code through. Bite it off in chunks.

For those whose role involves keeping the tools ready: Upgrade ASAP. Don't stop there.

For Cisco customers, implement LiveProtect to mitigate vulnerabilities between advisory release day and patching, to give time for that patching. Do this for everything you own.

Move beyond static domain blocking and implement behavioral detection that alerts on anomalous traffic patterns directed toward automation platforms.

Hone your focus to the vulnerabilities with the highest exploitability in your environment. KEVs are far less common among the sea of advisories, and their numbers have not risen proportionally with the AI-assisted deluge.

Focus on building defense-in-depth. Employ multiple protection systems, to cover for delays in patching. Implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), create custom IPS/Snort triggers to block pre-patched traffic using SnortML, deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models in software build chains.

Dive deeper into this conversation with the latest TTP interview with Yves Younan and vulnerability researcher Bella Fusari.

Don't swing at everything

Title: Researchers Warn OpenCode Quietly Patched Critical RCE Flaw, Leaving Users At Risk
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The Pillar Security team reported the vulnerability privately via GitHub Security Advisory with full reproduction material at the end of August 2026.

A month later, Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, confirmed it had received the report, but said malicious MCP servers are “outside their threat model.”

Pillar Security researchers said Anomaly patched the vulnerability on September 28 in version 1.18.33 – without a CVE or security advisory. “As a result, conventional vulnerability scanners and dependency alerts will not identify affected installations, potentially leaving enterprises unaware that they need to upgrade,” Pillar Security researchers warned.

URL Validation Falls Short of Preventing OpenCode RCE Attacks

Pillar Security researchers claimed that the standard fix isn’t enough to fully remediate this vulnerability, which they assessed should be allocated a critical severity rating (CVSS) of 9.8.

According to the researchers, URL scheme validation alone cannot prevent the attack because the malicious payload can be embedded in a seemingly legitimate HTTPS URL.

On Windows, the vulnerable open dependency passed the URL to PowerShell without properly escaping it, allowing the shell to interpret part of the URL as a command.

Although OpenCode added URL scheme checks in version 1.18.33, the researchers said the crucial fix was to update the dependency to a version that correctly quotes the URL, preventing PowerShell from interpreting the payload as executable code.

They recommend that developers avoid passing untrusted URLs through shell commands altogether, instead using argument-based process execution to reduce the risk of command injection.

OpenCode RCE Flaw Unrelated to Recent Console Security Breach

This vulnerability report comes a few days after OpenCode confirmed a security breach affecting its Console, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Speaking to Infosecurity, Pillar Security’s Cohen stressed that this newly disclosed vulnerability was not related to the Console breach.

“The breach hit a legacy system behind a hosted key proxy, and exposed provider keys users had stored there. The vulnerability we reported runs the other way: a malicious remote MCP server executing code on a developer's own machine during the OAuth handshake. Different target and attacker position,” he explained.

Nevertheless, Cohen highlighted that both incidents come down to the same thing, “Who you let hand credentials and inputs to an AI coding tool, and what that tool does with them.”

Title: Siemens Customers Targeted by ClickFix Attackers Exploiting DLL Side-Loading Flaw
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Siemens has warned customers that attackers are actively exploiting a dynamic link library (DLL) side-loading vulnerability in its Software Center to distribute malware.

The company has attributed the activity to the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign.

Romulus is a server hosting panel that was identified by Forescout researchers on October 14. The panel allows cybercriminals to deploy ClickFix tactics into an entire ecosystem which can be repeatedly used to deliver multiple forms of malware to victims.

ClickFix is a popular attack technique among cybercriminals. It relies on social engineering to trick the victim into running attacker-supplied commands on their own machine.

The Siemens blog, published on October 19, detailed how attackers are targeting CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS 8.4) to load malicious DLL files into a directory that the Siemens Software Center searches for. They use a genuine copy of the application with a valid signature and place their own files next to it.

The attackers then attempt to distribute these files to customers by using a ClickFix lure.

Version 3.5.8.7 of Software Center loaded helper files from its own folder without checking them, the firm admitted.

If a user follows the ClickFix commands, malicious code will execute on the device with the privileges of the affected application.

“Never paste a command from a web page into Win+R, the Run box or PowerShell. A real ‘I am not a robot’ check never asks for this,” Siemens wrote.

How to Defend Against the Romulus Campaign

Siemens urged Software Center customers update to version 4.0.9.8, which contains a fix for the flaw. Existing installations update automatically the next time they start.

Customers should also look out for the following indications that their PC is affected by the campaign:

"Siemens Software Center" in the start-up apps or Task Scheduler of a PC that never had it installed

A folder called SM Software Provisioning Service inside AppData\Local\Programs is created by the malware

Files named activate.bak or statinfosta.DB next to SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe

A folder called FTSuite containing a file ftc.uml inside AppData\Local

Network connections to 96.62.218[.]59

If a PC has been found to be compromised, customers should isolate the device, stop the process first, then remove the start-up entry and task and reset passwords.

Siemens added that detection tools should focus on the folder and suspicious behavior, not on the Siemens file fingerprint as the file itself is genuine.

Customers should also ensure that they only download Siemens software from official Siemens sources and block the active IP address and domain listed in the advisory.
